GUY BOYD MIZE
GRAND MASTER

GUY B. MIZE
Grand Master
Septemb er 29, 1961 - October 12, 1962

Guy Boyd Mize, who, on October 12, 1962, retired as Californ ia's
ninety-si xth Grand Master of Masons, was born in Ullin, a small rural
community in the southwe sterly corner of Illinois, on April 23, 1901.
His parents were Jacob L. Mize and Alice Eva (McMah an) Mize,
also native of Illinois. While they owned and operated a small farm
with the usual crops and animals, his father also maintained his own
general store and served as town marshal. He studied law to be prepared for his official duties as Justice of the Peace and Magistra te in the
town government. He was a lifelong student of the Bible, his avocation
being as teacher of a men's Bible class. This he pursued regularly and
faithfully until his death in 1927 at the age of 69 in Glendale, Californ ia.
His wife Alice was ever at his side and at 95 still maintains her own
home and is quite active.
Other relatives of the Grand Master are:
Homer, an older brother, of Grass Valley, California, and a sister,
Ellen Rains, of Minneapolis, Minneso ta. Two other brothers, one a twin
of the Grand Master, are deceased.
When Guy was six years old, his family moved to St. Louis, Missouri, where he attended grade schools and McKinle y High School. At
business schools he studied auditing and accounti ng and began his
business career as a cost accounta nt with Emerson Electric Compan y,
then engaged in making fans and motors.
In 1920 he spent two months in Glendale, California, but decided
to •r eturn to St. Louis. Another winter there convinced him that he preferred Californ ia's salubrious climate. He, therefore, returned to Glendale in the summer of 1921 and has since resided there. He was soon
followed by his J1arents and twin brother.
Being trained as an accounta nt, Guy worked first for Wilshire Oil
Compan y; eighteen months later he was employed by Pilcher and Cox,
prominent real estate subdividers in the early twenties. Then followed
three years as a senior accounta nt for the firm of Blackwell, Reed and
Compan y.
On April 10, 1929, he entered the employ of The John M. C. Marble
Compan y (now known as The Marble Compan y), an old and respected
mortgag e banking firm, as general auditor in charge of accounting for
its mortgage, bond and insuranc e business. He is still with the same firm,
having served in turn as head of property management, appraise r, secretary. vice-president, executive vice-president, and, since January,
1959. president. He has served on the board of directors for twelve years,
as well as on committees of state and national mortgag e banking associations, and, in 1959-60, was presiden t of the Southern Californ ia Mortgage Bankers Association. Along the way he studied real estate financing
and appraisin g in extension divisions of the Universi ty of Southern
Californ ia and the Universi ty of Californ ia (San Francisc o-auspic es of
N .A.R.E.B .) and has been registere d as a real estate broker since 1940.
F·rom 1940 to 1944 he served as a director of Goodwill Industrie s
of Los Angeles, contribu ting his real estate experience to the organiza tion.

In 1948 he was a member of the Charter Revision Committee for the
City of Glendale.
Brother Mize has been a member of the Central Christian Church,
Glendale, since 1921. Through this affiliation he met Ruby Evelyn Eubanks, who became his wife on June 20, 1925, a week after her graduation from U.C.L.A. (then University of California, Southern Branch).
To this marriage was born Guy, Jr. (veteran of the Korean War), who
is a graduate of U.S.C. and now a member of the staff of Coldwell,
Banker & Co. He is married to the former Gloria Goold and they are
residents of Los Angeles.
An interesting sidelight is that the Grand Master and his wife were
born within forty miles of each other but never met until after they both
were residents of Glendale.
The Grand Master was raised in Unity Lodge No. 368 on November 23, 1928. He first served as Treasurer and progressed through the
Chairs, serving as Master in 1939.
He was a member of the Credentials Committee in 1940, appointed
Inspector of the 86th Masonic District in October, 1944; Assistant
Grand Lecturer in October, 1950, and Trustee of the Masonic Homes
of California in 1954. He was elected Junior Grand Warden in 1958,
Senior Grand Warden in 1959. Deputy Grand Master in 1960, and
Grand Master in 1961.
He is a member of Unity Chapter No. 116, Royal Arch Masons,
Glendale; Unity Council No. 48, Royal & Select Masters, Glendale;
Glendale Commandery No. 53, Knights Templar, Glendale; the Los
Angeles Bodies of the Scottish Rite; Saint Gabriel Conclave No. 14,
Red Cross of Constantine; and a charter member and former treasurer
of Southern California Research Lodge. He served as president of Southern California Past Masters Association in 1955 and received the Honorary Legion of Honor, Order of DeMolay in 1952.
While Brother Mize was serving as Grand Master, in February of
1962, he was elected a member of the Board of Directors of the George
Washington Masonic National Memorial Association, Alexandria,
Virginia.
From this sturdy record and background has come the stamina of
our self-effacing Grand Master. In the interchange of duty, honor and
responsibility he has not sought the path of comfort but has humbly
faced the stress and spur of difficulty and challenge. Loyalty, compassion and gentleness have characterized his every act respecting home,
country and fraternity. He has not sought to master others but, steadfastly, he has lived by the laws, rules. regulations and landmarks of
Grand Lodge. By his recommendations he looked into the future but
left the decisions to his brethren. His modesty enabled him to remember
the simplicity of true greatness, the open mind of true wisdom, the
meekness of true strength. His labors should teach us the way to be a
true Grand Master and a Christian gentleman.

DEVOTIONAL SERVICE

created equal. Not only so, but such a position is utterly incapable of
historic or •scientific truth. If there is any truth which is self-evident, it
is that men have not been created equal, that they have never been equal,
and that they will never be equal. Jefferson knew this, of course. His
whole position is an amazing religious assumption. Men are created by
God and are equal before Him and His laws. They are endowed by
God with certain inalienable rights. Upon this magnificent postulate of
faith, this statement which flies in the face of all historical and scientific
facts, Jefferson and his aristocratic associates, established the United
States of America, which has been the most astounding success, governmentally, economically, and spiritually, in the history of the world!
The writer of the Hebrew Epistle, in the greatest faith chapter in
the New Testament, defines the meaning of faith with clarity and power.
(Heb. 11: 1 ) "Now faith is the assurance of things hoped for, the
conviction of things not seen." Faith is the assurance that the things
which ought to be-<:an be. But it is more than assurance; it is the motive
power which drives us to do something about what ought to be. By
faith-the devoted medical scientists believed that polio could be cured
and they did something about it. Through endless research, toil and
tears, they persisted until the cure was found. By faith we believe that
we can eradicate cancer, and through faith, we shall continue until the
cure is discovered.
But faith is also "the conviction of things not seen." The unseen
is not unreal-it is only unseen. Our constant fellowship with the unseen, and our utilization of it is now commonplace. No man has ever
seen an atom, but the atom is real and not merely an assumption. We
can see what it does and we know how it acts, but it still is unseen. A
pessimistic friend to whom I was recently expounding plans for our
future church building-to keep pace with our ever-expanding University, gloomily interjected, "Doc, it is all a waste of time and money.
Some day the Commies will drop a hydrogen bomb upon us and blow
us all to hell." I replied, "It may blow you to hell, but it will blow me
straight to Glory."
Electricity has relieved us of much of t)ie drudgery of our world.
It lights our homes and cities, speeds our electric trains upon their waiy,
drives our water-pumps, cooks our food, but we do not see it. We know
it only by its surging power.
Love is unseen. We can see the results of love making the world
a sweeter place in which to live. We know it in all the delights of a
lovely home, in blessed deeds of helpfulness and healing, but love itself
we cannot see. Though unseen it is real, the mightiest force in the world!
The ether around us in this great ball is pulsating and vibrating,
feebly or strongly with hundreds of ·radio programs from near and taroff radio stations. We cannot see the programs-nor the pulsating waves

FAITH FOR AN HOUR OF PERIL
THE VERY REVEREND JESSE RANDOLPH KELLEMS,

D.D .• PH.D •• S.T.D •• LL.D •• LITT.D.
Grand Chaplain
That this is a time of deadly peril, when, from day to day, we know
not what the next hour may bring to us, is obvious to every American.
Modern man now has the power actually to destroy the whole world.
Not only is this dreadly possibility within his power; there are evil men
who would do this monstrous thing and are deterred only by the certainty that the decent people of the earth would retaliate in such awesome manner that the attackers would themselves ·g o down into the awful
hell of fire and thunder of such a catastrophe.
The peril of this hour is the more frightening when we contemplate
the inaptitude of little, timorous men in high places. Unfortunately for
our times, we have no Winston Churchill to call the forces of God to
high endeavor, or to speak in tones of thunder to a world sinking into
despair. The feeble pronouncements from Washington sicken all men
of high courage who know that the whole rotten Communist system is
built upon sand. Atheism cannot win this titanic battle. Let us tell the
world so in words of courage and power. Only by a return to God, His
Word, His mighty promises and His invincible might, can our world
be saved kom utter destruction. Only by a return to faith, to the courage
of our founding fathers, and to the unshakable promises of Almighty
God, can this sweeping tide of atheism, immorality, and surrender to
tyranny be stopped.
A distinguished cousin of mine, Thomas Jefferson, wrote some very
strange words in the Declaration of Independence. Considering the
type of man Cousin Tom was, they were strange indeed. He was an
aristocrat of the artistocrats. We Randolphs did not consider his Jefferson blood to be very blue. But he was half Randolph, and obviously
from that noble strain his genius sprang. Great champion of the people,
he did not care for them individually. He was, however, very much concerned about the principles which undergird human liberty. He certainly made a tremendous assumption when he wrote, "We hold these
trnths to be self-evident that all men are created equal, and that they
have been endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable rights, and
among these are life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness." There is
truth, however, in the cynical paraphrase of the old Negro preacher that
"All men are created equal-and some more equal than others." But
there is not one sh['ed of scientific or historical evidence that all men are

upon which they ride, but-through the proper receiving-set, we can
tune in and behold a miracle! We see and hear-and are able to talk
to the whole world! Truly faith is the conviction of things not seen.
For a time of peril then, we must have faith-faith in God. This has
ever been the answer of our .Masonic Fraternity. It is indeed, the heart
and soul of Freemasonry. Again to quote the writer of the Hebrew
Letter, "By faith we understand that the worlds have been framed by
the Word of God; so that what is seen hath not been made of things
which do appear." (Hebrews 11 : 3) In what other possible way could
they have been framed, save by His Divine Word and Power?
In the beginning God-we must always begin with God. There is no
other place to begin. "By the Word of God-framed by the Word of
God!" "The heavens declare the glory of God, the firmament showeth
His handiwork."
But how can you prove the Word of God? The answer is, of course,
that I cannot do so. The Word of God is self-authenticating. If God
speaks, if He reveals Himself, He does not need me to interpret HimHe is perfectly capable of making Himself known!
Dean W. P. Patterson of Edinburgh, noted Gifford lecturer and my
own teacher, revered and admired, often said to us, "The Word of God
shines by its own light and prevails by its own might." The whole universe is full of God. It is mind and will and purpose. The basic assumption of all learning is that the universe is intelligible: we can read it,
measure it and understand it. If intelligible, then it is the product of
intelligence. Open your mind and heart and let God speak-for He does
speak in rock, and wood, and star, and flower. By faith and faith alone,
we can understand, for faith is the motive power of all research; the
certainty that we can find the answers, because we are thinking God's
thoughts after Him. We can find the answers because the universe is
not only the product of mind, but it is a universe of law. Have faith in
God, follow him, serve Him, "Dare the Heroes' March" with Him and
your life will be full of joy and victory.
In an hour of peril we must also have faith in our fellow men. It is
not only Christian, but it is also American to believe in the innate dignity of our fellow men. Man, created in the likeness and image of God,
is of superlative worth. He is capable of the highest and the best. We
must believe that, and do all we can as those who have the privilege of
education to help all men to that stature to which God intended they
should be brought. As Masons, we should be careful about the flippant
use of such terms as, the average man or the little people. These are
terms which have no place in our American vocabulary. Who has the
right to call any man "the little man" or an "average man"? By what
yardstick does any superior being measure the average man?

One of the mightiest texts in the Bible is the great word of the
Apostle Paul: "I can do all things through Christ who strengtheneth
me." ( Phil. 4: 12) Here then, is the gospel of imperial will, "I can, and
by the grace of God, I ·will." There are no impossibilities to men who
dare the march of faith!

13

Recall the words of Jesus, "If ye have faith as a grain of mustard
seed, ye shall say to yon mountain, 'Be removed, and it shall remove,
and nothing shall be impossible unto you.' " He meant tMs spiritually
and literally. I sailed once through the Panama Canal. and at the Culebra
Cut I saw .the place where a whole mountain of dirt and rock had
been removed by faith. By faith, we could remove Mt. Whitney, if
it were needed and we desired to do it. Faith created the mighty engines
and explosives of shattering power, which make it possible to do impossible things. Believe me, it is all by faith, "the assurance of things
hoped for, the conviction of things not seen.''
We must have faith in our country-believe in it, love it, defend it.
Among free men, love of country, as it appears in song and story, is
always centered in the love of land itself; its people, speech, history,
literature, and the institutions guarding its precious liberties, are extolled as having been born of the land. It is always, therefore, the homeland, the fatherland, the motherland, the nativeland.
Sir Walter Scott dips his racing pen in holy scorn as he writes of
the wretch who has no love of country:

.

"Breathes there a man, with soul so dead,
Who never to himself hath said,
'This is my own, my native land!' "
Or attend to the fairest love song that ever poured from a patriot's
heart as the immortal bard of Stratford extols his adored motherland, the
proud mother of the free:
This royal throne of kings, this septer' d isle
This earth of majesty, this seat of Mars,
This other Eden, demi-paradise,
This fortress built by nature for herself
Against infection and the hand of war,
This happy breed of men, this little world,
This precious stone set in the silver sea,
Which serves it in the office of a wall
Or as a moat defensive to a house,
Against the envy of less happier lands,
This blessed plot, this earth, this realm, this England;
This land of such dear souls, this dear, dear land.

Have faith in your country! Our fathers did not talk about "The
Americ an way of life." What silly twaddle is this? Who knows what
the American way of life is? It is, of course, what any individual American thinks it to be. They talked about freedom, and man's righ~s and
his £esponsibilities to preserv e the institutions which guarded their pr~­
cious liberties. They were in love with the land: they had conq~ered it
and tamed it, and they loved every rock and rill of it. It was theirs, and
they would shed every drop of blood to keep it.
Our land is great because it is free and good. The monstrous ty~ann~
of Communism which enslaves half the world cannot endure.' It is evil
and it must fail. The time approac hes when it will go down m fire and
blood to the hell from which it came. God speed that happy day!

GRAN D MAST ER'S MESSAGE
Guy B. MIZE, Grand Master

My Brethren:
Once again, through the inexorable passage of time, we assemble in
annual communication, not only to review that which is past but, what is
more important, to transac t our annual business and plan for the future.
This is the 113th Annual Communication of our Grand Lodge.
What an inspiration it would be if we could review this morning the
story of Freema sonry in this Jurisdiction as told by Masoni c leaders
of the past who have stood before their brethre n in annual communication to report on progres s during their terms as Grand Master. What
a privilege is ours, though, in being able to read of the accomplishments
of our brethre n in the Proceed ings which chronicle each year of California Masonr y. And now, we are privileged to add one more page
to the story and we are pleased that the opportu nity has come to us.
It is a humbling experience indeed for one to kneel at the altar of
Masonr y to receive the charges and assume the obligations apperta ining to the office of Grand Master. In the same attitude , I now stand
before you to give an account of my steward ship: acknowledging to
all my brethre n sincere thanks for their suppor t-not only to me as
an individual but, more important, to the Fratern ity of which we are
a part. In our deliberations this week, may we be guided by the teachings and princi)!lles of Masonr y; and may the presence of the Great
Archite ct of the Univers e be reflected in all our doings.
This has been a busy year but no more so, I am sure, than for
Grand Masters who have precede d me-fo r ours is a busy Grand
Lodge requiring much time and attentio n from those who serve it. The
monthly itineraries which have gone out to all concerned reflect a
considerable number and variety of interesting ceremonies. Exhibit s
attache d to this message will list in detail the various events and I
will report only certain highligh ts of the year.
May I, at this point, acknow ledge the support and assistan ce of
Past Grand Masters to whom I have turned for counsel, to my fellow
Grand Lodge Officers, to the members of the Ritual Committee, to the
Inspectors, to the Committeemen, to all in the Grand Lodge office who
assist the Grand Master in so many ways. To the Grand Secreta ry
and the Assista nt Grand Secreta ry-and here are •included both Brother
Henry D. Oliphan t, who retired June 30, 1962, after many years of
faithful and devoted service, and his successor, Brother Verne Hendrix-I pay a special tribute for they have been of tremendous help
to your Grand Master.

In the early part of this Masonic year came the sad news of the
passing of our Past Grand Master and Past Grand Secretary, Most
Worshipful Lloyd E. Wilson. It was with heavy heart that we convened Grand Lodge in this Auditol"ium and, using the simple burial
service of the Master Mason, paid our last fraternal tribute to our
illustrious brother.
Then, once again, the final summons came and this Grand Lodge
suffered the loss of a noble man, one whose name was favorably and
respectfully kown to Mason and non-Mason alike-our revered Past
Grand Master, the Most Worshipful Charles Albert Adams. Word
of Brother Adams' passing came to me as I reached the Hawaiian
Islands for my official visits to our Lodges there. Masonic services for
Brother Adams were conducted by the Grand Lodge with Most Worshipful Arthur M. Warren, Past Grand Master, officiating.
THE YEAR'S WORK

There was only one item of unfinished business referred to me at
the close of the 1961 Annual Communication, that of appointing a
special committee for the preparation of a new Trial Manual. I
appointed a committee of three, chairmanned by Worshipful Everett
Houser, and the work of the committee will be brought to your attention through a resolution presented by Worshipful Albert F. Ross.
Chairman of the Grievances Committee. The able services of the special
committee and the results of its labors have been approved by the Chairmen of the Jurisprudence and Grievances Committees and by your
Grand Master.
The Special Committee on Masonic Historical Monuments reporting at the 1961 Annual Communication made certain recommendations
as to procedures in protecting Lodge records. I directed at the beginning of the year that the work in regard to Masonic historical monuments be assumed by the Masonic History Committee. The latter is a
Standing Committee and, inasmuch as the activities of the two committees are parallel in most oinstances, I felt that the one special committee could be discontinued.
One of the favorite questions of a Grand Lodge officer is, "Which
way shall we travel?" Whether by car, by plane or, on occasion, by
train, the total mileage traveled during the year was quite impressive
and my only regret is that, with a business to think of, there was not
time to go into every section of our Jurisdiction and meet with all the
brethren. As it was, total mileage traveled approximated 36,000 miles
of which all but 10,000 miles were by air.
In the course of the year's travels, including able assistance on occasions when the Deputy Grand Master or the Senior and Junior Grand
Wardens officiated in my stead, six new Lodges, for which charters

of the schools. Particularly do we thank the press in those commund~
ties which gave factual, unbiased publicity to the ceremonies.
An unusual event took place in the cornerstone and plaque ceremony
in connection with the restoration of the original Masonic Temple once
occupied by Los Angeles Lodge No. 42. Scheduled, at one time, to be
destroyed by slum clearance and freeway projects the Lodge Hall
was eventually included in the State restoration project designed to
create a State Historical Monument consisting of buildings which once
housed businesses or organizations so important to the early life of Los
Angeles, when its population was approximately 1700 persons and all
activity centered around the old Plaza. When completed, the m~n~ment
will be one of the outstanding attractions for those who v1s1t Los
Angeles. It is to be expected that maniy thousands of Masons and friends
will, in due course of time, visit the Lodge Hall and admire the fixtures,
furniture and furnishings of a period dating back more than 100 years.
On August 25, 1962, it was our privilege to i>pen the Grand Lodge
in the present Lodge Room of Los Angeles No. 42, in the new Scottish
Rite Temple, and then proceed to the site of the Old Hall and there
lay the cornerstone of the restored building, which is in the area set
aside as EI Pueblo de Los Angeles State Historical Monument. Our
thanks go to the State of California and its officiaJ.s who approved the
inclusion of the Masonic Temple fa the restoration project: to the
Division of Architecture of the Department of Public Works, repre~
sented in particular by one of its members, our brother Orvel B. John~
son, who was in direct charge of the project: and to the several City
and County Boards whose approvaJ.s were so necessary in getting the
job done. For a number of years, while the project wa~ only in. the
planning or, really, dreaming stage, Grand Lodge had its committee

to help plan the project. Although the membership of the committee
changed from time to time, there was one member of the committee,

Brother Codon made the restoration of the Lodge Hall his personal
goal. and he lived with it for a number of years contributing time,
money, energy and ability.
The Masons of Caliifornia thank all who had any part in bringing
to fruition this Masonic monument which will be open for all time to
come--to Masons and non~Masons alike. Our lease with the State will
require us to furnish a custodian during suitable hours · in order that
the public may inspect the ·Lodge Hall as a part of the Monument.
We will also be obligated for certain operating expenses. The lease
provides that we shall have exclusive use of the Lodge Room at appro~
priate hours for Masonic meetings and it is anticipated that many
Lodges, as at the Masonic Temple at Columbia, will want to use the
Lodge Room for the conferring of degrees and for other special purposes.
I recommend that the Special Committee, designated as the Old
Masonic Hall in Los Angeles Committee, be recognized as a regular
Special Committee in the same manner as the Columbia Temple Com~
mittee and that it be a continuing committee. It will be necessary to make
the operation of the Old Hall of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 self~sustain~
ing to the fullest extent possible. In all probability, the Grand Secretary
will be the clearing house for engagements and will collect the fees to be
established for the use of the Hall. Rules and regulations governing the
operation of the Hall will have to be prepared by the Special Committee
in conjunction with the Grand Secretary, all with the approval of the
Grand Master.
Two Past Grand Masters came to the rescue during the year and
represented Grand Lodge when it was necessary for its Officers to be
elsewhere. A number of years ago. at the Mare Island Naval Shipyard,
Vallejo, a plaque had been placed on a building honoring the memory of
John Mills Browne, Commodore and Surgeon~General of the United
States Navy. Commodore Browne was a member and Past Master of
Vallejo Lodge No. 87 and was Grand Master in 1875, 1876, 1877 and
1878. Thanks to the interest of our brother, Admiral Honsinger, Com~
mander of Mare Island Naval Shipyard, we :were asked to officiate at
the placing of the plaque in a permanent location in Alden Park on the
Naval Base. At my request Past Grand Master Alfred Breslauer repre~
sented the Grand Lodge at the rededication ceremony on March 17,
1962, and the word which came to me was that Brother Breslauer offici~
ated in the able manner demonstrated on so many occasions during his
term as Grand Master.

HAWAII

One of the highlights of the Grand Master's year is his visit to that
part of the Jurisdiction most distant in miles but as near as his own Lodge
in the warm, fraternal spirit which reaches across the Pacific and brings
our two States together as one.
Accompanied by Mrs. Mize, I flew to Hawaii and spent five days
on the Island of Maui before plunging into the round of
Hana-Maui
at
official visits to the ten Lodges on the Islands of Maui, Hawaii, Kauai
and Oahu. There was sufficient time available to visit with the Officers of
each Lodge, our brethren on the Kona Coast of Hawaii, the York and
Scottish Rite Bodies in Honlulu and the Potentate and members of his
Divan of Aloha Temple in Honolulu. There were four official visits
when the Grand Master appeared in full regalia and was received with
Grand Lodge Honors. I am glad to report that on all other occasions a
more informal spirit prevailed, and it was not necessary to concern myself with what the tourists, dad in Aloha <Shirts and muu-muus, thought
as I strode hurriedly through hotel lobbies in tails and white tie.
The visit to the U.S.S. Arizona, through the courtesy of the Master
of Pearl Harbor Lodge No. 598 and Admiral Ray Needham, was a
sobering experience. The wreath which was placed on the platform over
the Arizona, in the name of the Fraternity, was with the hope that never
again will the people of any nation experience the tragedies of war such
as we did at Pearl Harbor. A new memorial structure was in the process
of being erected over the resting place of the U.S.S. Arizona. Scheduled
to have been completed and ready for dedication last December 7th, the
anniversary date of World War II, Admiral Needham said that the
completion and dedication was re-scheduled for Memorial Day, May 30,
1962. He was pleased that it was to be so for the dedication of the monument could then be in the spirit of devotion, heroism and patriotism for
one's country rather than as a reminder of hate for a tragedy which
could not be undone.

OTHER VISITS

Although your Grand Master was denied the privilege this year of
visiting neighboring Grand Jurisdictions on the occasions of their Annual
Communications, we were well represented at Arizona, Nevada, Oregon,
Washington, Idaho and British Columbia by other elective Grand Lodge
Officers. Other Jurisdictions than these extended invitations to their
Communications, and we regret that the pressures of business-fraternal
and otherwise-prevent ed acceptance in each instance. To the representatives of those Jurisdictions who are with us at this Communication,
and whom we will have the pleasure later of welcoming individually, we
bid you a hearty welcome and trust that you will find our hospitality
acceptable and that you will profit as much by being here as we will by
having you with us.
It was my privilege to attend the sesquicentennial celebration of the
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Louisiana in New Orleans on February 4, 5, and 6, 1962. The hospitality of our brethren in LoU<isiana
cannot be exceeded and, by the way of special events, Masonry was presented to the public in a most effective and appropriate manner.
Later in the month of February, I joined with the Deputy Grand
Master in attending the Annual Conference of Grand Masters of North
America, held in Washington, D.C., and the Annual Meeting of The
George Washington Masonic National Memorial Association at the
Memorial Build•ing in Alexandria, Virginia. California lost its member
on the Board of Directors of the Association in the passing of Past
Grand Master Lloyd Wilson but our Jurisdiction was once again recognized when your Grand Master was elected a Director to serve the unexpired portion of Brother Wilson's term. I would call your attention to
the completion of the twelve dioramas depicting events in the life of
George Washington which are now on display in the A<Ssembly Room
of the Memorial Building. Lloyd Wilson was one of the principal sponsors of the Dioramas, and they will constantly remind us of his devotion
to the George Washington Masonic National Memol"ial and of the
twenty years he served as a member of its Board and Executive Committee.
Also in our Nation's Capital. at the same time, attending the Annual
Conference of Grand Secretaries were our Grand Secretary, Edward H.
Siems, and our then Assistant Grand Secretary, Henry D. Oliphant. We
are happy to rep<;>rt that although Brother Siems has been Grand Secre-

I regret to report though that we had two instances of consolidations
of Lodges. The details of the consolidations will be found in the report
of the Grand Secretary. Although we dislike to see Lodges which have
been a valued part of this Jurisdiction pass out of existence, consolidations whic~ leave us with strong Lodges, rather than Lodges which may
be strugglmg to do a good job, are, in all probability, to be desired.
Changing times, relocation of population, other economic factors may
prompt more consolidations in the future.
The Committee on Lodge Financing has again experienced difficulty
with a few .Lodges which have embarked on programs governed by our
regulations but for which the necessary prior approvals of the Committee
were not obtained. Our regulations, as 's et out in the Code, are clear and
there can be no excuse for Lodges or Temple Associations failing to
comply. The Committee is for one purpose-to help-not hinder. In addition to being able to offer sound advice on building and financing problems, the Committee is in position to counsel on the problems inherent in
operating Lodge properties.
We can be proud of the esteem in which our magazine, The California Freemason, is held not only in our Jurisdiction but throughout the
Mason.ic world. The staff of the Freemason and the Correspondence
Committee labor hard, and we appreciate the high standards set in publishing the California Freemason. The Board of Control, Boards of
Relief, Committees on Sojourners, Masonic History, Education, Cemeteries, DeMolay-these, and the committee which are administrative, and
the ones which function during Grand Lodge Week are indispensable to
Grand Lodge and our thanks go to all of them.
It was my privilege to meet with the Board of Trustees of the Mas~nic Home~ of California on three occasions dul'ling the year and you
will be most mterested, I am sure, in their annual report. Our two Homes
are great monuments to Masonic charity and require the type of able,
dedicated Masons which we have, serving as Trustees, to insure a successful operation.
Although I have been speaking of Grand Lodge Committees, let us
never forget for one moment that the ultimate success of all that we do
hinges upon the loyal, enthusiastic support of the counterparts of the
Grand Lodge Committees. I refer to the work done by the constituent
Lodges at the local level. There is ample evidence to support my statement t~at more and more Lodges are accepting the plans, suggestions
and guidance of Grand Lodge Committees and this is good - for the
Lodge and for the Craft as a whole. Certainly the Public Schools Week
program was helped materially by the committees in San Francisco and
Los Angeles, operating independently of but in conjunction with local
Lodge committees and the Grand Lodge Committee.

Commit~ee the ~rogram of the past year and of several years immediately

It would take far more time than is at my disposal to adequately

in the Grand Lodge program. The reports of the many committees will

It is not proper, nor desirable, to single out certain Committees over

Please remember, my brethren, that the committees listed in your program were created to take care of definite needs in the over-all plan of

scenes, it is all for the benefit of Masonry and is deserving of your

I observed during the year the never ending efforts of the Committee
on Commercialism to restrain those who knowingly, or unknowingly,
violated our laws respecting commercial ventures, advertising, gambling,
and solicitation of gifts. In addition to suppressing the activities of the
few so-called Masonic magazines still operating in California by way of
solicitation of advertising, the Commercialism Committee carried on
extensive correspondence with appendant organizations relative to bazaars, food sales, rummage sales and the like. It was necessary for me to
issue warnings to two Shrine Temples because of infractions of Masonic
law. In like fashion, several Lodges and members of Lodges were reprimanded for not adhering to our laws, rules and regulations. The Commercialism Committee does not relish having to police the various organizations nor does the Grand Master enjoy meting out discipline. But,
when required, it must and will be done or Masonry will suffer. Fortunately, the necessity for discipline is not a major problem, and I know
that you who are here as representatives of your Lodges stand behind
our laws and those who must enforce them.
The painstaking examinations made by the Charters Committee of
the .five Lodges receiving dispensations made it easy for me to approve
the petitions for dispensations. It is interesting to note that these Lodges
achieved the distinction of being recorded on the Merit Roll of the
Memorial Temple and the Honor Roll of the Endowment Fund. It is my
understanding that there are excellent prospects of other Masonic Clubs
being ready to apply for dispensations in the not too distant future.

Early in the Grand Lodge year I received reports indicatin g tJ;i;at the
Culver-P alms Pyramid No. 57, Order of Sciots, had staged a Hobo
Dinner" party in its Lodge Rooms in Los Angeles and that civil. and
Masonic laws were v.iolated at the party by reason of the sale of liquor
without license. Upon ascertain ing the alleged facts to be true, I interdicted all Masons residing in the Jurisdiction of Californ ia from membership in said Pyramid . A copy of my interdiction, dated March 29, 1962,
i·s attached to this message for your consider ation and disposition.
Immediately after the issuance of my order, the head of the Supreme
Pyramid of the Ancient Egyptian Order of Sciots calle~ on me and
assured me that it was his intention to co-opera te fully with my order.

He arrested the charter of the offending Pyramid and that is where the
matter stands today. I can state further that it is my opinion the Pharaoh
of the Sciots has endeavo red to see that Sciot Pyramid s and their members obey the laws of Freemas onry.
In preparat ion for the Centenn ial Year of this Grand Lodge, an appropriation was made for the purchase of new regalia for Grand Lodge
Officers. The new regalia was worn for the first time at the opening of
Grand Lodge in October, 1950, and with this Communication will have
been in use for thirteen years. We have two "travelin g" sets of Grand
Lodge regalia, one being so shabby it should not be used. These sets are
customarily used away from this Temple. A study of Grand Lodge
engagements during recent years clearly shows an increase in number
from year to year, and we find ourselves, on occasion, in the position of
having two ceremonies scheduled on the same week end in different parts
of the State. I believe that it is necessar y to provide for new regalia and
make the following recommendation: That an appropri ation be made for
a new set of Grand Lodge regalia with the thought in mind that the
present set, used during the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge, be
considered as the reserve set and that the so-called traveling set be continued as such. The regalia being worn today is, or was, attractiv e when
new, but white velvet and elaborate gold thread and fringe are perishable and add consider ably to the cost of the regalia. I make no recommendation as to whether or not the new regalia, if approved , should be
of the same type we now have or the blue and gold as formerly worn.
Further, my recommendation contemplates other equipment as is needed
for ceremonies such as candle stick holders, vessels for corn, wine and
oil and a sword, etc.
The Finance Committee in its report at the last Annual Commun ication (see Page 311 of the 1961 Proceedi ngs) called attention to the fact
that Brother Lloyd Wilson had chosen voluntar ily to retire under the
physical disability provision of our Retireme nt Income Plan effective
January 1, 1962. He had elected to apply for a monthly pension of
$254.05 in order that, should his wife survive him, she would contiinue to
receive a monthly pension in like amount during the remainde r of her
life. The untimely and unforeseen death of Brother Wilson occurred on
November 2, 1961, before the necessary requirem ents for the pension
to begin January 1, 1962, could be completed. Grand Lodge was committed for the year ending December 31, 1961, to continue Brother
Wilson on his regulac <Salary. It was estimate d that it would take him
until December 31, 1961, to complete the special assignments previously
given to him by Grand Master Alfred F. Breslauer. Effective January
1, 1962, Brother Wilson was to receive $254.05 monthly from the
Retirement Income Plan and a supplemental monthly allowance in the
amount of $745.95. I ordered that payment be made to the Estate of
Brother Wilson represen ting the salary which would have been paid

25

PROCEED INGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFOR NIA

to him for the month of November, 1961, had he lived. On the basis of
need. and taking into consideration the fact that had Brother Wilson
lived for only a few more weeks the arrange ment for the pension protecting both him and Mrs. Wilson would have been completed. I further ordered that the sum of $254.05 be paid monthly to Mrs. Wilson
beginning December 1, 1961. I present the detail of my action to this
Grand Lodge for its approva l.
Bear in mind, my brethren , that provision had been made in the
budget for a supplem ental pension of $745.95 per month to Brother
Wilson , whereas I was only authoriziing a monthly paymen t of $254.05
to the widow, Mrs. Wilson . Grand Lodge, in the operation of the Retirement Income Plan, will further benefit in years to come in that its contributions to the Plan will be lessened by reason of the fact that some
$25,000.00 had been contribu ted by Grand Lodge as its share towards
future retirement benefits to be paid to Brother Wilson . With the appl4cation for his retirem ent and pension rights incomplete the plan will not
have to continu e certain reserves and Grand Lodge will benefit thereby .
As this problem now stands, there is no provision in the Retirem ent
Income Plan for Mrs. W Hson, nor should aniy paymen ts to her be considered in the light of a pension. The implications and establis hment of
precede nt as to employees or relatives of employees preclude the advisability of so labeling any such benefits which might be paid by Grand
Lodge. There is no question in my mind but that Grand Lodge should,
and will, make adequa te provision for the needs of Mrs. Wilson as they
may be from time to time, and I suggest that, following the policy established for the widows of other Past Grand Masters , the Finance Committee make provision in its budget for a monthly allowance to Mrs.
Wilson , the same to be charged to the Grand Master 's Relief Fund. For
guidance, the Finance Committee and the Grand Treasur er have available a study of Mrs. Wilson 's income and expenses for the period since
Brother Wilson 's death. I. for one, knowin g that at all times a fair
picture of the situatio n will be available, would be willing to accept
recommendations of the Finance Committee and the Grand Treasur er
each year as to an appropr iate monthly allowance designed to take care
of Mrs. Wilson 's needs.

RECOMM ENDATIO N No. 5
Question s have been propoun ded to me during the year in reference
to Lodge procedur es on requests for withdraw al or dimits from membership.
Section 447, CMC- Methods of Dimitting, states that withdraw al
may be accomplished at any time by a member of a Lodge, in good
standing . against whom no charges are pending, and whose dues are
paid, giving notice of his intention so to do at a stated meeting. Section
447 further states that a "certificate of the fact of such withdraw al'' may
be issued by the Lodge. No form for such certifica·t e of withdraw al has
ever been approved by Grand Lodge.
Section 448, CMC-F orm of Request for Oimiit, Section 449,
CMC-Fo rm of Dimit, Section 450, CMC - Dimit of Candida te, and
Section 451, CMC - Certificate of Standing offer ample evidence of
the dimit being the necessar y evidence of the steps required for severance
or transfer by affiliation of membership.
Section 557, CMC-Af filiation, clearly shows that an applican t for
affiliation must produce a dimit from the Lodge of which he was last a
member (Californ ia or otherwis e) or furnish a written request to his
Lodge for a dimit as a condition necessar y to applying for membership as
an affiliate. Evidence in the form of a dimit, in such a case, is most helpful
not only to the applican t but to the Lodge as well.
A member desiring to withdraw from membership in his Lodge cannot secure a dimit unless he is in good standing at the time of giving
notice, has no charges pending against him, and whose dues are paid.
Thus he may be consider ed worthy of, although not entitled to, a recommend atory certificate except by vote of his Lodge as provided for in
Section 447, CMC. However , the vote of a majority of members present
for the issuance of a recomme ndatory certifl.cate may well be a decided
minority of the total membersMp of the Lodge.
Generall y speaking, it is not the present custom in the business world
to issue a letter of recommendation to an ex-employee, addresse d to
whom it may concern. Exempla ry conduct in the past is no guarante e
that it may continue in the future. Not all Grand Lodges provide a dimit
in the form of a recomme ndatory certificate. The conditions under which

a regular dimit can be obtaine d in our Juris~ic~on ~ons?tut~ a ~ecom­
mendation for the dimitting brothe r and there 1s httle justification,
1f any,
for preferr ing one member over anothe r.

DECISIO N No.

1

Questi ons have arisen respecting investment of funds under Section
403 CMC, as follows:
1. Do the provisions of said section apply to Lodge Templ e or Mason
ic
Templ e Associations? Under Section 402-1 of CMC the Lodge
must hold title to the building and/or land used or suitable for temple
purposes and ~n which it has invested Lodge funds: and under
Section 402-2 a Lodge or Lodges shall own a controlling interes
t
in memberships or shares of a corpor ation which holds title to such
proper ty used or suitabl e for temple purposes. Since a Lodge
or
Lodges in either event controls and in effect owns the proper
ty
of such associations, it appear s that the funds of such associatiions
are subject to the invest mpt rules laid down by Section
403
including the rule requiring submission of propos ed investments
to the Investment Adviso r used by Grand Lodge.
2. Respecting saving s accoun ts and investment certificates in saving
s
and loan associations under catego ry 3. ( c) of Section 403 CMC,
is it require d that propos ed investments in •such accounts and certifkate s be submitted to the Investm ent Adviso r used by Grand
Lodge? The services of the Investm ent Adv·isor relate to securities only, such as stocks and bonds. Strictly speaking accoun ts and
certificates in saving s and loan associations are not securities. They
are in effect deposits of money backed by an instrum entality of
the
Federa l Govern ment.
My decision, concerning the two questions, is as follows:
The provisions of Section 403 of the Mason ic Code apply to
Lodge Templ e Associations and to Mason ic Templ e Associ a-

5. Support for our public school system has been one of the prime
purposes of Grand Lodge for more than forty years. Perhaps,
because of certain opposition no cornerstone ceremony has been
conducted in the City of Los Angeles for a public school for more
than twenty years. The ceremony in laying the cornerstone of
Palisades High School was well attended and enthusiastically
applauded by all, including teachers, parents and school officials.
It is hoped that it will represent a break-through to a revival of
such ceremonies. Personally, I would not have chosen Sunday to
perform the ceremony but the time element was not in our hands.
The date was selected by the school officials and it was up to us to
take the ceremony or leave it. Because of our long-standing interest
in public schools, it is my opinion that the cornerstone laying ceremony at Palisades High School. conducted on Sunday, was in
accord with the spirit of Masonry.
My deciision is therefore, as follows:
Cornerstone laying and dedication ceremonies for public school
buildings or other exclusively public buildings may be conducted
on Sunday without infringing the spirit of Masonry.
DECISION No. 4
In considering the subject of Lodge ·rosters, and the extent of
information concerning members pertinent and proper to be published,
I am of the opinion that it is beneficial to Lodges and their members
that certain ·information as to each member be available.
In reviewing our law as it now stands, particularly Section 334-c,
I see no prohibition to including in Lodge rosters the business or vocation, address, and telephone number of members in addition to home
address and telephone number.

DECISION

Our law embodied in Sectfon 334-c, California Masonic Code does
not prohibit the listing of the business or occupation, business address
and telephone number of members in a Lodge roster.
DEc1s10N No. 5
I was asked if a brother who had willed his body to a university
for medical research and who, in his will, had requested a Masoniic
funeral service could receive the same. His request was supported
by his widow and by the members of his Lodge, it being noted that
the deceased brother had a long and distinguished record of Masonic
service.
Section 604, CMC states in part that "every Master Mason who
dies in good standing is entitled to burial with Masonic honors, regardless of the disposition which is to be made of his remains." No mention

38

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

is made as to whether disposition is prior or subsequent to a funeral
service.
Section 605-g, CMC holds that the Masonic funeral service is
symbolic.
In answer to the question put to me, I held that the Lodge making
inquiry could conduct a Masonic funeral service for the brother who
had willed his body to a university for medical research.
DECISION

A Masonic funeral service may be held for a deceased brother who
dies in good standing and for whom proper request for burial with
Masonic honors has been made, regardless of the disposition of his
remains or the fact that his remains may not be present at the funeral
service.
DECISION No. 6
Question at hand is whether a Council of Allied Masonic Degrees
(attached to the Grand Council of Allied Masoni~ De~rees ?f t~e
United States of America) whiich is stated to have existed m Cahforma
since prior to September 27, 1957, as ,a non-degree body, can now moor
to itself a Royal Ark ,Mariner Lodge which does confer degrees.
It is further stated that membership in a Chapter of Royal Arch
Masons is a prerequisite to membership in a Council of the Allied
Masonic Degrees. This prerequisite is established because most of the
degrees under the jurisdiction of the Grand Council have ~ Royal Arch
prerequisite as well. This, however, creates a problem with respect to
certain members of Lodges of Royal Ark Mariners from other jurisdictions, who are not, of necessity, Royal Arch Masons and who cannot, because of this lack of a prerequisite degree, and perhaps also
because of the membership limitation by number, hold fraternal communication with their fellow Royal Ark Mariners in the United States.
The Grand Council of Allied Masonic Degrees meets this problem
by authorizing each of its constitu~t. Co~ncils to h~ve "moored" to it
a Royal Ark Mariners Lodge, perm1ttmg 1t to open m that degree only
and to receive visitors and members who are not Royal Arch Masons.
Each "moored" Lodge, therefore, generally has affiliated with it a few
members at least who are not members of the parent Council of Allied
Masonic Degrees.
None of the organizations listed above has ever been established,
sponsored or sanctioned by the Gran~ Chapte: of R?yal :Arch Masons
of California or by any other Masomc body m Cahforma.

No. 7
In 1956 a member of a Lodge, holding a certificate of life membership, against whom no charges were pending, applied in writing for
withdrawal of membership, which application was read at a stated
meeting. Acknowledgement of the request for withdrawal and its reading at a stated meeting was made in a letter from the sec,retary of the
Lodge to the brother requesting withdrawal. No certificate of withdrawal, more properly termed, a dimit was issued by the Lodge to
the brother.
DECISION

In 1962, said applicant requested reinstatement to membership,
and the Master of said Lodge now seeks a decision on procedure.
DECISION

Under Section 447, CMC, action by the Lodge on the request for
reinstatement to membership by whatever means is unnecessary. In
the absence of a dimit issued by the Lodge, membership never terminated and no reinstatement proceedings are required.
Membership not having terminated, the applicant is entitled to all
the rights pertaining to his li£,e membership. Under Section 575, CMC,
since the applicant was never legally removed from the Lodge Roll,
the Lodge is obligated to Grand Lodge for payment of accrued per
capita taxes on the applicant.

DECISION No. 8
The inquiry is whether it is lawful for a Tabernacle of the Holy
Royal Arch Knight Templar Priests to operate in California.
The facts submitted are as follows:
1. The Order has 33 degrees ranging from Knight of the Christian Mark to Holy Royal Arch Knight Templar Priest.
2. Membership is by invitation only and is limited to those who
have been installed Commanders of Commanderies of Kn~ghts
Templar.
3. Tabernacles have been chartered in some 24 states of the
United States.
4. No Tabernacle has ever been chartered in California and
none has existed here.
5. Said order is not sponsored, controlled, approved nor even
recognized by any York Rite Body of California.
This Order having 33 degrees which it can confer must have a
ritual. Consequently, it comes within the prohibition of Section 332.1,
CMC.

The establishment of a Royal Ark Mariner Lodge in the Jurisdiction of California by a Council of Allied Masonic Degrees. (attached
to the Grand Council of Allied Masonic Degrees of the Umted States
of America) is prohibited by Section 332.1 of the CMC.

Establishment of a Tabernacle of Holy Royal Arch Knight Templar
Priests in the Jurisdiction of California is prohibited by Section 332.1,
CMC.

IN CONCLUSION

And now, my brethren, it is time to conclude this report. My
stewardship for the year is ended and while I see things to be done,
I am not unhappy or worried for able servants of Masonry stand ready
to lead the Craft to new heights. The torch which was lighted so long
ago continues to burn and it serves as a beacon to free men.
Masonry has been challenged on many scores-but only by those
who would control the mind and bend the will of man to their own
ideologies. Masonry is for free men-men free to worship God according to their own personal beliefs-men free in the pursuit of life, liberty
and happiness. These freedoms were of paramount importance in the
minds of those Masons who helped write the Constitution of our
Country.
We are accused, on occasion, of being a religion-albeit, a false
religion. This, we deny, for ,it is not true, but as Masons we are proud
to acknowledge our belief in a Supreme Being.
Listen to the words of Carlos P. Romulo, former President of
The Philippines and recently recalled from his post as Ambassador
to the United Nations:
"I am going home, America-farewell.
"For seventeen years, I have enjoyed your hospitality,
visited every one of your 50 states. I can say I know
you well.
"I admire and love America. It is my second home.
"What I have to say now in parting is both a tribute and
a warning: Never forget, Americans, that yours is a
spiritual country.
"Yes, I know that you are a practical people. Like others,
I have marveled at your factories, your skyscrapers
and your arsenals.
"But underlying everything else is the fact that America
began as a God-loving, God-fearing, God-worshipping people, knowing that there is a spark of the
Divine in each one of us. It is this respect for the dignity of the human spirit which makes America invincible. May it always endure.
"And so I say again in parting, thank you, America, and
farewell. May God keep you always-and may you
always keep God."
Thus spoke a man who, though neither an American nor a Mason,
had caught the underlying force and spirit of Americanism and Freemasonry.
Inscribed on the Royal Hawaiian Coat of Arms used by Royalty
until 1898 are the words of King Kamehameha:
"Ua Mau Ke Ea Oka Aina I Ka Pono"
"The life of the land is preserved in righteousness."

Grand Master
The message was received with a standing ovation and was referred
by the Deputy Grand Master to the Committee on Distribution.

FREE AND ACCEPTED MASONS

GUY

B. MIZE

GRAND MASTER

To ALL LoDGEs AND MASONS WITHIN AND
UNDER

Tms JURISDICTION:

Brethren:
It has been brought to my attention that on January 20, 1962, a group
of Masons organized and meeting under the name of Culver-Palms
Pyramid No. 57. Order of Sciots held a party desc:riibed as a "Hobo
Dinner" in rooms adjacent to or a part of their regular meeting place at
10120 Venice Boulevard, Los Angeles, California and that, as a part
of refreshments, liquor was sold open~ and without license to persons
attending the party.
Evidence clearly shows that those engaged in the handling and
selling of liquor were Masons and members of Culver-Palms Pyramid
No. 57, Order of Sciots; that although ·it was claimed that attendance
at the party was supposed to be limited to members, their wives and
friends, the facts are that the door to the lodge quarters was unattended; that during the course of the evening, police officers walked
tn and purchased tickets entitling them to obtain drinks at the bar
~erated by meinbe:ris of the Order of Sciots; that arrests were made,
all of which brought Masonry into disrepute.
Although officers of Culver-Palms Pyramid No. 57, Order of
Sciots disclaimed knowledge of Masonic and civil law relating to sale
of liquor with or without license, the offense to Masonry was not
lessened by their doing so, and it is to be noted that statements were to
the effect that similar parties had been staged on previous occasions
and under similar circumstances.
Such gross violation of Masonic law as dt relates to all Masons resdding within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted
Masons of California cannot go unnoticed. The good name of Masonry
demands that appropriate action be taken to insure that any and all
who hold membership in our Fraternity will respect Masoniic law and
custom.
NOW THEREFORE. as Grand Master, I hereby interdict membership in the Culver City-Palms Pyramid of Sciots by all Masons
within or under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California. This
means that all such Masons must sever and terminate membershdp in
said Pyramid of Sciots and that no such Mason may hereafter become
a member thereof.

PROCLAMA TION

CoNsTITUT ION OBSERVAN CE MoNTHs

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWME NT MONTH

It is written ·in a religious work of old, "As for him who voluntaril y
performs a good work, verily God is grateful and knowing."
How meaningfu l this is to Masons of the Jurisdiction of the Grand
Lodge of California , who have created voluntaril y the Masonic Homes
of California and the Masonic Homes Endowme nt Fund, with which to
assist financially in the support of the Homes. This good work redounds
to the honor of all Masons, and our guests at Union City and Covina,
who benefit by your generosity , are grateful and knowing.
The month of May climaxes the attention focused each year on this
most worthy enterprise . I call on each member of the Fraternity to give
attention to the call for financial support of our two Homes through a
suitable contributi on to the Endowme nt Fund. The total need is great.
The individual burden, if all Masons respond, is light. May the Great
Architect of the Universe prosper, direct and counsel you in all your
doings.
It is directed that this Proclamat ion be read at the April and May,
1962, Stated Meetings.
Dated: February 1. 1962.

GIFT PRESENT ATION
(1)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:

WHEREA S. the Holy Bible, above all else, contains within its
revered chapters that which is the rule and guide of a Master Mason's
faith, and
WHEREA S, the Holy Bible, is, in fact, the ultimate symbol of a
Master ·Mason's obligation to his God, his Lodge, hfs Masonic brethren
and himself, and
WHEREAS . the Holy Bible and the open Lodge are synonymou s
and, therefore, of necessity, harmonious, and
WHEREAS . for all Masonic history it has. on occasion, been
deemed appropriate to present a Holy Bible to a Master Mason,
NOW THEREFO RE BE IT RESOLVE D, that the Holy Bible
upon which he has been obligated may be presented to a Master Mason,
in open Lodge, at the conclusion of his Third Degree ceremonies.
Respectfully submitted.
WILLARD M. HUYCK, Master, Lodge No. 662
RALPH F. CooPs. Past Master, Lodge No. 662
Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes, and on
Ritual.
GIFT PRESENT ATION

(2)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREA S. it is the custom in most Masonic Lodges in the State
of California to present to newly raised Master Masons, Bibles. pins,
rings and other symbols of the fact that they are Master Masons, and
WHEREA S, it is in the best interests of Masonry that such presentations be made in a ·solemn and dignified manner in order to impress
upon the individual the responsibility entailed in wearing or possessing
such symbols, and
WHEREAS , such interests can best be served by employing the
dignified surrounding s of a Lodge room.
NOW THEREFO RE BE IT RESOLVE D. that Bibles. pins. rings
and other paraphernal ia indicative of the fact that a person is a Master
Mason may be presented, accompanied by appropriate wording, in open
Lodge after the completion of all degree work for the evening but before
the closing ritual is performed.
Respectfully submitted.
BENJAMIN L. SusMAN, Master, Lodge No. 529
Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes, and on
Ritual.

MEMBER SHIP QUALIFI CATION
(4)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS . Section 51 lg of the California Masonic Code prohibits
a Lodge from receiving an application for degrees from , one who has
served a term in State Prison, and
WHEREAS , Grand Lodge in the past has made exceptions to said
rule which permitted a Lodge to receive such an application (See 1958
Proceedings, Pages 28, 298 and 30, 285), and
• WHEREAS , our Masonic Law permits a Mason who serves a term
in Stat~ ~rison .after he becomes a ·M ason to be restored to his full rights
and privileges m the fraternity thereafter when the circumstances warrant such action, and
WHEREAS , we feel that the service of a term in State Prison should

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

not in and of itself bar a man from Masonry, but that it should be one
of the many and all the circumstances of a man'·s life which should be
taken into consideration in determining the qualification of a candidate.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 511 of
the California Masonic Code be amended by adding at the end of said
Section the following:
"Provided that one who has served a term in State Prison and who
has since lived properly should not by reason of the service of said prison
term be deemed ineligible for Masonry."
Respectfully submitted,

PHYSICAL QUALIFICATIONS
(5)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, there are many worthy and well qualified men who
have been wounded, maimed, or otherwise physically disabled in the
defense of our country in its wars, and others similarly worthy and well
qualified who, through misfortune or tragedy have also become physically disabled or maimed, and who are literally unable to comply with
the physical requirements of our laws and are therefore denied participation in our privileges, and
WHEREAS, this is contrary to our teachings and precepts, particularly that of Brotherly love, and
WHEREAS, we no longer work in operative Masonry but speculative only, these physical requirements are obsolete,
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that all references to physical
sufficiency or physical qualifications for the degrees contained in our laws,
rules, regulations, edicts, decisions, or any other matter on this subject,
written or unwritten, having the force of law, be rescinded.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the prescribed ritual for the

APPLICATION FOR DEGREES
(7)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the reputation of the Fraternity rests upon the individual Mason and his knowledge of our Masonic Law, and
WHEREAS, it is repugnent to our moral and Masonic sensibilities
to find a Master Mason aspiring to, or occupying a station, or being in
an official capacity in a concordant or prerequisite body, without sufficient
knowledge of our Masonic Law as contained in the California Masonic
Code, and
WHEREAS, the actions of individual Masons who govern and
compose prerequisite or concordant bodies by their negligences and
ignorance of our law could cause Master Masons to have formal charges
brought against them of such a serious nature as may result in suspension
or expulsion from the Fraternity, and
WHEREAS, Master Masons without knowledge of our law have
allowed their particular affiliate body to be brought into disrepute and
caused the Fraternity to come under censure and derision from other
groups and the public in general. and
WHEREAS, upon receiving the Master Mason Degree, a Mason
is enjoined to preserve unsullied the reputation of the Fraternity and in
an effort to preclude infractions of our Masonic Code by concordant or
prerequisite bodies or individuals composing such a body, at least an
elementary knowledge of Masonic Law and Custom should be required
to keep themselves and/ or those under their jurisdiction in complete
compliance with, and without deviation from, the accepted laws and
regulations of the Fraternity.
BE IT THEREFORE RESOLVED. that Section 527 "Form of
Application for Degrees" question fifteen of the California Masonic
Code, be amended by inserting after the words "Candidate's Lecture of
the Degree of Master Mason" and before the words "and in no event
within twelve months after you have received the Degree of Master
Mason?" the following words:
and shall have satisfactorily passed. an examination
on Masonic Law as prescribed by Grand Lodge.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that this examination shall be
administered in such form and manner as prescribed by Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,
ROBERT L. WALKER, Master, Lodge No. 512
JoHN C. LINDER, Senior Warden, Lodge No. 512
LLOYD H. SHELTON, Past Master, Lodge No. 512

JOHN A. McCmsH, funior Warden, Lodge No. 512
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. Sectio~ 61?4. California Masonic Code states, "Every
Master Mason who dies in good standing is entitled to burial with
Masonic Honors"-and Section 605 reads, "to constitute burial with
Masonic honors the funeral service authorized by the Grand Lodge must
be used," and
WHEREAS. the foreword in the instructions of The Funeral Service, as adopted ~y th.is Grand Lodge states, "The funeral service may
be held (a) entirely m the Lodge room, or ( b) entirely in a chapel or
home or church. The forms of the two services are different. In each
case, the 'Committal' is to be delivered at the final resting place, or at
the place_ wh~re. the ~asonic service is concluded. The language of the
two services 1s identical. It is ritual and must not be deviated from nor
are interpol~tio~s to b_e permitted e~cept that a eulogy may be deli~ered
at the place indicated in the service, ' and
WHEREAS, it is further stated, "Care should be exercised to comply with any reasonable wish of the family. If any special requests are
made or. th~re are any un~sual conditions, consult with the Inspector
of the district before denying the request or attempting to adapt the
service to the circumstances," and
WH~REA~. an incr~asing number of requests are being made for
a Masonic Service to be given only at the final resting place, and
WHEREAS, the entire Masonic Service, following a church or other
fraternal service is not desired by the family of the deceased, and
. WHERE~S. the only way the Masters and Inspectors can comply
with these reasonable requests is to violate our law.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that a suitable Funeral
~ervice, to be given at the place of interment, be prepared for consideration at the next Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge.

BURIAL WITH MASONIC HONORS
(10)
.

.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A.~· of_ California:
WHEREAS because of a Police Report disclosing that a Brother
Master Mason i~ good standing had been charged w_ith c?mmitting _a
murder and then suicide, the accused was denied burial with Masomc
Honors, and
WHEREAS. many instances have developed th~t the accused
(according to Police Reports) had bee~ brought to Trial by Jury and
subsequently acquitted or found not gmlty as charged, and
.
WHEREAS. the Master of his Lodge had requeste~ advice from
proper authority, which authority had none of the relative facts, was
poorly advised, and
.
WHEREAS. the accused was a Master Mason in good stand1?g,
of high morals and general .good reputa~ion'. even to the extent of bemg
considered for appointment to an office m his Lodge, and
.
WHEREAS. many members of his family, member>S of his ~ge
and of the Craft at large with whom he had been closely associated

61

were dissatisfied and considered that the accused was rendered a grave
injustice upon being denied burial with Masonic Honors, and
WHEREAS, it is our indispensable duty to aid and assist a distressed worthy brother Master Mason,
THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: "In the event that it appears
that an alleged felony has been committed and the accused thereupon
committed suicide, the Master and the Wardens are to determine
whether or not the accused is to be buried with Masonic Honors. As our
Civil Laws protect the accused, in that a man is innocent until proven
guilty of the crime of which he is accused, it must be borne in mind that
a Police Report is an official preliminary investigation but does not necessarily establish the final proof of guilt of the accused, nor the conviction
of the accused for the crime. Furthermore, if there is reasonable doubt
of the accused's guilt because of alternate or remote possibilities involved, he should receive proper consideration to be buried with Masonic
Honors, provided that he was a Master Mason in good standing at the
time."
Respectfully submitted,
CLAUDE J. PALMER, Past Master, Lodge No. 212
JosEPH ScARDAMAGLIA, Past Master. Lodge No. 212
ALFRED ANDERSON, Past Master, Lodge No. 212
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, and on Policy and General
Purposes.

RESEARCH LODGE OFFICERS
(11)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the Research Lodges are seriously hampered by the
existing requirement of Section 385 California Masonic Code that the
Master and Wardens must be Past Masters of a Lodge, and
WHEREAS, the status of the Master of a Research Lodge should
be clarified to distinguish him from the Master of other Lodges,
BE IT RESOLVED: That Section 385 of the California Masonic
Code be amended as follows:
(A) Amend Paragraph 10 to read as follows: "No officer or former
officer of a Research Lodge shall, by reason of that position alone, be
a member of Grand Lodge. Sections 490 and 491 of the California
Masonic Code shall not be applicable to one who has served as Master
of a Research Lodge, only, and the Master of a Research Lodge shall
not, upon death or completion of his term of office, by reason of that
fact alone, become or be known as or designated as a Past Master, and
shall possess none of the !tights, powers or privileges of a Past Master of
a Lodge."
(B) Amend Paragraph 5 thereof by adding the following: "provided, however, that when the Master-elect or a Warden-elect or a
Senior Deacon appointed, is not a Past Master of a California Lodge,

62

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

before he can be installed he must produce a certificate from the Inspector
of the district in which the Research Lodge is situated certifying to the
proficiency of such officer in the opening and closing ceremonies."
( C) Strike out Paragraph 18.
Respectfully submitted,

RESEARCH LODGE APPROPRIATION
(12)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 385 of the California Masonic Code establishes a special classification of constituent Lodges to be known as
Research Lodges, and
WHEREAS, said Section grants to the constituent Research Lodges
the authority to "gather and preserve Masonic Information" and to
"maintain a library," and
WHEREAS, the lack of necessary funds has prevented the establishment of those libraries authorized by said Section, be it
RESOLVED, that the sum of $500.00 be appropriated to each constituent Research Lodge, the funds so appropriated to be used for the
acquisition of a basic Masonic Library.

WHEREAS, prior to 1961, the Grand Lodge Week Activities
Committee had as its responsibility and duty the following: the ar~anging and handling of the Grand Master's party, formerly, t':o dinners and entertainments at the Palace Hotel. one for approximately
1 000 delegates, and the other for some 350 of their ladies on the same
e~ening, presently, a musical program of high calibre held in the auditorium of the California Masonic Memorial Temple for some 3,200
delegates and their ladies; the annual trip to the Masonic Home for the
Aged at Union City, transporting some 1,200 to 1,500 perso.ns by ?us,
and arranging for box lunches for this number; together with various
sight-seeing trips, tours, and luncheons, and
.
.
.
WHEREAS, since the completion of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, an unofficial committee of some four to six members of
Grand Lodge handled the sale of tickets and the arrangements for the
daily lunches served in the Exhibit Hall of the Temple during .each
annual Grand Lodge Communication for the comfort and convenience
of some 2.500 delegates in attendance, and
WHEREAS, in August of 1961, the responsibility for the arranging
and handling of the daily lunches for delegates was given to the Grand
Lodge Week Activities Committee with no additional committee members, the former unofficial committee having resigned en masse, and
WHEREAS, in order to perform efficiently and satisfactorily the
many simultan~ous duties required of it in a short space of time with a
minimum of complaints from Grand Lodge members, the Grand Lodge
Week Activities Committee is in positive and immediate need of additional manpower, now therefore
BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 192 of the Ordinances as contained in the California Masonic Code be amended in such a manner
as to permit the Grand Lodge Week Activities Committee to consist of
(not less than nine members, and not more than) eleven members instead of the present seven members.
Respectfully submitted,
LowELL H. BECKENDORF, Past Master, Lodge No. 462

WHEREAS, Grand Lodge of California approves the ideals, aims
and purposes of the Order of DeMolay and requests Masons to "lend
their moral and personal support" to the Order of DeMolay, according
to the provisions of Section 333f, California Masonic Code, and
WHEREAS, the future of our Masonic Fraternity lies in the Youth
of our present day, and
WHEREAS, we feel that proper and direct guidance of the Youth
of today will provide untold wealth in a better citizenry of tomorrow, and
WHEREAS, we feel that as a result of this guidance, our Masonic
Fraternity will directly benefit in the form of better future members, and
WHEREAS, the Youth of today does need encouragement and influencing in the right direction in their activities, and
WHEREAS, this encouragement and influencing is an opportunity
to serve our Country by helping guide the Youth in the proper direction,
and
WHEREAS, it is the Policy of Grand Lodge of California as attested to by the Most Worshipful Past Grand Master Stewart in 1956
(Note, 333f California Masonic Code), that a Masonic Lodge might
have permission to sponsor Chapters of the Order of DeMolay,
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED, that Section 333r be
added to the California Masonic Code, and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Section 333r read as follows:
"Masonic Lodges, by resolution of the Lodge in Stated Meeting, with
the approval of the Grand Lodge of Masons in California, may sponsor
Chapters of the Order of DeMolay, and may expend funds, in nominal
amounts, with the approval of the Most Worshipful Grand Master of
Masons in California, to provide equipment, supplies and furnishings
for the sponsored Chapter of the Order of DeMolay."
Respectfully submitted,

Procedure on receipt of charges. Upon the presentati on of such

SPECIAL PRESENTA TIO NS AND ADDRESSES
Past Grand Master Henry C. Clausen introduced Frederic H.
Stevens. Past Grand Master of the Philippines, who in turn presented a
fifty Year Veteran Award to Will H. Taylor, Past Grand Master of
the Philippines. A standing ovation was accorded Brother Taylor. He
responded with appropriate remarks.
Past Grand Master Leo E. Anderson addressed the Grand Lodge
regarding Masonry in South America as he saw it during his recent
visit there. He presented to Grand Master Guy B. Mize a copper
plaque and stand as a gift from Tupac Amaru Lodge No. 42 of Lima,
Peru. Grand Master Mize accepted the gift with gratitude.
Grand Master Mize requested Brother Samuel Steelman to approach the east where Past Grand Master Edgar V. Stewart, Jr. then
presented to him a copy of Preston 's Illustrations in Masonry. printed
in 1821, as an expression of appreciation by the Board of Trustees for
legal services rendered to the Masonic Homes and for which Brother
Steelman continually refuses to render a bill. Brother Steelman responded with remarks appropriate to the occasion.
Nohea 0 . A. Peck. Grand Master of Masons in Japan, expressed
fraternal greeting s and, as an expression of appreciation from the Grand
Lodge of Japan, presented a copy of its Constitution and Code to Grand
Master Mize.
At the request of Grand Master Mize, Brother Orvel Johnson, a
member of W ashing ton Lodge No. 20, approached the east. He in turn
presented to the Grand Lodge of California three original paintings,
representing the Lights of the East, West and South Stations, which
bad hung in Columbia Lodge No. 28. They had been preserved by request of the artist, Brother Joseph Spear, to be subsequently placed in an
appropriate Museum or Masonic Temple. Grand Master Mize responded on behalf of the Grand Lodge and directed that the paintings
be hung in the Columbia Temple at Sonora.
Brother Matthew M . Codon, Past Master of Los Angeles Lodge
No. 42, requested permission to address the Grand Lodge. A plastic
plaque, made by Brother Don L. Stoffer, a member of Vesper Lodge
No. 84, was presented to Grand M aster Mize by Brother Codon. The
plaque displays a square and compass together with two of the original
hand made spikes used in the construction of the Old Masonic Hall of
Los Angeles Lodge No. 42 . The Grand Master requested Brother Codon
to provide an appropriate stand and suggested that it be displayed in
the Old Lodge Hall at the City Hall Plaza, Los Angeles.
