REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand LodgeF. & A. M. of California:
I have pleasure in presenting my second annual report as Grand
Treasurer.
Attached will be found all of the financial reports and audits of the
Grand Lodge. Masonic Homes of California and the California Masonic
Memorial Tempie. These reports cover in detail the complete financial
history of our Grand Lodge for the past year and careful attention
should be given to the various items contained therein.
I particularly call your attention to the financial status of our Masonic Homes. We can point with pride to our efforts on behalf of those
who are committed to our care. The Trustees have done an outstanding
job in providing for the ever-growing nee~s of our. residen~s. The .~a­
sons of California likewise have met their commitments m providmg
gifts and bequests and by their support of our Endowment F~nd. The
annual per capita tax levied by this Grand Lodge for the mamtenance
of the Homes is very modest indeed when compared to other Grand
Lodges, and the Trustees should be complimented for their efforts in
keeping the operating costs to a reasonable level.
I feel it incumbent also to comment on the work of the Investment
Committee. chairmanned by our Assistant Grand Treasurer, W. Paul A.
Pflueger, who is outstanding in his chosen field of finance. The Gra~d
Lodge is fortunate indeed to have such an array of talent to handle its
investments. Nowhere except in Masonry could you expect to find such
men, unselfishly giving freely of their time and effort, and with such
exceptional and beneficial results.
APPROPRIATIONS AND DISBURSEMENTS

All appropriations and disbursements have been carefully reviewed
by the professional auditors as provided by Section 191 C.M.C.
Detailed records and vouchers are on file for inspection in the office of
the Grand Secretary.
The budget approved at the last Communication has been strictly
adhered to and as a result of careful planning, a budget surplus of
$27,720.21 has been produced. The various Boards and Committees,
as well as our genial and most efficient Grand Secretary, are to be
complimented for their efforts.
Supplementary appropriations were approved by the Grand Master
on March 9, 1962, as follows:
Pay of Members Annual Communication ............ $ 600.00
Workmen's Compensation Insurance Premium
provided for Constituent Lodges .................... 1,100.00

Supplemental Pension, Lloyd E. Wilson
At the 1961 Communication the Finance Committee, with the approval of the Grand Lodge, arranged the retirement of Past Grand
Secretary Lloyd E. Wilson. The terms of the retirement provided for
his full retirement under our Pension Plan and authorized the payment
by Grand Lodge of a supplemental pension of $716.00 per month: all
to be effective January 1, 1962 (Page 311 ) •
Under the Retirement Plan Brother Wilson chose the opt·ion to
accept a reduced sum ( $251.05) in order to provide a similar amount
for Mrs. Elsie Wilson in the event of his death after retirement (Page
1OA Retirement Income Plan).
Unfortunately the Great Architect of the Universe in His wisdom
saw fit to remove Brother Wilson from our midst before this plan could
be carried out. A s a result the program arranged for Mrs. W ilson was
of no avail and no funds could legally be provided for her under the
Retirement Income Plan.
Recognizing the injustice of the turn of events, the Grand Master
after consultation with the Chairmen of Finance, of Jurisprudence, of
Policy and General Purposes, and with the concurrence of the Grand
Treasurer ordered a monthly payment of $254.05 from the funds of
Grand Lodge to be paid to Mrs. Wilson. This matter no doubt will be
reported by our Grand Master and the reference herein is for the record
only.
The work as Grand Treasurer is a very rewarding one and I am
grateful to the Grand Lodge for the privilege of serving this great
Fraternity.
I express to my associate, W. Paul A. Pflueger, Assistant Gra nd
Treasurer, and to our Grand Secretary, M. W. Edward H. Siems, my
warm thanks for their willingness to serve at every opportunity.
To the Brethren of the Grand Lodge I off er my deep appreciation for
the trust which they have placed in me.
Fraternally submitted,
ARTHUR M. WARREN
Grand Treasurer
Refel'red to Committee on Distribution.

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

SEVENTY-FIVE YEAR BUTTON

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
I have the honor to present to you my Second Annual Report as
Grand Secretary.

I wish to report that Edward Gardiner Dodge, a member of Santa
Barbara Lodge No. 192, became eligible for a Seventy-Five Y ear
Veteran Button on June 18, 1962. This award was presented to him
on July 12, 1962.

UNFINISHED BUSINESS

LODGE UNDER DISPENSATION

The following matters were continued from the last Annual Communication to the present one:
1. Masonic Historical Monuments, page 239, 1961 Proceedings.
2. Trial Manual. page 279, 1961 Proceedings.
3. Trial Record No. 1554, page 274, 1961 Proceedings.
4. Trial Record No. 1726, page 278, 1961 Proceedings.

Woodland H ills Lodge, U .D. was instituted on June 14, 1962.
This Lodge did not collect dues fo r the year ending June 30, 1962.
Therefore, in accord with precedent the G rand Master at our suggestion, directed that Woodland Hills Lodge be not required to pay the
per capita tax. It is respectfully requested that this be approved.

CHARTER ENDORSEMENTS

I wish at this point in my report to bring to the attention of the
Officers of the Lodges in particular, and the membership in general,
the result of some of the activity of this office.
During the past few years there have been about 6,000 to 7,000
applicants for the Degrees each year. Once an applicant has been elected
in a Lodge it is only a matter of a few weeks, or months, before he
becomes a Master Mason. Hence, the number of cards in the file
indicating Candidates in process should remain faidy constant.
About a year ago an analysis of the Candidates' file disclosed tha t
it actually contained about twice the usual number of names. Much
to the staff's sur,Prise it was learned that many average size Lodges
had from 12 to 41 names in the fi le. In some instances this represented
as much as 7% of the total membership of the Lodge. These Candidates
have shown no interest in going beyond the First or Second Degree.
They have been inactive for more than five years. Hence, they were
eligible for the application of Section 546, C alifornia M asonic Code,
which reads in part:
"If a Candidate does not present himself properly qualified for
the Second and Third Degrees within a period of five years from
the date of his ini tiation as an Entered Apprentice, the Master
<Shall direct the Secretary to forward to such Candidate, by reg i s~
tered mail to his last known address, a notice advising him that
unless he shall present himself for advancement on or before a
specified date (at least sixty days in advance) his fee s for the
unconferred degrees and all of his previous contributions will be
declared forfeited."
This Section of our law was enacted to make it possible to keep a
Lodge membership up to date, but it raises some serious questions.
The potenNal is somewhat a larming. Some of these cards date as far
back as 1943 which indicates that either Section 546 should have been

MEMBERSHIP

Change of Meeting Place:
Truth Lodge No. 628 has changed its meeting place from Los
Angeles to North Hollywood. Benevolence Lodge No. 631 has changed
its meeting place from North Hollywood to Los Angeles. Florence
Lodge No. 649 has changed its meeting place from Los Angeles to
Walnut Park.
These changes of meeting place have been officially approved under
the authority of the Grand Master, and the Grand Secretary now
requests authority to properly endorse their Charters.
Consolidation of Lodges:
All requirements of the law respecting consolidation having been
complied with by San Francisco Lodge No. 360 and Victory. Lodge
No. 474 they consolidated, effective November 29, 1961. with the
approval of the Grand Master, the Lodge to be known as San FranciscoVictory Lodge No. 360, located at San Francisco.
All requirements of the law respecting consolidation having been
complied with by Surprise Valley Lodge No. 235 and North East
Lodge No. 266 they consolidated with the approval of the Grand
Master, effective July I. 1962, the Lodge to be known as Surprise Valley
Lodge No. 235, located at Cedarville.
The Grand Secretary requests authority to properly endorse these
Charters.

invoked a long time ago or, by Lodge Action, time should have been
extended for the conferring of Degre~s. It seems to be a real indictment
of some of our investigatin g committees. It may also be a further indictment of the Lodge Officers for not doing a proper follow-up after the
applicant is elected to membership. Regardless of what may have created
this situation, the Officers of each Lodge may be well-advised to rev·iew
their own situation. They will then be in a better position to determine
a course of action to solve their peculiar problem, should one ex ist in
the Lodge.
It will take more than a year to complete the task we have undertaken. We started with Lodge No. 1 and are reviewing the condition
of each Lodge in numerical sequence. It is a time-consuming task to
communicat e with each Lodge concerning these Candidates. Lodges
not yet contacted could help us by reviewing their own files. A real
effort should be made to rekindle the interest of the worthy Entered
Apprentice or F ellow Craft before declaring a forfeiture under Section
516. C .M.C.
The second observation recorded in this report is the result of
another special study dealing with suspensions for non-paymen t of
dues, Article VI, Sections 571-582, C.M.C. The law is very clear. There
is no latitude as to its intent. There is, however, ample leeway as to
its application.
The Lodge has no option but to suspend a Brother when he loses
interest and refuses to pay his dues. unless the delinquent dues committee (Section 577-£) or Officers of the Lodge are able to convince
him of the worth of Masonry. If. on the other hand. there is a reasonable hope that he may change his mind, the Lodge could either remit
his dues or at least grant further time (Secion 579(a) (b) ) .
The concern here is twofold: In 1962 the number of Brethren losing
membership in their Blue Lodges through suspension for non-paymen t
of dues was 1511, which is almost double the number suspended ten
years ago. Membership in 1953 was 213.639 against 2·H,212 in 1962.
The suspensions are all out of proportion.
A special study of 116 suspensions revealed that 41 had maintained
good standing for 20 years or more with no prior suspensions . One
member was suspended for non-paymen t of dues after 51 years of
unblemished membership. Another Brother, a dual member, was suspended a fter 37 years of unbroken membership.
There may be justification for each of these suspensions , but are
we, who are in positions of responsibility, doing our part before the
final s uspension is declared? The magnitude of the problem seems to
justify recording it here with the hope that our leaders will, in their
own way, render unto every man his just due. It would seem that, if
a Brother had proven himself. suspension for non-paymen t of dues
should be delayed until every effort has been made to ascertain the

79

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

cause. This is particularly important when we realize that the number
suspended during the year represents approximate ly 25 % o f all applications received during that period.
The purpose of this report is to make all of the members aware of
the problem in the hope that before final. drastic action is taken every
effort will be made to avoid the necessity of suspension.
What we are saying is that interest in our Lodges is a t a low ebb.
Could it be that by keeping in closer touch with our members, either
by special letter or by personal calls or committe activities, we could
eliminate much of this problem. We must continue to guard well our
West Gate. but once men have proven themselves let us do all we can
to maintain their interest in this great Fraternity of select men.

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The report this year must concern itself chiefly with the program of
expanded candi?ate instruction now about to be launched. This program
Is designed ~o impart to the advancing candidate knowledge relating
not only to his degrees but to the Masonic world around him.
To permit a fuller exposition of this problem and our hoped-for
solution, the report will only briefly touch on the other activities 0 £ the
Ritual Committee.
Six meetings of the Ritual Committee were held during the year,
including a full school for the Assistant Grand Lecturers, again held in
Pasadena. Other meetings coincided with Divisional Conferences as
follows:
Division VI
San Pedro Temple
March 16-1 8
Division v
Hesperian Temple
April 13-15
Division III
Santa Rosa Temple
May 4-6
Division IV
Pohona Temple
June 1-3
Divisions I & II
La ke Tahoe Temple
June 15-17
Conference schools were in each case under the direction of the
Assistant Grand Lecturer of the Division. Work in most schools was
excellent and I must particularly commend the Inspectors of Divisions I
6 II. as well as their A ssistant Grand Lecturers. for the almost flawless
exemplification o~ the work. The change over the years in these two
divisions is remarkable and their pride in the work shows knowledge
and appreciation of the lessons of Masonry.
The Inspectors and Officers Coaches of our Hawaiian Lodges received special schooling from Assistant Grand Lecturer Arthur J. Kahn,
who made the trip to Hawaii on behalf of the Grand Lecturer. Continued improvement is noted in his report of the work of the Lodges of
these districts.
Se.ction 156 C~C (1st) requires the Grand Lecturer "to supervise
and direct the Assistant Grand Lecturers and the Inspectors in the performance of their duties.... ".
Section 161 CM C requires the Inspectors (2nd) "to require any
Master of a Lodge in his District to convene his Lodge for lnspection(9th) to report the working condition of each Lodge in his District to
the Grand Lecturer on or before the first day of July of each year.( 10th) to examine the books and records of each Lodge to determine if
its manner of transacting its business conforms to our laws, and to report to the Grand Master any violation of law.
In the performance of his duties he shall be the Representative of
Grand Lodge in his District. ...".

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Our law, while delegating much power and responsibility to the
Inspector, specifically recognizes that wit hin the Lodg~ the M~ster is
the one person empowered to discharge all the executive functions of
the Lodge ( CMC 482). All other Lodge officers are under his direct
superintendence.
. . ..
This particularly applies to the Lodge Secretary whose duty 1t is to
obey the will and pleasure of the Worshipful Master".
.
This clearly points up the impracticality of an Inspector actmg also
as Lodge Secretary. E ach of these positions is one of hono~ and ~is­
tinction. Combined in the person of one man, we have the 1mposs1ble
situation of one man serving both as servant and master, as the auditor
and the audited, as the captain and the quartermaster.
I have, therefore, taken the stand that, except in emergency, and
then only for a limited time, no Inspector shall continue to function as
a Lodge Secretary. Without in any sense subordinating the ~mp~rtance
of service in either field, I do not believe that the dual capacity 1s compatible with good order and discipline.

Our answer is this-that each Lodge contains within itself the manpawer, the dedication and the interest for the task. The candidate's
coaching staff meets the challenge. In the Lodge with many candidates,
the staff is large. With few, it may consist only of one or two men but
we believe that here, with proper direction. lies our solution.
In the Insta lla tion ·service. primary responsibility for education is
vested in the Master. To him the Installing Officer says. " It is your
province to spread and communicate light and instruction to the brethren
of your Lodge". The Wardens, too, are instructed, "You are assiduously to assist the Master in the discharge of his trust, diffusing light
and imparting knowledge to all whom he shall place under your care".
It is, therefore, the plan of the Grand Lecturer to place responsibility
within the Lodge in the person of the Senior Warden who shall, under
the direction of the Master. carry out the Candidate's instr uction.
This is to be accomplished by schooling coaches in Masonic matters
through the use of the Candidates Coaches Handbook, through Lodge
or District Coaches schools, and forums utilizing, additionally, the Proceedings, California Masonic Code. the Masters H andbook and other
official material.
We propose that candidates' coaches be presented, after properly
qualifying . with a certificate of recognition , as well as a copy of the
Candidates Coaches Handbook.
The C andidates Coaches Handbook is to become available to Lodges
at cost. I t is the result of many months of study and research on the
part of many interested men. I would be derelict if appreciation were
not voiced to the many who have read proof and constructively criticized
the makeup of the articles . Particular mention must be made of the use
of articles from Northern California Research Lodge as background
material.
For the Candidate, we propose a revision of the present introductory
booklet into an expanded work to be entitled, "Information for C andidates." This booklet will contain a personal letter to be signed by the
Master, welcoming the Candidate to our door. We also propose the
division of the Monitor by Degrees and the use of it after each degree
by the Candidate and his coach in that degree.
Instructions to Lodges and to Inspectors will accompany the initial
supply of C andidates Coaches Handbooks. Orders for your present
coaching staff should be made to the supply room.
With the tools here given, we believe that the Masters, Wardens
and Coaches of our Lodges will produce, over the years, a better informed a nd more eagerly interested membership.
Respectfully submitted,

100

CANDIDATE EDUCATION

I turn now to the matter which has occupied the interest of your
Grand Lecturer for the past two years. Delays caused by circumstances
beyond my control have now been overcome and I can report to you
on a beginning at last completed.
I call it a beginning because no plan of action should be so static
that change cannot occur in it. Our truths are unchangeable but our
means of implementing them must grow with the times. I therefore ask
you to accept this as such a beginning.
The question which comes first to mind may well be, " What are we
trying to do in Candidate education?" Masters have been troubled by
the inability to relate Masonry's age-old ritual to the facts of presentday fraternal life. Men coming into our Lodges are often lost again
after a few weeks or months because they do not understand Masonry
as a present-day force in the world.
It is our job to save these men for Masonry, for Masonry's great
task of brotherhood, for Masonry's challenge of charity in a world where
the state is usurping our duties to the orphan, the widow. the aged and
the distressed. Understanding must begin with understanding ourselves,
our institution and our place in the divine plan.
We are geographically too widely scattered for visiting lectures
by our more informed brethren. In our present seminars, valuable as
they are, we touch only a relative few. We need then to touch each candidate as he comes in. We need to meet him with an informed instructor
and guide who can impart to that candidate some of his own zeal for
Masonry and his knowledge of it.
Where then do we get our faculty for this educational endeavor?

D ONALD G. CAMPBELL,

Grand Lecturer
Referred to Committee on Distribution.

Again it is our pleasure to pay homage to the Superintendents of our

Worshipful Gail H. David's report on the activities of the senior
citizens at Union City is appended to this report and will indicate a
number of new activities that our guests are now enjoying under his
supervision. His job of continually trying to please some 380 of our older

brethren and their ladies is not an easy one, and his devotion to his task

Worshipful Robert M. Henry's report on the youngsters' activities

The report of the Necrology Committee, to be g~ven later in this

On November 2, 1961. while the Northern members of the Board
were in session, word was received of the sudden passing of Most
Worshipful Lloyd E. Wilson, who until his recent retirement served as
Secretary of the Homes Board. The Board adjourned in his memory and
have since spread upon their minutes a resolution memorializing this
Brother who served us so long and so well.
On May 1, 1962, we were notified of the unfortunate pas-sing of
Most Worshipful Charles Albert Adams as a result of an accident.
Brother Adams. one of the "two Charlies" so much beloved by all the
brethren in California, was for forty-two years a member of the Masonic
Homes Board aRd since his statutory retirement had sat with the
Trustees as an Emeritus member. An appropriate resolution was sent to
his family in remembrance of this ninety-fou r year old young man whose
name had been synonomous with the H omes Board for nearly a half
century.
Several times during the past year Lodges have presented applications for admission to the Homes , particularly to Union City, and a fterward have admitted that a more thorough investigation on their part
might have disclosed the ineligibility of the applicant. In a number of
instances the applications were then withdrawn. When we send our
Social W orker out to investigate an application which a Lodge has
presented. it oftentimes involves considerable expense which could be
saved by a more thoughtful approach on the part of the Lodge. We urge
the Lodges, therefore, to give due consideration to all requests for admission.
When there is a definite need which cannot be met by admission to
either home, our program of assistance which we call Outside Relief is
available, and we handle many such cases each year. They require the
same careful scrutiny on the Lodges' part before presenting the formal
applkation.

CHILDREN's HoME AT COVINA

Whereas our report to you of June 30, 1961, indicated a total population in our Children's Home of thirty-eight (an all time low), our Superintendent's report as of the same date this year shows a total of forty.
nine, with twenty-three youngsters admitted during this fiscal year, one
of the most active periods in recent years.
His report will also show the continuing programs being carried out
by and for the children, with honors coming to the Home from many
quarters through their activities.
Four of our young men from the Home graduating from high school
have been awarded scholarship assistance for college by the Board of
Trustees as their scholastic records merited this consideration.
You will be interested to know that our increase in population in
the Covina Home was in no way due to the broadening of the rules
of admission permitted by action of the Grand Lodge in 1961. All
of our new admi·ssions to this date have qualified under our old long
standing requirements. As this report is being prepared, _howe~er, we
do have two cases under advisement, either or both of which might result in our first admissions under the new legislation.
Our continually rising per capita costs give your Board of Trustees
great concern. If cost is the sole concern, the Board will be the first to
admit that the Home can be operated on a less expensive scale. We can
eliminate some of the fine features which over many years have made our
Home one of the outstanding Masonic Homes of the country. But we,
the Trustees, honestly believe that that is not what you would have
us do. By this we do not mean that we are not watching every expenditure and exercising every prudent economy; bu~ ~e refuse.. ~nless
ordered by you to do so, to curtail the many opportumties and privileges
which add so much, not only to the pleasure, but to the broadening
experiences of these young people whose guidance to normal adulthood
has been given into our hands. We feel this is a sacred trust.
We are not unmindful of the fact that the trend in this field of social
service is toward the placing of wards in foster homes, and we receive letters from some of you occasionally suggesting this approach as
a matter of economy. We are definitely of the opinion, however, a~ter
careful consideration that we would be violating our trust by adopting
any such program.
Our Endowment Fund which is so generously augmented each year
by you, through the excellent offices of the M~sonic H_omes End?w~ent
Board, is also the recipient of many substantial legacies, o~ten m~p1red
by our Children's Home. Generous bequests also are re~e1ved, directly
by the Homes Board, earmarked in many case's for the Children s Home.
We are confident that we are keeping faith with these many donors by
the continuation of the type of personal care we are presently providing
for our youngsters.

MASONIC Ho ME AT UN ION CITY ( DEc OTO)

During the past fiscal year the population at the Decato Home at
Union City has increased to an all~time high of 382. This has caused
a waiting list for men and women, as well as couples, of as many as 18
people at one time. The many applications continuing to come caused
us to commence an expansion program which would accommodate not
only additional residents but also provide proper dormitory facilities for
male employees and couples that are employed by the Home. It was
obvious that these latter facilities for staff members would have to be
constructed first so as to make available the areas needed for a residential facility. Construction began about the fir st of July. It is expected that
these three buildings will be completed by the end of the year.
At the present time, plans are being developed for a new residential
haU which will accommodate 91 people. This will include two-room
apartments for approximately 40 couples which can be converted to
single-person use should the demand require. This building will be
trected where the old hospital building now stands. This new hall will
be dedicated to P.G.M. Charles A lbert Adams who served on the

FINANCE

Despite strict budgeting and persistent efforts on the part of the
Superintendents of both Homes and the Trustees, o~r operating c~sts
continue to rise. This is due to rising labor costs, increased medical
charges. the increase in the average age of the Deco~o resi_dents, and
the number of new applicants for admission and for outside relief.
Were it not for the valiant efforts of the Endowment Board, and
the support given to us by our brethren and frien_ds. we \:ould ha~e
to look to the Lodges for additional funds. Beside the mcrease m
expense, we are faced with a loss of revenue due to the div_ersion f~om
reserves of substantial sums to provide for the new construct10n required
to service our additional Decoto population. For each $1.000,000 converted to buildings we suffer a loss of approximately $40,000 of investment income per year.
The Trustees are reluctant to seek an increase in the per capita tax
the Lodges and are meeting the decrease in receipts and increase in
~~penses by transferring from reserves whenever possible. Obviously
this cannot continue indefinitely.
The auditor's final figures for the 1962 fiscal year disclosed a gain
on the sale of securities of $170,501.23 without which we would have
shown a deficit. This is, of course, a non-recurring item and was produced largely through the sale of securities to provide cash for our
current construction program.

discussed by the Trustees on a number of occasions. In 1919 Grand

REPORT OF THE SUPERINTENDENT COVINA HOME
To the Board of Trustees of the M asonic Homes of California:
It is with great pleasure that I present my fourteenth report as
Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina, for the
year ending June 30. 1962.
HOME MEMBERSHIP

As of June 30. 1962, the population of our Masonic Home Family
numbers forty-nine children - thirty boys and nineteen girls. During
the fiscal year of 1961-1962, twenty-three children have been admitted
to the Home. fifteen boys and eight girls. Twelve children left the Home,
three after graduating from high school. eight returning to their
families or guardians, and one entering the Navy. All of the graduates
plan to continue their education through scholarship assistance by the
Home.

families are in the Covina Home under the membership of their father.
This fall. nineteen children will be in high school, eight will be in junior
high, eighteen in grade school. one in kindergarten, and three in college.
The twenty-six families are here on applications from twenty-six
Lodges.

Movie night is a popular one, to which many of the children invite

the use of the "date Car," and use this for their special events. Transportation by car or bus is provided for other affairs such as dances,
athletic contests, Award Banquets. etc.
V1sITATIONS

Sundays continue to bring countless members of the Fraternity to
visit the Home and grounds with their families and friends. The Lodges
have responded very well in cooperating with the Home"s visitation
program. Lodge or group visitations are the third Sunday of each
month. Reservations are taken for a maximum of four hundred persons
on this visitation Sunday, and Lodges may hold their group visitation
not oftener than once every two years. Picnic accommodations are
available as well as guided tours by the children. Reservations must be
made in advance and are taken in the order of their receipt. Frequently,
Alumni come out. on the day the Lodge which sponsored them is
scheduled to visit.
HEALTH

The health of each youngster in the Home is a major concern with
every member of the staff. The Magan Clinic continues to be our supervisory health consultants, where the children are taken for regular physical examinations and any additional medical care they require. For their
eyes, they see Dr. McCormick for routine matters, Dr. Namikas, an
oculist, for more complicated conditions. Dr. Pancoska covers the routine
dental care, Dr. Teal. orthodontia. Where help by other specialists is
required, it is supplied. Every effort is expended to keep the children
in excellent physical condition.
DoMESTIC Sc1ENCE CorrAGE

On October 2, 1961, five of the older Senior Girls moved into the
Domestic Science Cottage under the supervision of Mrs. Munger
(Senior Girls' Housemother). For the remainder of the school year,
1961-1962, the girls assumed the responsibility of the usual problems
of maintaining a home. They originated their own menus, shopped for
the supplies they required through retail channels, and prepared their
own meals.

116

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

The girls were assigned a definite budget, and were required to
keep their expenses within the allotted sum. Each month they reviewed
the expenditures that would be needed, re-budgeted, and arranged
for a conference with the Superintendent to determine whether or not
the proposed monthly budget was feasible. The remainder each month
was divided among the five young ladies.
At Christmastime, on the evening of the Home Party, the girls held
an Open House to which the Trustees were invited. Many times during
the year the Domestic Science Cottage entertained guests for supper,
and served refreshments after Home functions.
All of the girls matured immeasurably as a result of this experience,
and gained practical knowledge that will be essential for them as future
homemakers.
THE ALUMNI
The real test of this or any other Home is how the children feel
about it after they graduate. Our contact with the Alumni is a living
thing-like a charged wire. One of the most important mediums in this
relationship is the annual Newsletter. The 1962 edition is the finest ever
published, and about one-half of its contents is devoted to the Alumni,
either in the form of letters they have written or in the departments
which describe the Reunions and vital statistics in their lives. Copies
of this edition were mailed to all Alumni who were contributors, those
who had sent in wedding, birth, or change of address notices, those
who visited personally, and all those who attended any of the Reunions.
In addition, a copy was mailed to each Lodge sponsoring a child in the
Home, Grand Lodge Officers, members of the Board of Trustees, Past
Grand Masters, and members of the Endowment Board.
The number of Alumni Reunions increased this year to four: the
regular Covina gathering on the second Sunday in September, the
Sacramento Picnic on the first Saturday in June, the Reunion Dinner in
San Francisco on the Saturday preceding Grand Lodge, and a Reunion
Dance in Covina on the last Saturday in October. Each one was successfull and well-attended, with all present happily anticipating the next
year's event.
Whenever the Alumni from one of the Services are in the area, they
come "Home" to Covina. They call up about advice in regard to their
problems, and in every way regard the Home as a pillar of strength in
their background. What is even more touching is the expression of
gratitude from the young people themselves.
Another expression of gratitude was received in the mail this week.
While it has been directed to my attention, it was meant for the entire
Masonic Fraternity of California. I am therefore taking the liberty of
enclosing it as part of my annual report. It expresses sentiments in
writing that I have been privileged to have heard over the years.
Covina, California
June 15, 1962

"Dea!l' Friends,
"Last night my son Bill graduated from the Charter Oak High
School. and I was a proud and happy mother as I witnessed this event
- the first big milestone in what we hope will be a successful career.
This also marks the official end for Bill as a regular member of 'the
family' at the Masonic Home.
"That is why I am taking this opportunity to put in writing, as a
matter of record, the thoughts that are in my heart. Seven years ago
(lacking three days) a little boy, eleven years old and two years past
the death of his beloved father, was placed in your care. It was a
terrific responsibility on my part to make such a decision, and I spent
many anxious hours considering the implication of two words: 'relin:iuish custody.' But the decision was made, based on what I felt would
':>e the welfare of this precious boy of tender age.
"Neither he. nor I. have ever regretted that decision for one moment.
In fact, if his father had left him a fortune it would not have been of as
much value as the love, and care, and training, Bill has had in the shelter
of the wonderful organization of Masons. I have gone to the Home
practically every Sunday for seven years, and in all that time I have
never found one word or action that a loving and watchful mother would
not approve of wholeheartedly. His care and surroundings have been
far better than I could have provided for him, and I will be g·r ateful to
my dying day for this 'legacy' from his father.
"So now as we mark the end of boyhood, and the commencement
of his manhood my hopes and prayers are that he will continue to build
on the strong foundation that has been laid, and that he will fulflll and
justify the trust, faith, and confidence so many fine people have placed
in him. And as he becomes the kind of man we can all be proud of, most
of the credit will rest with you.
"With sincerest gratitude,"
(Mrs.) Ruth G. Barraclough
May I add my expression of appreciation to the Craft and to the
Board of Trustees for the privilege of association and service with the
fine young boys and girls who indeed are a source of pride to our
"Family at Covina.''

Respectfully Submitted
ROBERT M. HENRY, Superintendent

ANNUAL REPORT OF THE
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
The Masonic Homes Endowment Board hereby submits its 30th
Annual Report for your thoughtful consideration, covering the fiscal
year ending June 30. 1962.
W1tLS AND B EQUESTS

This year. the Homes Endowment F und received $63,612.17 in bequests. representing final and lasting tribute to our great work of
"caring for our own."
Additional effort was expended this year to stimulate the making of
bequests. by the brethren, in favor of the Masonic H omes and the
M asonic Homes Endowment Fund . This Boa rd requested the Lodges
to send in the names a nd addresses of a ll attorn eys who are members of
the Craft. As a result, more than 1500 na mes have been received a nd a
booklet on " Wills and Bequests." written by M. W . Joe L. Shell,
P.G.M .. has been mailed to each such attorney. Brother Ra lph H. Head,
who was a member of the Homes Board of Trustees for many years, in
addition to many other Masonic a ssignments, arranged to have the
booklets printed at no cost to Masonry. Also. the Lodges ordered an
a dditional 50,000 small pamphlets entitled "I Give and Bequeath,"
written by brother Everett Houser, for mailing to members.
I NCOME FROM T HE ENDOWMENT FU ND

The earnings from the Endowment Fund for the past fiscal year
a mounted to $468,000.00, which amount was credited to the cost of
operation of the H omes.
I NDIVIDUAL PARTICIPATION

This year, 11 3,346 brethren made contributions to the Homes Endowment Fund, for a net increase of 3,613 contributors over a y ear ago.
The number of contributors has been steadily increasing each year but,
even so, more than 130.000 brethren made no contribution to the Endowment Fund this past year. These figures should be of concern to the
Lodges that we may join in a concerted effort to materially increase the
number of contributors, that all may share in this great M asonic
endeavor.
CASH CONTRIBUTIONS

Individual contributions through the Lodges amounted to $696,787.15, for an increase of $51 ,333.39 over the previous year. These
figures do not include bequests, memoria ls, ·special gifts, etc., which
are shown elsewhere in this Report.

Lodge

PRINTED ITEMS

This past year, again, the Lodges ordered more than 1,250,000 printed items of information about the Homes and the Endowment to mail
to the members. This year we went all-out for using pictures in the
pamphlets and other printed items, believing that next to a personal
visit to the Homes is to see the pictures of our beautiful Homes and
their facilities, and pictures of the wonderful children and elderly who
live in those Homes. All such pictures were taken at no cost to the Craft.
The Lodges ordered 203,000 of one particular picture pamphlet. They
also ordered 200,000 Grand Master's Proclamations for mailing to
members, and 300,000 contribution envelopes. All such printed items
were written, composed, caused to be printed, and distributed by and
under the supervision of the Endowment Board. Obviously, a great
amount of additional work was done by the Lodges in mailing the printed

122

123

items, together with countless thousands of letters and other items
prepared by the Lodges and sent to members. Much of the work done
by the Lodges necessarily falls upon the Lodge Secretary and all such
Secretaries are to be commended for their untiring work. along with the
work of the other Officers, Endowment Committeemen. etc.

"WHEREAS: Brother Oliphant has generously shared his allotted
time with the Chairman of the Endowment Board on numerous occasions, and

ENDOWMENT BOARD PERSO NNE L

Brother James B. Baker found it necessary to resign from the
Endowment Board during the year. because of business pressure, and
brother H ershel! E. Griffin of Santa Ana was appointed to serve the
balance of brother Baker's term on the Board.
Brother Harold R. DeTuncq moved his residence far from the
Bakersfi eld area for which he had been appointed to serve, and therefore
resigned from the Board but has not yet been replaced.
Brother Orno E . Tyler. who served the San Diego area for more
than twenty years as a Member of this Board. decided to "retire" from
his strenuous duties on the Board and Frank R. Porath of San Diego
was appointed to serve that area.
Our thanks go to these three brethren for their devoted service to
this Board, with an extra special thanks and appreciation to Brother
Tyler for his unusually long service. Their work will live on through
the years by the additional funds which were added to the Endowment
through their devoted efforts. and those funds will be earning income
for the Homes for countless years into the future.
THANKS TO HENRY OLIPHANT

Brother Henry Oliphant. who was Assistant Grand Secretary until
his retirement on June 30th of this year, has always been considered one
of our staunchest supporters of the Endowment Board during his entire
more than twenty years as Assistant Grand Secretary. He was our
"Grand Assistant" of this Board. and gave so freely of his time and
effort to assist the Board and to support the Endowment Cause at every
opportunity.
In grateful appreciation of his great service to this Board, the
Masonic H omes Endowment Board. meeting in regular session , unanimously adopted the following resolution and ordered a copy thereof
delivered to Brother Oliphant:
" WHEREAS : Brother Henry D. Oliphant. Assistant Grand Secretary. has, over the years. held quarterly meetings with Secretaries of
the Constituent Lodges in some areas (less frequently in other areas)
throughout the State. and
"WHEREAS: Brother Oliphant has always allocated a generous
amount of time at each of these meetings to the discussion of Masonic
Homes a nd Endowment matters. and

"WHEREAS: It is the unanimous feeling of this Board that a
measurable part of the success of this Board may be attributed to Brother
Oliphant's continued brotherly cooperation, not only at these meetings.
but through h is efforts in office procedures.
" THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED: That the members of the
Endowment Board, individually and collectively, express to Brother
Oliphant, through this resolution, their sincere app reciation for his un~
tiring. friendly, and courteous efforts in helping this Board year after
year. and to wish him in his coming retirement HEALTH. HAPPINESS. and ENCOURAGEMENT in his every undertaking."
OuR APPRECIATION TO ALL

The Homes Endowment Board is simply a service department.
furnishing material. ideas. suggestions and encouragement to the Lodges,
but the real credit for the success of this Board lies in the hands of the
many thousands of officers, committeemen and members who are "on
the firing line," from the Grand Master to the youngest member in the
Lodge.
Most Worshipful Guy B. Mize, Grand Master, has given his wholehearted support to this Board direct, as well as directly to the brethren
as he traveled over the Jurisdiction, giving talks to the many Masonic
meetings.
Our Grand Secretary, Edward H. Siems, P.G.M., the Assistant
Grand Secretary and their entire staff have all given complete cooperation and support. We had a most ardent supporter in Henry D. Oliphant,
while he was Assistant Grand Secretary until his retirement, and he
has volunteered his promise to do everything in his power for this
C ause, even in his retirement. Now, we are receiving equally fine
enthusiasm. cooperation and support from brother Verne W. Hendrix,
our new Assistant Grand Secretary.
Our Grand Lecturer, Brother Don G . Campbell, has always been a
most enthusiastic and helpful supporter of the Hornes Endowment and
has given much encouragement and assistance to this Board in general
and to its Chairman in particular. That spirit has permeated to the
Assistant Grand Lecturers and Inspectors, and the Inspectors are constantly passing it on to the officers of the Lodges. We cannot give too
much credit to the Grand Lecturer, the Assistant Grand Lecturers and
the Inspectors.
The final results, however, lie principally with the Masters, Secretaries
and Endowment Committees of the local Lodges because the final decision is left to them to determine how much of our Endowment publicity

124

items are to be sent to the members; the amount of verbal and bulletin
publicity; and how many letters to members regarding Endowment contributions are to be sent to members. As an example of the tremendous
amount of work involved, this year the Lodges ordered from this Board
and sent to members more than I% million printed items of information about the Homes and the Endowment plus countless thousands of
letters and other items composed and prepared by the local Lodges and
sent to members: and approximately 113,000 contributions were received
by the Lodges from their members and a like amount of individual receipts prepared and sent to the contributors. Much of this work is done
by the Lodge Secretaries, and to them we give our special praise.
All of the above mentioned brethren are both workers and givers,
and we have reason to believe that the workers are also the most liberal
givers, on average. However, our many thanks also go to those who are
givers only, many of whom go far beyond the "token" contribution and
make substantial gifts year after year. To all workers and contributors,
therefore, we express our sincere gratitude.
THE COMING YEAR

The number of elderly residents at our Home for the Aged is at an
all-time high and filled to capacity. with a considerable waiting list.
Construction will soon start on an additional building to house the increased number of residents. No Endowment Funds will be used in the
construction, of course. Most of the cost of construction will come from
the special fund built up from bequests but the income-producing securities now held in those funds must be liquidated to pay the cost of construction which will result in a loss of income from that source. The
cost of operating the Homes is constantly increasing and will increase
all the more as the number of residents increases. They must be cared
for, and we pride ourselves that "Masonry Takes Care of Its· Own."
For the coming year, then, we might adopt some such slogan as "The
need is greater. Work harder and give more."
In conclusion, we humbly request an appropriation of $16,000.00 as
our budget for the coming year.
Respectfully submitted,
THE MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

of Relief.

ways and means of improving this situation. It has completed a survey
and study of all Lodges within the jurisdiction of Grand Lodge. Maps
depicting member and non-membe r Lodges of Boards of Relief have
been prepared and services rendered by our Boards for these Lodges
have been analyzed. As a remedial measure. in order that our Brethren

throughout th~ Junsdtet1on that they will be encouraged to join existing

I~ will off~r .the average Mason, "the sideliner," an opportunity to actively participate and practice Masonry in its various facets, for where,
my Brethren , can the tangible evidence of Masonry practiced out of
the Lodge be s.o evident.as in a Boa rd of Relief. It is regrettable that space
~oes not permit the setting forth of specific instances of the heart rendering examples of blessed relief.
The unprecedent ed population growth in California, with its accompanied proportion of sojourning Brethren, together with the much
~ublicized recession throughout the country have caused considerabl e
mcrea.sed activities in our Boards of Relief and Employmen t Bureaus.
Notw1thstan.ding this additional work that has been thrust upon them.
they have discharged their duties promptly and without discord. It is
the uns~l~sh labors o.f t~ese dedicated Masons, who give so generously

REIMBURSEMEN TS TO MASONIC BOARDS OP RELIEF

It has long been the policy of this Grand Lodge that no worthy
Brother sojourning in our Jurisdiction, or his immediate family. shall
suffer for the necessities of life, or have other than a decent burial upon
their demise, regardless of the willingness or ability of the Brother's own
Lodge to reimburse us. Our Grand Lodge undertakes to reimburse any
Board of Relief for such unrecoverable advances. During the past Masonic Year our Boards of Relief advanced more than $36,941.00 to sojourners and their dependents. All such advances were carefully scrutinized by one of our Executive Secretaries and efforts were made to obtain
reimbursement from the sojourner's home Lodge. It is gratifying to
report that out of $36,941.37 advanced during the year, only $50.00
was not repaid, in accordance with the following request to Grand Lodge
for reimbursement :
REIMBURSEMEN T TO THE SAN FRANCISCO BOARD OF RELIEF

The San Francisco Board of Relief has requested reimbursement in
the amount of $50.00. This matter, which has continued over many years,
involves a very worthy Brother from Scotland and his wife for whom
the Grand Lodge of Scotland made some provision but not sufficient for
their essential needs. The Brother is now deceased. The widow has expressed her sincere gratitude to our Grand Lodge and believes she can
now adjust her mode of living so that further assistance will no longer
be necessary.

REPORT OF TRUSTEES,
CALIFORNIA MASONIC MEMORIAL TEMPLE

A thorough examination of the existing sound system revealed that
improvements should be made to it. Accordingly, corrective measures
were taken involving new vertical column speakers back of the stage;
new ceiling speakers in selected locations; the elimination of certain
speakers in various locations; and the construction of an alternate control board remote from the Master Control Station.
The above work has been accomplished, and the results have been
most gratifying. Further operational adjustments can now. readily be
made to accommodate the diversified list of demands as required by our
tenants.
The Board has already received favorable reaction and comment
concerning these improvements, and feels certain that there will be an
ever-increasing demand for our facilities by those in the entertainm~nt
field. and by organizations for convention purposes. The Frate~mty
itself benefits public-relations wise from such use. because of the national
publicity given when our auditorium is used by such organi~ations as t~e
American Bar Association, or by such performers as Mau:1c~ Chevalier
or the Limeliters. The Boar<l feels certain that revenues will mcrea~e by
such use. and of course the more the auditorium is used, the larger will be
our revenue from the operation of the garage, which is rented on a percentage basis.
It is gratifying to note that the number of visitors to the Temple is
increasing yearly-due, in part, to the policy adopted by the Board of
Trustees last year in having the Temple open for inspection on Saturdays
and Sundays.
Due to the constant vigilance of Brother Alvin A. Horwege, Building Manager. and Harry Haines, his assistan~. a~d to .the co~perati?n
of their able staff. the building has been mamtamed m keeping with
the highest standards. It has been gratifying to know that this has been
accomplished at a minimum expense.
In keeping with the Board's previous decisions to publish a supplement to the Open Book. the names of subsequent donors (those not
having contributed prior to the original publication) are being carefully segrega ted-anticipating this second listing of names. We now
have several thousand names to be added. Any member wishing to be
included as a "Builder of the Temple" has time in which to make his
contribution, and assure his name being listed in the Open Book.
As of September I, 1962, we have 531 Lodges on the Merit Roll, and
84 "HONOR DISTRICTS." Space does not permit us to here list all
Me11it Roll Lodges, but we do salute and list the "HONOR DISTRICTS."

This is the Eighth Annual Report issued by the Board of Trustees
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
The Board of Trustees met following the close of the 1961 Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge, as is required by the By-Laws, for
the purpose of organization. The election of Brother Ira W. Coburn,
Deputy Grand Master; Brother Elmer W. Heald, Senior Grand Warden; and Brother Theodore Meriam, Junior Grand Warden, was formally reported to the Board, and on motion duly made, seconded and
carried, they were elected members of the Board of Trustees. Appointed
to the Board by the Grand Master was Brother Jay A. Robinson. The
Board elected the following officers: Ira W. Coburn, President; Frank
Harwell, Jr., Vice President; Paul A. Pflueger, Treasurer; and Edward
H. Siems, Secretary. As part of this report, we submit the reports of
Lybrand, Ross Brothers & Montgomery, Certified Public Accountants,
and Brother Alvin A. Horwege, Building Manager.
During this Masonic year, the members of the Board of Trustees
have worked to a great extent as operative Masons, authorizing such
improvements to our Temple as were necessary to make it the most
desirable place in the Bay Area for concert performances and convention purposes.
Even before this Masonic year began, certain recommendations had
been made to the Board to make the auditorium more acceptable for
public use. and during the present year, the following work was actually
accomplished:
1. Raising of the stage 3' 1Yi" from floor level. (The stage can be
disassembled and stored.)
2. Installation of portable backdrops and wings.
3. Installation of spotlights in the ba lcony- located in two permanently designed enclosures.
4. Installation of a sound-proof. air-conditioned projection and
spotlight booth suspended from the rear of the balcony.
5. Installation of attractive ticket booths in the main lobby.
6. Upon recommendation of Dr. Vern Knudsen of the University
of California in Los Angeles, one of the recognized authorities on acoustics, and upon the recommendation of H. M. Engle, Structural Engineer,
the following work was completed:
In order to further control sound reflection, the wall surface's at
the rear of the auditorium were replaced by surfaces of perforated hardboard and plywood, and the upper portion of the walls was laid out with
splayed panels, the fada of the balcony was rounded to provide further
deJlection.

To the Trustees of California Masonic Memorial Temple:
Brethren:
It is with much pleasure that I submit this, my fourth and final report as Manager of the Californ ia Masonic Memoria l Temple.
Many changes and adjustme nts have occurred in the T emple operations since we opened our doors in April, 1958. As a result of our experience s, patterns of policy and procedur e have develope d, which I
believe will lead to successfu l future growth. and to the continua nce
of an atmosph ere of dignity and high regard in the community.
In the beginnin g. it was anticipat ed that the major source of revenue
would come from the exhibit area for conventi on usage, and, in fact,
during each of the first two years, ten conventions were handled. Early
in the 1960-61 Masonic year, however , the Board of T rus tees, noting
the sharp decline in con vention occupanc y because of additional fac·ilities provided in neighbor ing hotels, realized that the auditorium should
be placed in a better position to attract the concert field.
The auditoriu m had been originall y designed for fraternal use, and
included a number of physical features consider ed somewha t unusual
by the general entertain ment business. As reported last year by the
Board of Trustees , the stage was redesign ed, and action was taken to
make certain practical changes more in keeping with suggestio ns made
by the concert .trade. In addition , acoustica l treatmen ts ha ve been completed ·in the auditorium, and two ticket booths have been added in the
main foyer. Work is still continuin g on the sound sys tem, and adjustments are being made to fit the different acoustica l requirem ents.
All of these changes have met with enthusia stic response from entertainm ent manager s, and the use of the auditorium for concert purposes has materially increased . This is demonst rated by the fact that
during the year 1961-62, the auditoriu m's usa ge for outside activities
increased 42 per cent-64 days being utilized in such occupancy. The
exhibit hall, on the other hand, was used by only one conventi on, and
miscellaneous usages accounte d for another 22 days-a decrease of 10
days from last year. The increase in the auditorium rental, however ,
has resulted in an over-all boost in gross revenue above last year's total
intake. The Fall of 1962 and the Spring of 1963 will bring to our auditorium one of the finest concert seasons since the opening of the T emple.
One factor related to the stepped- up use of the auditorium is the
increased use of the garage in handling the attending crowds. As a
consequence, the annual garage revenue has now increased to well over
$50,000 per year.
Our Visitors' Register points up the interest of not only the Fra-

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ternity. but the general public as well in our Temple. It includes the
names of guests from all corners of the earth. and 4,820 visitors have
been recorded during the past year. (Large numbers failed to register.)
In making this, my last report after nearly five years as Building
Manager. may I express both to the Board of Trustees, and to the
others with whom I have worked, the pleasure in, and the appreciation
for. the challenge which has been mine. I am grateful. too, for their
advice and support in handling the numerous interesting problems with
which we have been confronted. I also here extend to my friends
throughout the State, whom it has been my privilege and pleasure to
have known during the almost 19 years of association with the Grand
Lodge F. & A. M. of California, my assurance that memories of our
close association will be cherished throughout the rest of my life.

Your Committee is happy to report that all Lodges whose Proceedings were not approved at the 1961 Annual Communication of Grand
Lodge have since complied with the law in all respects and their action
is now approved.
We suggest that applications for changes of by-laws by constituent
Lodges be presented in sufficient copies that one copy thereof can be
referred to the Committee on By-Laws at the time of such application
for approval.
Your Committee further suggests that the constituent Lodges be
required to use the certification form in Section 366 C.M.C., which
forms are available at the Grand Secretary's office, when applying
for approval of an amendment to their by-laws.
An additional suggestion of your Committee is that a certi.Bcate
form, similar in purpose to that in Section 366 C.M.C., be prepared
for use of constituent Lodges asking approval of resolutions for removal
or change of meeting place, pursuant to Sections 372 or 373 C.M.C.,
and that this form clearly indicate which of the two sections of the Code
is involved. Such a certificate form, prepared by the Grand Secretary's
office, would be of great assistance to the constituent Lodges.
We find that Section 343 C.M.C. has been variously interpreted.
We, therefore, suggest that it be clarified for the benefit of the constitu~
ent Lodges.
The Committee wishes to express its sincere appreciation to the
overwhelming majority of Lodges who have carefully followed the

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History presents the following report:
The members of the Committee unanimously express their appreciation to the Grand Lodge and especially to our Grand Master, Brother
Guy B. Mize, for the privilege of serving. We have found the Grand
Master to be friendly. cooperative, sympathetic and understanding and
it has been an enjoyable experience to serve under him this year.
ITEM 1. In the original, first Proceedings of this Grand Lodge. the
Grand Secretary is listed in rank above the Grand Treasurer. In the
reprint of these Proceedings, in 1858. the ranking is reversed and these
Officers rank as they do today. There is no explanation for this reversal.
Brother Stanley Gustavson. of this Committee. did some research and
found that the original ra nking of these two Officers was intentional
and was no mistake. At the time. 1850, the Grand Lodge of the District
of Columbia, one of our three original Grand Lodges, ranked their Secretary above the Treasurer. as was true of their constituent Lodge.
California No. 13, now our California No. 1, and this ranking continued for several years a fter 1850. When or why the change was made
to the present order of ranking we do not know as the Proceedings a re
silent on this point. All the other grand jurisdictions. in 1850, ranked
their Officers as we now do. We report on this merely as a matter of
historical interest. because the transposition has been bafflling.
ITEM 2. During 1961, there existed a special Grand Lodge Committee on Historical Monuments which this year Grand M aster Mize
combined with the History Committee a nd which reported at the last
Grand Lodge session as follows, in part: " ..• It is ... the recommenda-

\

159

tion of this Committee that the Grand Lodge offer its assistance in furnishing designs for the installation of fire proof safes or vaults (for the
preservation of valuable. historical rec~rds) to be .constructed by the
members of the Lodges, of sufficient size to contam these records •. It
as clearly indicated to your Committee that these Lodges are askmg
~r technical advice and are not soliciting financial a id from Grand
Lodge."
The History Committee has stood ready at all times to give all
possible assistance to the Lodges when called upon to do so and not
ne call has been neglected nor one request turned down but we must
0
dvise that we have not had a single call for technical advice such as
:as proposed in the Report of the Masonic Mon~ments Committee. In
the balance of their report, they pointed out that m many Lodges valuable records were unprotected and in danger of loss by fire: lndee.d, the
records of the History Committee amplify and substantiate this observation. It is presumed that this regrettable condition still persists. If
your Lodge wishes technical advice on the preservation of records. we
suggest that you solicit assistance throug~ the Grand Secretary who
will refer your inquiry to the proper committee.
ITEM 3. We conceive it to be the primary function of a History
Committee to write history as it is made. on the spot. at the time'. As .a
matter of routine work, we are maintaining a running file on all historical occasions as they occur. One or more members of the Committee
has been in attendance on all history-making events. They have been
written up as a report on the event and filed in the Committee's files
for future reference.
A secondary function of the History Committee, as we see it, is to
study the history of our past in order to learn it; to uncover any mist~~es
in our historical archives and to correct them to the best of our ability
so fut ure historians may not make or copy the same errors. W~ co~~
ceive it to be our obligation to teach the Craft about our California
historical heritage so they. too. may s hare with pride the progress that
Freemasonry has made since coming to this Stat~. This .we h.ave a~­
tempted to do through speakers, speaking on histor1~al sub1ect~ m California Masonry; in the publication of papers on history subiects, and
in the showing of colored, illustrated slides. As in the past. several
committee members have appeared a t various places throughout the
jurisdiction on b ehalf of two of these phases of hi7,tory education . The
colored slide-lecture of pioneer Lodges and people . SOME CAME BY
LAND AND SOME CAME BY SEA." is still being requested by
Lodges and Masonic Districts in Northern and Southern California and
we have filled all such requests.
Two new illustrated lectures are in preparation and will shortly he
ready for release. They are titled, "THE TRAGEDY OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIPORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OP THB

CRABB EXPED ITION ," and "PION EER FREEM ASON RY IN
SOUT HERN CALIF ORNIA ." Work on "The Crabb Expedit ion,"
is nearly complete. Not so advance d is "Pionee r Masonr y in Souther n
Califor nia," principally because we had to await completion of the old
Lodge Hall of Los Angele s No. 42, which was dedicated on August
28th last. These two lectures will be made available to the Lodges on
a loan basis. That is, upon application a Lodge or Masoni c District
may receive the pictures through the mail. A manuscript will accompany
the slides which can be read as the slides are shown. In this case the
Lodges need a reader, a projectionist and a suitable screen and projector.
Also, these two lectures will be given with a lecturer, upon application.
He will bring his own equipment and will lecture as the pictures are
shown. A bulletin to all the Lodges will shortly be sent out describing
how these lectures may be obtained.
The tragedy of the Crabb expedition occurred in 1857 at Caborc a,
a small village about one hundre d miles south of the Arizona border in
the State of Sonora, Mexico. There were seventy -eight members in the
expedition, most of whom were outstan ding and well known citizens of
Northe rn Califor nia communities. as well as Officers and members of
Masoni c Lodges in Californ ia and elsewhere. In a six-day armed encounter with units of the Mexica n army, they were forced to surrend er
to the Mexica ns on April 6, 1857, and on the next morning, April 7th,
they were shockingly killed to a man. Maniy of our Lodges and people
of the towns were horrified. The incident took on nationa l importance
through the intervention of the State Departm ent at Washin gton. Because the expedition was immediately labelled "a filibustering affair,"
which it was not, it was spoken of in hushed tones and in the Grand
Lodge Communication of May, 1857, no mention was made at all except
veiled allusions by the Grand Master, William Henry Howard , in his
address to the Grand Lodge. After a time the matter died down altogether and was forgotten. Several Lodges, on learning of the death of
one of their members at Caborc a, spread the death notice on the minutes
and in at least one instance appoint ed a committee to investigate the
tragedy . Throug h two of these minutes, at Martine z and Benecia, the
Grand Lodge Committee on Masoni c History learned of the affair in
1948, while prepari ng material for "l 00 Years of Freema sonry in California." During the past fourteen years, the Committee has research ed
the incident, including a visit to Caborc a and the extensive taking of
pictures of landma rks about the town that prominently figured in the
affair. It is these pictures, supplem ented by some local views, which
comprise our lecture which tells the true and complete story of the entire
incident, including its shocking aspects. Up to the present, the expenses
incurred in the development of this story have been home by the individual Committee members, at no cost to the Grand Lodge.

161

ITEM 4. The historical records of the Grand Lodge consist almost
entirely of the Proceedings. These volumes contain all the transactions
of the Grand Lodge proper to be written as well as irreplacable statistical material. In 1857, when it was clearly apparen t to the then Grand
Secreta ry, Brother Alex Abell, that an insufficient number of copies of
Proceed ings were being printed each year, he request ed and received
permission of the Grand Lodge to i'eprint the first seven years, at his
own expense, and by 1858 the invento ry of Proceed ings was ample for
foreseeable generat ions to come. Each year, the Grand Secreta ry carefully estimates future needs and orders enough copies to meet the
estimate. Even so, due to unforeseen demand s and other factors, the
number of copies made has not always been sufficient. Your Committee
regi'ets to report that a situation confron ts us today which, to historians
and, we believe, to the Grand Officers, is most alarming. For thirteen
of the years, out of the past 111 years, there are no extra copies in
reserve at all, the only two copies in our hands being in the Grand
Secreta ry's and the Grand Lodge Library collections. Volume s for several other years are in extremely short supply. To meet the needs of
future generat ions there ought to be at least one hundre d copies of
each year's Proceed ings in our inventory. To reprint just these thirteen
volumes alone, as was done in 1857, it is estimat ed the cost today would
be close to fifteen thousan d dollars. Based on considerable observation,
this Committee feels that old Proceed ings in the hands of the Lodges
find very little use. Many volumes are buried away in closets and attics.
With the loan and mail service now in effect by the Grand Lodge
Library, any student of Masonr y or Officer of a Lodge, can borrow
books from the library merely for the asking and with a sufficient number of Proceed ings on hand there is no reason why they, too, could not
be borrow ed. In order to avoid the cost of reprinting, this Committee
recommends that each constitu ent Lodge make a donation of its collection of Proceed ings to the Grand Lodge of California. It is well known
that hundred s of copies of P.roceedings in the Lodges have been destroyed by Bre, by rodents, and lost by forgetful borrowers. It is an
absolut e certaint y that they would be well protecte d in this building
. and preserv ed for student s and researchers. We suggest that Masters
and Senior Warde ns present make a note of this recommendation and
bring the suggest ed donatio n of these badly needed records before your
Lodge for appropr iate action.
It has been a custom that the incoming Grand Master be furnished
with a complete set of Proceed ings for his own persona l use, to be returned to the Grand Lodge upon his death. Due to lack of underst anding
of the heirs, they have not always been returne d and in some cases are
disposed of with the Past Grand Master 's library collection, thus being
lost to the Grand Lodge. It is our recommendation that in future all

162

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

copies of Proceedings loaned out by the Grand Lodge be stamped in
several places, in indelible ink, "Property of the Grand Lodge of Califorina, F. & A. M .. San Francisco, California."
ITEM 5. A matter requiring some negotiations, and which we are
extremely happy to report here today, was the acquisition by gift of
113 pieces of Lodge papers comprising all that remains of the records
of old Violet Lodge No. 138, formerly located at Spanish Flat, California. Violet Lodge was dispensated in 1859 and surrendered its
charter in October, 1879. These papers were presented to the Grand
Lodge as a gift by Brother E. 0. Sawyer, Jr., (retired Lieutenant Colonel U.S.A.) of Hollywood, California. A member of the Committee
first found the papers in a book store, in San Francisco, where they were
for sale. He prevailed upon the book dealer to furnish the name of the
owner of the papers. Negotiations with Brother Sawyer resulted in him
donating the papers to the Grand Lodge. They were appraised to a
value of $750 and since the donation actually was made to the Masonic
Homes of California, a charitable organization, it was income tax deductible in that amount by the donor. However, the value of the papers
lies in their rarity as well as in their historical value as these are the
only papers of a gold rush Lodge. or any Lodge. becoming extinct prior
to the fire and earthquake of 1906, in possession of the Grand Lodge.
All similar records , material. libraries, etc .. were destroyed by the fire
which followed the earthquake. The papers of Violet Lodge reveal a
typical. true story of life in a gold camp Masonic Lodge. The name.
"Violet," has perplexed the Committee as it has no known Masonic
connotation and the papers fail to reveal why or how this particular
name came to be chosen. It remains open only to surmise and conjecture
which, your Committee hopes, was pleasant in the contemplation to the
members of Violet Lodge.
Conclusion. The Committee wishes to report that it was not found
necessary to spend the entire two thousand dollars appropriation which
was budgeted for our use this past year and about twelve hundred dollars
was turned back to the general fund of the Grand Lodge on July 1,
last. In consequence, we are reducing our request for funds this year
and ask that the sum of $1200 be appropriated for our use during the
coming Masonic Year and hereby request this amount.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
We are pleased to repo rt that a lease on the second floor Lodge
Room of the restored Old Masonic Hall has been executed between
Grand Lodge and the State of California, as owner, and the City of
Los Angeles, as operator, of Pueblo de Los Angeles State H istorical
Monument. A copy of the lease is on file in the Grand Lodge office. The
lease is similar in general terms to that which exists between Grand
Lodge and the State on the Masonic Temple at C olumbia.
.
On August 25, last, Grand Lodge, under the direction of Most Worshipful Guy B. Mize, Grand Master, met on the site at 416 N~rth .M ain
Street. In the presence of a large gathering of Masons and their friends,
together with City and State officials, the Grand Master laid a cornerstone and dedicated a plaque in the restored Lodge Room.
With the execution of the lease and the completion of the ceremonies
by Grand Lodge, we had anticipated that we could ask that this Committee be discharged. However. certain minor but necessary wor~ on
the building remains to be done and the members of your ~om m1ttee
feel that we should continue to cooperate with the Construction Supervisor for the State until the restoration of the Hall is fully and finally
completed.
Therefore, we recommend the continuation of this Special Committee for another y~ar.
Under the terms of the lease we are required to pay for all utilities
and provide janitorial service. It is anticipated that the Lodge Room
will be rented to Lodges for special occasions at a rental figure to be
determined. The Committee recommends an appropriation of $1,000.00
as an operating expense fund. against which will be credited all receipts
from rentals.
The other members of this Committee again wish to express their
appreciation to Matthew M. Codon, Past Master of Los Angeles Lodge
No. 42, who has been a member of the Committee from its inception.
Brother Codon has been untiring in his work with S tate and City officials
and the successful completion of our participation in this project has
been due largely to his elf orts.
Respectfully submitted,

A considerable portion of your Committee's activities are in connection with appendant bodies seeking support of the public in sales
of tickets to shows, carnivals, dinners, bazaars, rummage sales, etc. One
organization, in particular, offended when several of its units advertised
affairs at which liquor would be served. Attention of the offending groups
was immediately called to our laws, rules and regulations, and assurances
were received that there would be no further violations.
A cemetery in this State, established some ninety years ago by a
Masonic Lodge for Masons, over the years has gradually lost its Masonic
characteristics and for some years has been open for burials to all Caucasians despite the fact that it still carries the word "Masonic" in its
corporate title. Our Grand Master has been in correspondence with the
responsible parties to have the word " Masonic" removed from its title.
Masonry, either from ignorance, indifference, or inadvertance on
the part of certain individuals who should know better, has a difficult
time to keep its name free from the taint of commercialism. Unceasing
vigilance is necessary if we are ever to blot out this stain.
Your Committee desires to express its sincere thanks and apprecia~
tion to those Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors and other members of
the Craft who were so generous of their time and were helpful when
called on for assistance. To our Grand Master, Most Worshipful G uy
Mize, our special thanks and appreciation for his forbearing advice,
kindly counsel and assistance. He has been most helpful. Your Committee feels highly honored and pleased to have had the honor to have
worked and served with him.
Respectfully submitted.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee concludes its twelfth year of activity,
and herewith renders its report for the twelve months ending June 30,
1962. Each year's report gives a certain amount of historical background
and basic information, which should be helpful to those attending Grand
Lodge for the first time.
The Prudent Man Rule in modified form was adopted by Grand
Lodge at its 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges a Prudent
Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
was formed for the purpose of administering the investable funds of
Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes of California, and the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund. The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent Lodges, but Grand Lodge makes the services
of its investment advisor available to the Lodges. Many Lodges are now
making use of this service, as evidenced by the fact that a total of 276
Lodges have made inquiry regarding the service. Under recent date
Moody's Investors Service reported as follows:
"We have files on a total of 276 Lodges and of this number we
consider 163 to be active, the balance inactive. * * The so-called inactive
Lodges are those w here we have received no response from the Lodge
itself to our periodic requests for a statement of investments and available cash. In these cases we have made certain to write to the Lodge
secretary now in office before removing the name of the Lodge from the
active list.
"Lodges making initial inquiry of us during the past year amounted
to nine.
.. At the time of our last interim report on May 14, 1962. the approximate total market value of the portfolios of the active Lodges stood at
$7,920.000. This compares with a figure of $6,470,000 one year earlier.
"Activity has been fairly constant during the year with some 278
requests from the Lodges for portfolio reviews, 46 telephonic consultations, nine personal visits to our office, plus some 346 written communications."
The Investment Committee hopes that the Lodges are making full
use of this valuable service.
The Investment Committee is composed of the Grand Treasurer, the
Assistant Grand Treasurer . the Chairman of the Finance Committee. the
President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees or a Trustee of that
Board designated by him, and the Chairman of the Masonic Homes
