Endowment Fund contributions made throu gh the Lodges amounted
to $696,787.15 for the year ended June 30, 1962. Other gifts and bequests for the Masonic Homes amounted to $298,612.00. The Masonic
H omes Board of Trustees determines how these gifts and bequests are
allocated-these alloca tions a r e made in accordance with specific bequests, or in the absence of such, at the direction of the Trustees. The
Endowmen t Fund contributions remain in that Fund, and only the income is used.
The Investment Committee was informed a t the February , 1962,
meeting that two construction projects were to b e undertaken immediately at the Home for Aged at Union City ( Decoto), at a cost of approximately $1.250,000. While the money would not be needed for about
a year, nevertheless the Committee concluded to make funds available
as soon as possible, which was done. The major amount was invested in
one year bank certificates of deposit. Inasmuch as bank savings now earn
interest from date of deposit to date of withdrawal. this too has come in
good stea d for readily available funds.
May we also call attention to the fact that the total portfolio has
increased since November, 1950. from $6,124,471 to $15,909,690, or
about 159.77 %. and a t the same time the income has increased from
$120.598 to $639,757, or 430.49%. As mentioned above, $1,215,000 was
withdrawn for the new Decoto hospital in the year ending June 30, 1960,
and $128,000 was withdrawn in the year ending June 30, 1962, to fund
the unpaid balance of the Grand ·L odge Pension Fund.
May it also be mentioned that in spite of some decline in prices and
one Grand Lodge withdrawal. investment ·i ncome as of June 30, 1962,
is greater than the preceding year-$639, 757 in 1962 vs. $605,814
in 1961.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
LODGE FINANCING
To the Most W orshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
The Committee on Lodge Financing respectfully submits its report
for the past year. A review of the activities of the Committee during this
period indicates definite progress in the construction, maintenance and
operation of Masonic Temple properties. This excellent progress is reflected in the annual financial s tatements >Submitted by the Masonic
Temple associations relative to their financial transactions a nd other
matters relating to Masonic T emple construction and operation. During
the past year 255 Temple associations and Lodges have submitted financial statements, pursuant to the requirements of Section 200 of the
Masonic Code. These financial statements reveal tha t each year more
and more interest is being taken in the proper efficient business and
financial affairs of Masonic Lodges, and as a result of this interest there
is a constant diminishing of the number of Lodges and Temple associations operating at a loss, while the vast majority of Lodges are now
indicating a n income in excess of expenditures in their operations. This
is resulting in the establishment of necessary cash reserves and. more
importantly , the s etting up of actual cash depreciation accounts that will
be so beneficial to the Lodges in the future. The financial reports definitely indicate the effectiveness of Temple associations in conducting
the financial affairs of the Lodges.
During the past year the Committee on Lodge Financing has received, processed and approved 67 applications for consent to purchase
property, start construction , make capital im provements upon existing
properties and other matter's in connection w ith the operation of their
Temple facilities. The Committee granted consent to 10 requests to
trans fer funds from Lodges to Temple associations for the purpose of
building, improving and maintaining their properties; 15 requests to
purchase property for the construction of their own Masonic Temples;
l 0 requests to form non-profit Temple associations; 14 requests to make
capital improvements and 10 requests to start construction on their new
Masonic homes. In all, including miscellaneous items. Committee action
was required on approximately 100 transactions.
The Committee wishes to commend the various Lodges and Temple
associations for their interest and their full cooperation in all matters
relating to the business affairs of their facilites. Also. to commend the
brethren for their earnest endeavor to fully comply with the requirements
of the Internal Revenue Service and the Franchise Tax Board in ma tters
relating to their tax status. The Temple corporations are making the
required amendments to their Articles of Incorporation , if necessary. in
order to definitely establish and maintain their tax exempt status for
non-profit ('.Orporations.

174

175

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRANO LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

The Committee wishes to direct the attention of the Lodges and
Temple associations to the importance of having ample insurance coverage on their facilities. It has been discovered in some instances that the
item of workmen's compensatio n (required by State Law ) is not included in insurance schedules. Such insurance is most important to protect anyone engaged in the construction and maintenance of the Temple
and its lack might well prove to be very costly and embarrassin g. It is
the suggestion of this Committee that the insurance structure be reviewed from time to time to determine that it is in proper order.
The Grand Lodge presently has implemente d a group insurance
program for fire coverage on Masonic Temples. In most instances it
provides broader coverage at less premium cost. It is strictly a voluntary
program made available to Temple managemen t and/ or Lodges. It was
submitted in answer to many inquiries on the subject.
The volume of corresponde nce has been, as usual. extremely heavy
and the Committee has made innumerable visits to Lodges and Temple
associations at their request to discuss, advise and consult with them
relating to problems confronted in their Temple financial programs.
These meetings have been most fruitful and in all instances solutions
to the problems have been satisfactoril y consummate d. The Committee
intends to continue meeting with the brethren and assisting whenever
called upon in order to aid them in any manner possible regarding their
Temple affairs.
The yearly activities of the Committee are set forth in detail on the
following pages of this repor t and will be included in the published
proceedings .

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
What our young people learn to believe in, and admire today, will
determine the kind of world in which they and we will live tomorrow.
It is the responsibility of this generation to guide the educatonal processes which will make tomorrow's world. If we as Masons wish tomorrow to have a climate in which Freemasonry will thrive, we must
exert constant vigilance in regard to the academic and ethical realm in
which our young people spend half their waking hours for about twelve
of their most formative years.
We are sure this, as well as the great shortage of teachers, was in
the mind of the late Charles Albert Adams when he conceived and
brought into being Public Schools Week, under the auspices of this
Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. The perpetuation of Public Schools
Week for forty-three years, and its almost universal spread into other

183

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

states, cannot be attributed to a great need on the part of the American
people to celebrate another week, or the publicising of this Grand Lodge
or Freemasonry in general. It can only be because such an observance
is of assistance in the creation, generation or increase of interest in our
Public Schools by our own members, and by Mr. and Mrs. John Q.
Public which is, of course, our ultimate aim.
Any activity which promotes this interest. whether it be held during
P .S.W. or at some other time, complies with the spirit of our undertaking
and is to be commended. Outstanding in this category are Public School
dedicatory and corners tone ceremonies which local Lodges have arranged for Grand Lodge to perform. Details of these are omitted here
as they will certainly be reported in ample form by the Grand Master.
From the report system, which was used this past year, much interesting information has been obtained, not the least of which indicates that
at least 500 Lodges had some sort of participation during P.S.W. (There
mus t be many more, but at the date of this writing this is the report
return.)
A great majority availed themselves of the posters which were produced and sold by "The Coordinating Council for Public Schools
Week." This Council has no direct connection with the Grand Lodge
and works with both Masons and non-Masons alike, but its leadership
is all Masonic and they have furnished this Committee with a financial
statement of their activities over the past two years. This statement
reflects that profits made in the first year were totally expended in additional services during the second year. No monies whatsoever have been
spent for personal services, and the responsible members of the Council
have assured your committee that these policies will continue in the
future. It is our understanding that this service will again be offered
to the Lodges next spring, and that there will be offered a p ackage deal
which will include both posters and window stickers.
We received a large number of comments (actually compla ints)
concerning the 1962 dates. The dates originally announced w ere for
April 23 to 27. Immedia tely following the 1961 observance, school people began to express objections to the dates as announced , beca use there
would be no time whatsoever following Easter V acation in which to
make preparations. In consequence of this, the change was made for
their benefit, but it worked a severe hardship on many Lodges.
Some of the projects as reported should be of interest particularly
to the Senior W a rdens present. These observances range from virtually
no cost to those which require per capita expense which is sizable.
The time to sta rt planning is immediately upon your return from
Grand Lodge, or before, so we trust that the Senior Wardens who do
not already have plans under way hear something which will strike
a spark.

The following is only a sampling of some of the activities reported.
This list could easily be five times as long:
Arrange bus tour of school facilities for Lodge members and public.
Bus tour of community for new teachers.
Speakers before Service Club meetings.
Radio and TV announcements and programs.
Post Office and postal meter cancellations.
Honor Educators.
Entertain School Board members.
De Malay members as speakers.
Participate in career counciling.
Posters-get junior organizations to distribute.
Group organizations, particularly in metropolitan areas, appear to be
the most successful method of getting the job done. The San Francisco
Masters and Wardens Association activity. under the able chairmanship of Raymond H. Levy, is an outstanding example among many.
Your Committee has been assured by the Grand Lecturer that in the
future it will have even greater cooperation from the lnspectoral Corps.
This could lead to additional cooperative efforts which would be of
benefit in many instances. It is the recommendation of this Committee
that its membership be increased to fifteen at this Communication. The
added members, strategically located, would allow closer cooperation
with the Inspectors, and thus give better overall coverage in assisting
the Lodges and Districts.
Within the 'past sixty days your Committee has been charged with
the responsibility of implementing a program which is described in the
following letter on the letterhead of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted M asons of the Philippines :

"The Grand Master

Most Worshipful Sir and Brother:
You may have heard of the tremendous need in the Philippine public
schools for textbooks of all kinds. The Japanese sys tematically destroyed
all textbooks in the English language during the last war. Despite the
efforts of many Americans, this situation has never been substantially
alleviated. Part of the reason. of course, is the population explosion in
the Philippines.
The Philippine Government reserves over twenty per cent of its

184

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

budget for public school education. Despite this fact, we have found
that on the average three school children are using one textbook. The
English language is generally used throughout the Philippines, and
the public school system in the Philippines was founded and nurtured
by Americans and is patterned after the American School System. Consequently, any American textbook on any subject will be useful. Furthermore, there is such a vacuum that even if a book is outdated. it will be
useful.
The United States Navy is prepared to transport free-of-charge
any and all books that you may be able to send us. In the event that you
can collect books through your Subordinate Lodges. kindly arrange with
the nearest U.S. Navy Installation to ship them to the West Coast Director, Project Handclasp, Eleventh N aval District, San Diego, California, in accordance with the instructions contained in CINCPACFL T
5726.l ( 42) 24 April 1962.
When we receive the books, we shall distribute them on a proportional basis through our 117 Subordinate Lodges in the Philippine Archipelago (we also have Lodges in Guam, Okinawa and Japan) . This will
fit in with our program of public service and education which we have
initiated in connection with our Special Golden Jubilee Communicatio n
to be held on December 19, 1962, which we hope you or some members
of the Grand Lodge will attend.
We hope that you will ask all of your Subordinate Lodges to do all
possible to collect used textbooks and to arrange for shipment to us.
We understand that in many areas in the United States, textbooks which
are outdated or are in less than good condition are destroyed. These
books would be highly acceptable and very much appreciated by the
teachers and by the school children in the Philippines.
We are doing our best to fight the forces of communism and it seems
to us that if this program is successfully carried out, we will be making
a two-pronged attack on communistic activities. First, by improving the
educational level of the children, we will be combatting ignorance. Second, the fact that the gift has been made from America, will enhance
immeasurably the goodwill which exists between Americans and
Filipinos.
You can be assured that we will see to it that your Grand Lodge and
your Subordinate Lodges get full credit for all donations made.
I hope to attend the Grand Masters' Conference in Washington next
year, and hope to meet you there if I do not see you here next December.

This is a most challenging program and your Committee, realizing
that its correct name is Public Schools Committee and not Public Schools
Week Committee, is anxious that we help in " Project Handclasp."
There are two approaches: ( 1) Contact your local school authorities
in an endeavor to obtain textbooks which they might have available;
and ( 2) contact your own members and their friends for those two or
three to a dozen old textbooks which are stored away.
We solicit your enthusiastic cooperation in this matter, to the end
that we assist our daughter jurisdiction toward success in a truly worthy
endeavor, and at the same time give our Grand Officers reason to be
proud of this jurisdiction on the occasion of their visit to the Golden
Jubilee session.
Before concluding this report, your Committee wishes briefly to
record its sincere appreciation to :
Most W orshipful Guy B. Mize, Grand Master, for giving us the
privilege of serving our schools and this Grand Lodge. For his
tremendous capacity, zeal, understanding and cooperation in connection with Public Schools.
Our predecessors in office who have laid the firm foundation on
which we are building.
The Masters and Committee Chairmen who carried the ball
throug bout the Jurisdiction.
The California Teachers Association whose cooperation over
the years has been of untold assistance.
To school teachers and administrators without whose assistance
we could° not succeed.
Looking to the future. let us be ever mindful that as our Public
Schools have always been a grass-roots institution and so should we keep
our program in the local Lodges, with guidance and help, not dictation,
coming from the Grand Lodge Committee.
Assure yourselves that your own local schools are not degenerating
into being merely mills of learning as in the Soviet Union. Keep your
Public Schools- Symbols of Freedom.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Today I would invoke the symbolism of these "Whirling Wheels,"
the title which I have chosen for this oration, to assist me in developing to the Craft the tribute which is upon my heart.
The outer wheel, circumscribing the infinite universe, we naturally
ascribe as Masons to God, its author and creator. The inner wheel
we may view as man, or more particularly for our present purposes,
as Masons, strug·gling through the ages to achieve individual dignity
and true freedom under God.
Both outer and inner wheels are whirling because both the universe
and all which it contains are dynamic, mov.ing and developing-not
static. Each wheel presents basic concepts which are essential to my
theme.
Fif'st, we turn to the outer wheel of God's infinite power which
includes all else. The great light of our faith illumines this wheel with
its mighty opening words-"In the beginning, God ... . " Here operates
the eternal and immovable God upon whom, in this changing world. we
may always count as a fixed source of love and strength. Here, in short,
is the Almighty, Omnipotent and Infinite Creator of the whole universe
symbolically surrounding and protecting us.
Some time ago, the distinguished editor of the California Freemason
printed a verse which described God'-s creation of our particular earthly
planet in these colorful words:

rounded by the protective comfort of the outer wheel of God's infinite
presence.
Finally, and yet of essential importance to us, we know this Infinite God to be a personal God - the God of Abraham, Isaac and
of Jacob. More than this, He is the God of all mankind-a dynamic,
present and active God today just as He has been and will continue to
be as the outer wheel whirls on.
Within the orbit of this outer wheel we find the whirling inner
wheel which symbolizes you, my Brethren, as representatives of all
Freemasons of every age. And this inner wheel has four flashing spokes
which taken together represent the four age-old goals of the Craft. The
first is the achievement of individual dignity. The second is the winning
of individual freedom. The third is the accomplishment of national
freedom. And the fourth is the establishment of individual freedom of
worship.
Because our forefathers in the Craft have built well toward the
establishment of these freedoms, the rights which they bestow are ours
to enjoy, to defend and in our turn to expand. Their heroic accomplishments are no dry bones of history. Rather, they shower down
upon us, and envelop us in star-dust as the guardians of their treasures.

188

"A fire-mist and a planet,
A crystal and a cell,
A jelly-fish and a saurian,
And caves where cave-men dwell;
Then a sense of law and beauty
And a face turned from the clodSome call it evolution,
And others call it God."
Today, of course, we know that this planet earth is but a speck in
the total universe and that numberless worlds are indeed around us, all
framed by the same Divine Artist. We are thoroughly space-minded,
and our scientists constantly expand their knowledge of space and simultaneously strain upward and outward in their practical calculations as to
how to propel man toward the very stars. Yet the whirling outer wheel
of our imagery assures us that our God is a great God: that wherever
man's imagination or his techniques may ultimately permit him to soar
-and far beyond that extreme point-there will be found the same
Divine Artist. Be assured, my Brethren, that man is no chance collection of particles, created and then turned loose to flicker briefly
amid surrounding chaos-but stands in his Maker's image ever sur-

For no matter how far back our gaze or imagination carries us.
whether it be to the skilled members of a college of artificers in urban
Rome, or to the lonely watchers in Babylon and the deserts of Egypt
who carefully pl<?tted the courses of the stars and planets long before
the building of the pyramids, we shall find the same origins and the
same basic drives motivating and leading upward those whom we Masons are proud to call "Brother." For all mankind is kin, and what
dedicated men of all ages seek is, ultimately, not material nor of this
world. Rather, "they seek to escape the duality of their natures, to
achieve an essential unity; to transcend the material, to rise out of the
earthly -into the fullness of the spiritual." In short, they seek to harmonize the whirling inner wheel which is symbolic of their lives and
action, with the rhythm of the celestial outer wheel.
Through generation after generation, above the clank and vibrations
of material progress, Masons have continued to labor and to listen for
an omnipotent voice. And the motivation which drove them to do so
survived the rise and fall of mighty empires, and the whip-lash and
retribution of tyrants in every age. That motivation we call basically
man's struggle for freedom, his journey upward upon what Lord Tennyson described as "the great world's altar-stairs, that slope thro'
darkness up to God." For man has ever sought to rise from anonymous slavery to individual dignity and freedom, and once launched

191

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

upon those twin quests has gone on to struggle for national freedom and
the priceless privilege of worshipping his Creator in his own way. Hence
the four spokes of the inner wheel.

Out of serfdom, out of ignorance, out of the denial of the right even
to stray from their chani:e places of birth-yes, out of next to nothingness-there had emerged through the power of Freemasonry the priceless possession of human dignity. Men of the Craft were indeed recognized as individuals, and to prove it for aU time, they possessed their
individual marks with which they stamped their handiwork. Moreuver,
they had created a great class of men who were in truth made free to
travel wherever their skills were in demand. Here were indeed Freemasons, and men cloaked with that mantle of human dignity without
which man could never go forward to achieve those full freedoms which
made up the spokes of the inner wheel.
1£ you would experience, even across long centuries, something of
a personal, physical bond with these ancient Brethren, you may find
that experience as I did in the company of Most Worshipful Brother
Shell. Not long ago, we stood together in a very old cathedral in Austria. And there, amidst the music and liturgy of a religfous ceremony
not ours, we reached out our fingers and touched. on one of the soaring
arches of the cathedral. the master's mark of our Masonic Brother whose
hands, together with his fellows', had erected that mighty building centuries ago. With such a physical bond, my Brethren, one almost literally
sees before him, stepping out through the mists of the past of long
ago, the stalwart form of a living Brother, a fellow Mason and a mighty
champion of freedom. And one is proud indeed to be his follower in
that great quest.
There is another brilliant jewel of the early Craft's accomplishment
upon which I presume ta speak. If authority for such comment be needed,
it may be found in the teaching of the Ancient Charges and Regulations,
which demand of us that "you agree to hold in veneration the original
rulers and patrons of the Order of Masonry." To what further jewel of
accomplishment do I. then, refer?
To nothing less than the example of the great care and concern of our
early Brethren in transmitting their ideals and aspirations to the young
men who were growing up around them. They spent time with these
youths, they worked with them, and they gradually opened their minds
and vision to the worthiness and keen desirability of achieving fellowship and membership among the enlightened ones. Youth responded,
as it always has, to the adventure-dangerous as it might be-of fighting for high ideals. And when those high ideals were understood to be
persona] dignity and the freedom of all men, interest became enthusiasm and enthusiasm became dedication. Thus at the portals of Masonry,
sons knocked at the door and sought admission as had their fathers.
Friends followed friends. And thus. joining the Masters of the Craft,
there was a perfectly natural progression, a built-in admiration and
devotion, which provided a steady replenishment and growth for the
Order.

190

In Tolstoy's War and Peace, there appears a moving scene between
Pierre, Count Bezukhov, and an elderly traveller who is recognized by
the ring he wears as being a Freemason. The Mason, in reply to a
suggestion that his brotherhood suffered from a delusion, replies :
"I should never dare to say that I know the truth. No one can attain
truth by himself. Only by laying stone on stone with the cooperation
of all, by the millions of generations from our forefather Adam to our
own times, is that temple reared which is to be a worthy dwelling
place of the great God."
Our ancient Brethren, though largely bereft of material pleasures,
personal possessions and the blessings of freedom, instinctively knew
this truth, and realized that the first key to the stone by stone erection
of freedom consisted of knowledge. And so they patiently began to
observe, to study and to reflect-all in ages when formal teaching was
the special prerogative reserved to kings and priests. The book of
nature lay open before their inquiring minds, and from it they read and
began to understand something of the secrets of the skies and something
of the everyday workings of simple natural laws, as well as being
drawn to the realization that all these things pointed unerringly to the
existence of one great Creator. As they slowly opened the vistas of
their minds, so too they increased the skill of their hands, and began to
bring to bear their new knowledge in the production of ever more beautiful objects of their Craft.
In this expanding process of acquiring personal dignity and freedom,
they early adopted two principles. The first was to establish a means
of preserving their growing body of knowledge at a time when the art
of writing was largely closed to them. This they did, with an effectiveness to which we can testify, by the use of symbols, selected from
the Craft's most expressive tools and implements. The second was to
protect for themselves, their a pprentices and fellows, the precious s~
crets of the skills of the Craft which permitted their application to ever
more complex and stupendous edifices. This they achieved by the use
of secrecy- made functional by the concept of the tiled lodge wherein
learning was imparted and protected from profane ears.
I recall these events to you, not as a presentation of pages of M<Y
sonic history-for there are present far more learned historians than
I. Rather, I cite them as the means whereby our early Operative Craft
made one of the most dramatic strides forward ever made by man in
his long quest for freedom. For observe, and s well with pride at what
had been achieved by our Brethren.

But note, I beg you, the critical fact that this invigorating Bow of
young Entered Apprentices, this transformation of boys into Craftsmen
who fought to understand and improve the world as well as themselves,
was solidly supported by active and continued personal contact with
members of the Craft.

Thus the never-ending struggle of men, and of Masons, has come
down to us. Slowly, over the generations, the rhythm of the inner
wheel becomes more in harmony with the outer. Slowly. but magnificently, the spokes of indi¥idual dignity, personal freedom, national free,,, dom and freedom of conscience have expanded and held firm.

Mine is no function or intention of critical comment as to the degree
to which Masons of our day may fail in seeing to it that they work
thus steadily with young men and bring to them that spark of enthusiasm which in turn will bring them to our doors as eager recruits. Mine
rather is but the function of the remembrancer; for once the rays of
recollection and realization flash before your minds, certain it is that
your own keen intellects as Masonic leaders will unerringly point the
way whereby the Craft of today may improve itself in the performance
of this great Masonic privilege and duty.

All these events-all these accomplishments over the centuries-are
both our common birthright and a part of the swirling clouds of glory
which surround and adorn each one of you. Of these things are you
made. And for these things, to which each one of you have added so
much by your own devoted labors, I sing your praise.

But let us return to our inner wheel and examine briefly the two
remaining spokes which represent the right of all men to national freedom and religious liberty. We all know how the torch of individual
freedom, once lighted by our ancient Brethren, kindled the determination of men through century after century which followed to achieve
still more complete freedom for all mankind. This unceasing quest for
freedom is at the very core and essence of Freemasonry, and, together
with its humble dependence upon God, readily explains both the attrac..
tion and the power of our Order.
As rapidly changing scenes of the past Bick past in memory, we see
our Brethren standing behind the barons who forced Magna Charta
from King John of England at Runnymede in 1215. We see them as
they furnished the French Revolution with much of it·s strength and
with its great rallying cry of "Liberty, Equality and Fraternity!" We
see them in Indian dress at the Boston Tea Party, warning a foreign
monarch that there were limits of oppression beyond which his subjects could not be pressed.
We look at the scenes of heroism at Valley Forge and elsewhere
throughout the Colonies, and we see the mystic seal of the Square and
Compass deeply impressed upon our nation's fight for freedom. We
watch the Constitutional Convention of 1787 which followed victory
and see there the careful labors of Freemasons. And we read with
pounding pulses the ringing words of freedom's charter which they
wrote in the immortal preamble of our Constitution.
As political liberties expanded there grew apace the right of every
man to believe and to worship God as he sees fit-and here again we
thrill as we see the handiwork of our Brethren in sweeping away the
strangle-hold which long had held men's consciences in thrall.

But truth demands that I stop not here with words of praise-for
it must also be said that the continued possession of our freedoms demands of us both vigilance and exertion. H eed the words of Goethe's
"Faust":
"Whate'er you have, bequeathed you by your father,
Earn it in order to possess it . ... "
Strong as we are in our nation's military might, we are but slowly
awakening to the realization that deadly danger surrounds us. For
all too long we Americans have indulgently gauged others by our own
peaceful intents and purposes. We have been far too prone to assume
that our libert>ies and freedoms are automatically to be ours foreverwithout exertion by us. We have tended to think of our Constitution
in terms of a rare document kept safely on d isplay at Washingtoninstead of seeing, in its the living bulwark which our Brethren raised
against arrest. torture, loss of our property and death itself, withou t
due process of law.
Now that we have begun to realize more and more the chilling possibility of nuclear attack against us , all too many of our citizens are
thinking of meeting any such attack on a "survival only" basis. Yet I
assert that any such timorous objective may well destroy free civilization, taking us along with it. "Survival only" is not a policy. It is the
delusion of a nation marked for suicide. It is a faulty stone which I
pray that you, as Master Craftsmen, will firmly reject. The great
Edwin Burke described the danger very neatly when he commented.
"All that •is necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do
nothing." Let us heed those words and never lay down our working
tools.
To you, the very flower of Freemasonry. must go the leadership
in this resurgence of spirit-this recovery of an understanding long
buried in the rubbish of the Temple. In the words of the Prophet Isaiah,
the call is made to you to " •. . J.ift up a standard for the people!" That
you will succeed is not open to doubt. Your stature in the Craft, your

194

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

proven abilities as leaders, and the clarity of your vision . al.I combine
to assure that the mighty structure of freedom so tru~y bmlt ~y our
predecessors will rise to new heights by your accomplishments m our
times. And, thus, with our labors ended, we shall w~tch. the ..whirling
wheels move on. as " •.. time and the world are ever m flight.
My Brethren, I salute you.
"I do not know beneath what sky
Nor on what seas shall be thy fate;
I only know it shall be high.
I only know it shall be great."
The Grand Oration was received with a standing ovation.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
During the past few years the principal duty of your Committee
has been the publication of California Freemason. The year 1962 saw
the completion of Volume 9, and Volume 10 will be issued quarterly
during 1963.
The format adopted in 1959 has been continued, the magazine having 48 pages, 6 inches by 9 inches, and is produced by the offset process.
The first eight pages and the last eight pages are in two colors. There
is a liberal use of pictures.
The original function of the Committee has not been overlooked
and the Proceedings of sister Grand Lodges have been studied to obtain
information of interest to California Freemasons. These reviews have
been published in the magazine.
The California Freemason is an official publication but its articles
do not necessarily present the opinion of Grand Lodge. It has attempted
to maintain sound Masonic standards and to give our readers Masonic
information and inspiration , but it must always be understood that its
statements are not necessarily the official position of the Grand Lodge
of California. Articles are printed which ha ve some Masonic connection and which are educational, informative, stimulating and even provocative. News of Grand Lodge activities is presented as well as unusual
and outstanding items about ind ividual Lodges, but a quarterly is not a
news magazine and space is not available to mention every local happening.
Bids were sought for the publication of the quarterly for the ensuing
year. By the authority of the Grand Master and the Deputy Grand
Master, the contract for 1963 was awarded to Stecher-Traung Lithograph Corporation of San Francisco.
There has been a small increase in the number of forward-looking
Lodges which send the magazine to their entire membership. This practice has been a real stimulan t to membership interest. The arrangement
for blanket subscriptions is that if a Lodge adopts a resolution so to
do, each member will be mailed the quarterly and, in January of each
year, Grand Lodge will bill the Lodge at the rate of not to exceed 60
cents for the number of members shown on the last A nnual Return.
Changes in membership during the year do not affect this charge.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Sam Walter Foss wrote in his "The Coming American":
"Bring me men to match my mountains
Bring me men to match my plains."
Our nation has repeatedly called its citizens to summits of crises :
Valley Forge, Bull Run, the Depression, Guadalcanal, Cape Canaveral.
Repeatedly we have sent forth men of strength, wisdom and courage
to meet the moun'tains. Leaders of those men have been untold numbers
of Masons.
This year as we celebrate the one hundred seventy-fifth anniversary
of the signing of the Constitution of the United States of America, we
are in dire need of intelligent statesmanship and capable public servants
who do not compromise with honor and right. We must not stand by with
apathetic eyes as we witness the daily inroads that are being made into
the rights and privileges which were written into and provided by that
great document. We as Masons must provide the men to meet those
mountains. For as Ralph Waldo Emerson so wisely wrote:
"For what avail the plough or sail
Or land, or life itself-if freedom fail?"
These annual observances by our Lodges must not be just an answer
to the Grand Master's proclamation. They must be vital and enthusiastic.
They must bring the message of freedom not only to Masons but to
your friends, your neighbors and the entire community. They must accomplish what the great Athenian statesman Pericles wrote:
"I would have you day by day fix your eyes upon the greatness
of your country until you become filled with the love of her; and,
when you are impressed by the spectacle of her glory, reflect that

198

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

it has been acquired by men who knew their duty and had the
courage to do it."
Because of the requirement that this report had to be in the hands
of the Grand Master by September 1st, it must of necessity be void of
any accounting of this year's observances. We can only say that reports
of program planning have been most encouraging and point to an out.standing year.
Again this year the Committee visited many of the district officers'
meetings to offer their assistance in the planning of the various observances. The response by the Inspectors to the Grand Master's suggestion
that committeemen be invited to visit one of their district officers' meetings for this purpose, was very fine. To these devoted Masons-our
sincere appreciation. We believe these visitations are productive of
better planning and the resulting observances thus more successful.
Our preamble and flag program this year- a single item of the
Preamble to the Constitution printed on parchment with the American
flag printed in color-was received most enthusiastically. Over one
hundred thousand of these items were distributed by Lodges throughout
the State to schools, churches, civic groups, etc.
Your Chairman would like to add a personal note to this report. I
have been a member of this Committee for seven years. To me, the original appointment of Grand Master Ned Stewart, and continued reappointments by succeeding Grand Masters have been a real pleasure
and a distinct honor. With real pride I have seen this Committee grow
from just "another list of Past Masters on the Roster of Grand Lodge"
to an enthusiastic and dedicated group of Masons who are sacrificing
time and effort to do a good job for Masonry. This has afforded me
much pleasure and personal satisfaction. Because it has always been
my firm belief that no one should be continued too long in a specific job
and because I believe that new "blood" and new leadership are required
periodically to produce continued progress towards the goal which we
all must strive, I have requested the incoming Grand Master to appoint
a new Chairman of this Committee. He has accepted this request.
My Brethren, let us truly hold the Constitution in true veneration
and protect it with our hearts and minds and actions. Remember that
"deterioration of any government begins with the decay of the principles
on which it was founded."
Respectfully submitted,

T o the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
At the 1961 Communication of Grand Lodge the dispensation of
Scepter Lodge U.D. was continued for an additional year. During the
current Masonic Year five more Lodges have been instituted. In addition, one petition for a dispensation has been certified by the Grand
Secretary to the Grand Master and referred to the Committee on Charters for investigation. The investigation is in suspense, pending appointment of the Committee on Charters by the incoming Grand Master.
Four of the Lodges petitioned for charters. These are Scepter, Los
A lamitos, Victoria Palms, and Woodland Hills. They submitted their
records and sent delegates who appeared before the Committee on Char.ters. In some cases there were errors or omissions in their records. Some
of these were minor and others were more substantial. Some of them, at
least. would not have occurred if closer attention had been given to the
California Masonic Code and to the manual prepared by the Committee
on Charters w hich had been issued by Grand Lodge to them.
In any event. the errors and omissions were of a character which
could be rectified. and such has been accomplished or assurance given
that it would be done. Therefore, in a basic sense, their work and proceedings prove satisfactory; they have produced certificates that their
respective Masters and Wardens proposed are each thoroughly skilled
in the work and )ectures, and they have shown that they are clear of all
indebtedness.
The Committee on Charters therefore unanimously recommends that
charters be granted and numbers assigned to the four petitioning Lodges
as follows:
Scepter Lodge No. 808 at West Sacramento, in the county of Yolo.
Los Alamitos Lodge No. 809 at Artesia, in the county of Los Angeles.
Victoria Palms Lodge No. 810 at Riverside, in the county of Riverside.
Woodland Hills Lodge No. 811 at Canoga Park, in the county of
Los Angeles.
Triad Lodge U .D. at Montebello, in the county of Los Angeles, was
instituted on August 28. 1962. The Lodge, having worked under dispensation such a short time. did not petition for a cha rter but requested
that its dispensation be continued for the ensuing Masonic Year. Its
delegates met informally with the Committee. and we unanimously concur in the request of the Lodge and do recommend that the dispensation
be continued.
Comment is required with respect to the status of Old West Lodge

200

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

U. D. The dispensation was. originally granted September 13, 1962. The
Lodge was instituted October 2, 1962, and held its first Stated Meeting
the same evening. On the advice of this Committee, it has not surrendered its dispensation nor forwarded to the Grand Secretary its by-laws,
books of records, etc., however brief they may be. The reason for such
advice will be explained.
California Masonic Code, Section 309. provides in part that a "dispensation shall terminate upon the first day of the month in which the
next succeeding Annual Communicatio n shall be holden and shall then
be returned to the Grand Secretary, together with the by-laws, books
of records, and returns of the new Lodge to that date .... ".
Thus, if reliance were placed on the dispensation as originally
granted we would be confronted with a dispensation which by virtue of
its date terminated under Masonic Law on October 1, 1962.
The Grand Master rectified that situation by re-dating the dispensation October 2, 1962, the date upon which he instituted the new Lodge.
Inasmuch as the Lodge did not come into existence until it was instituted, it obviously could not comply this year with that portion of
Section 309 requiring return of the dispensation, etc., to the Grand
Secretary the day before it was instituted.
Thus. Old West Lodge U.D. is a Lodge of which this Committee
must take cognizance, but is one upon which no action need be taken
at this Communicatio n. The dispensation with the new date is the one
under which the Lodge exists. and does not terminate until the first day
of October, 1963. This will result in the Lodge having the opportunity
of either petitioning for a charter at the 1963 Communicatio n or of requesting at that time that it be continued under dispensation for the
following year.
This portion of our report is for information, and requires no action.
Reference is made to that portion of the Report of the Grand Secretary relating to consolidation of Lodges, which has been referred to
this Committee.

and Victory Lodge No. 474, the Lodge to be known as San FranciscoVictory Lodge No. 360, located at San Francisco, was accomplished in
accordance with the law.
It further appears that the consolidation of Surprise Valley Lodge
No. 235 and North East Lodge No. 266, the Lodge to be known as Surprise Valley Lodge No. 235, located at Cedarville, was accomplished
in accordance with the law.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In the sincere belief that the promotion of Masonic Education can
provide one of the best answers to the universal Masonic problems of
attendance and membership, your Committee has this year explored.
experimented and attempted many forms of Masonic education.
In conformity with the custom of the past seven years the Committee,
in conjunction with the Research Lodges, has planned a Masonic Education Seminar for Tuesday, October 9. at 7 :00 p.m., in the California
Masonic Memorial Temple. Grand Master Guy B. Mize in authorizing
the seminar spoke of it as a "feature of Grand Lodge Week." Your Committee is indebted to our Grand Master for his guidance, support and
encouragemen t throughout the year. We urge that the evening Masonic
Education Seminar be made a regular feature of Grand Lodge Week.
This year, classroom panel. and question and answer sessions will
be held in the ground floor meeting rooms from 7: 00 to 7: 45 p.m. and

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worsh ipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M . of California:
Your Committee on Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges has had
under consideration several applications for recognition from foreign
Grand Lodges, including two recently formed, as well as conditions in
Cuba and in France, and reports as follows:
INDIA

A new Grand Lodge of India was constituted and the Grand Master
and other officers installed on November 24, 1961. Preparations for the
creation of this Grand Lodge had been going on for at least two years
by a joint committee representing the Grand Lodges of England, Ireland
and Scotland, and members of the Lodges in India . The new Grand
Lodge was consecrated by the Grand Master Mason of Scotland and
constituted by the Deputy Grand Master of Ireland . and the officers
were installed by the Deputy Grand Master of England.
The Grand Lodge of India is entirely regular and we recommend
that the Grand Lodge of California ex tend formal recognition. The
acting Grand Secretary is Brother M. P. Dube, Freemasons' H all, Janpath, Post Box 681 , New Delhi, India.
LUXEMBOURG

In our report at the last Communication we noted that the Grand
Lodge of Luxembourg had applied for recognition and recommended
that the question be held over for another year.
The Grand Lodge of Luxembourg has been in existence since 1849
but has not heretofore been recognized by us. It has recently, however.
severed relations with the Grand Orient of France and the Grand Orient

206

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

of Belgium, neither o f which bodies is recognized by the Grand Lodge
of California. All information we are able to secure indicates that the
Grand Lodge of Luxembourg is now entirely regular and merits our
recognition.
We, therefore, recommend that the Grand Lodge of California
extend fraternal recognition to the Grand Lodge of Luxembourg, the
Grand Secretary being Brother Leon Hamus, P . 0. Box 260, Luxembourg (Grand Duche).
SOUTHERN AFRICA

The Grand Lodge of Southern Africa was formed on February 18,
1961, and has applied to this Grand Lodge for recognition.
This new Grand Lodge is made up exclusively of Lodges formerly
under the obedience of the Grand Lodge of The Netherlands. It has
ninety-four Lodges and about 5,000 members. The Grand Master installed April 22, 1961, was M . W . Graham Botha , formerly Deputy
Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of The Netherlands in South Africa.
The new Grand Lodge of Southern Africa is regular and has been
recognized by the Grand Lodges of England, Ireland a nd Scotland.
We recommend that the Grand Lodge of California extend formal
recognition to the Grand Lodge of Southern Africa, its headquarters
being in the National Mutual Building, Church Square, Capetown.
CUBA

Prior to September 22. 1962. at least. the situation of Freemasonry
in Cuba under the Castro regime had not been clear.
In March, 1959, Juan Jose Tarajano was elected and installed Grand
Master of Masons in Cuba, and in March, 1960, w as re-elected and
installed to serve a second year. By November, 1960, he and a number of
other Grand Lodge officers deemed it necessary to get out of Cuba because of the trend toward Communism, and its threat through infiltration to engulf Freemasonry.
On November 15. 1960, Brother Tarajano delegated his powers to
the Deputy Grand Master, and on the following day arrived in Miami
where he was joined by some of the other Grand Lodge officers. The
Deputy Grand Master also decided to leave, but he was not able to get
to Florida. With some difficulty he managed later to go to Venezuela
where we understand he now is. Brother T arajano, who had meantime
received the Great Seal of the Grand Lodge of Cuba, issued a statement
on December 31, 1960, in which he reassumed his duties as Grand
Master, and on the same date declared a temporary recess in all Masonic
activities in Cuba. He and his group appear to have observed carefully
the Masonic rules of propriety as to the Grand Lodge of Florida and
were made welcome there. Grand Master Larson of Florida by his

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

207

proclamation of March 6. 1961. and the Grand Lodge of Florida, by
action taken April. 1961 , recognized Brother Tarajano as in truth and
in fact the Grand Master of Cuba with the privilege of residence in
Florida, and of continuing from there the existence and operation of
the Grand Lodge of Cuba.
However, it appears that the Castro government did not at that
time suppress Freemasonry in Cuba as Freemasonry had been suppressed in some other countries. When Grand Master Tarajano, and
later on the Deputy Grand Master, left Cuba. the Senior Grand Warden
took over as the ranking officer left in Cuba and carried on until March.
1961. Then at the regular ·s emi-annual communication of the Grand
Lodge, Jorge Cuervo Calvo was elected and installed Grand Master.
From reliable information furnished us, it appears that although the
Grand Lodge building in Havana was taken over by the government,
together with all other office buildings in the city, the four Masonic
floors in the Grand Lodge building had not been disturbed until recently. It appears that most of the Lodges in the Grand Lodge of Cuba
have been working under the direction of Grand Master Calvo, one
exception being Caribbean Naval Lodge at Guantanamo Naval Base
which has given its allegiance to Brother Tarajano in Miami as Grand
Master.
The Inter-American Conference, consisting of Latin American Grand
Lodges. went on record, after investigation by a commission sent to
Havana, as affirming the validity of the Grand Lodge of Cuba then
working in Cuba. While the Masons in Florida. and Brother Tarajano
and those associated with him, have been of great assistance in rendering Masonic service and relief to Cuban refugees who are Masons. competent legal opinion was that under the circumstances there could have
been no such thing as a Grand Lodge of Cuba in exile. and that the
legally established Grand Lodge of Cuba in Havana still had jurisdiction
over the 30,000 or more Masons in that country. Some Cuban Masons
now in the United States have not been able, however, to secure dues
receipts from their Lodges in Cuba nor replies to communications, and
without current dues receipts, of course, they could not visit California
Lodges.
On September 25, 1962, the newspapers carried a press release from
Mexico City to the effect that Cuban troops had occupied the Masonic
Grand Temple in Havana, arrested its officers (including Grand Master
Calvo) and outlawed the organization. This report was confirmed by
the Grand Executive Secretary of the Inter~American Masonic Con~
federation, General Eduardo Rincon Gallardo. We have no information
other than press release; however, those members of Lodges under the
jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Cuba who may wish to affiliate with
our Lodges are not prevented by reason of this suppression from so

doing if they can prove reasonably that they have been in good standing in Lodges under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of Cuba (see
Sec. 557-3rd C.M.C.). Because less than two weeks have elapsed since
we learned from press notices of the suppression of Cuban Freemasonry
and because of the lack of definite information as to the precise situation now facing Freemasonry in Cuba. the Committee does not feel that
it can make any recommendation at this Communication.
FRANCE

As your Committee has reported at several communications during
the past few years. the situation of Freemasonry in France has been a
cause of concern.
The Grand Lodge of California at present recognizes two Grand
Lodges in France, the Grand Lodge Nationale and the Grand Lodge of
France. A third jurisdiction, known as the Grand Orient of France. is
the largest in membership but is irregular and is not recognized by this
Grand Lodge or by any other with which we are in fraternal relations.
The Grand Lodge Nationale is entirely regular and is universally
recognized.
The Grand Lodge of France has been officially regular. at least in
the past few years. but according to the best information we can secure
it has not been entirely succesful in enforcing regularity in many of its
constituent Lodges. Fraternization and intercommunication between
Lodges and members adhering to the Grand Lodge of France and those
adhering to the irregular Grand Orient seem to continue in spite of
official action of the Grand Lodge itself. We understand also that the
Holy W ·r itings are not always used, and that many members of constituent Lodges have not bee.n obligated thereon. Only nine other grand
jurisdictions in the United States now recognize the Grand Lodge of
France.
Your Committee feels that it is not wise in the interest of Freemasonry for this Judsdiction to continue to recognize two competing
Grand Jurisdictions within the Republic of France; and to continue to
recognize the Grand Lodge of France would be to condone a certain
amount of irregularity which that Grand Lodge is itself apparently
unable or unwilling to control. Since the other Grand Lodge. the Grand
Lodge Nationale. is entirely regular, it is our thought that until the
situation in France has been corrected, we should confine our recognition to this one Grand Lodge about which there is no doubt.
For the above reasons your Committee recommends withdrawal of
recognition from the Grand Lodge of France. with the expressed hope
that this step on our part will help to bring about a closer union of those
Lodges in France which wish to be entirely regular and to adhere strictly
to the Ancient Landmarks.
Respectfully submitted.

Adopted.

PHIL N. MYERS
WILLIAM RHODES HERVEY, }R.
ALFRED F. BRESLAUER

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON MASONIC CEMETERIES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
At the request of the Grand Master. Brothers Gillett and Chapman
prepared this report in order that Grand Lodge may be informed of the
current status of matters which have occupied our attention during the
past year.
It is our sad duty to repor t that the Chairman of the Committee,
Worshipful Samuel E. Leddel. was called to the Lodge on High September 28, 1962. Our beloved Brother wa·s long active in Masonic, religious and civic affairs in his home area of Long Beach and will be sorely
missed.
Briefly. our duties under Sec. 204, C.M.C.. fall into three categories:
( 1 ) cemeteries owned or operated by Grand Lodge; ( 2) cemeteries or
sections thereof owned or supervised by constituent Lodges and ( 3)
problems of any nature arising by reason of the connection or usage of
the name of our Fraternity in relation to any burial ground in California.
The cemeteries owned by Grand Lodge are as follows: (a} Columbia Cemetery, situated in what is now Columbia State Park. about four
miles from Sonora. It adjoins the renovated Columbia School and is near
the Columbia M asonic Temple, which was restored to its original condition by Grand Lodge twelve years ago. The school is a show place
for vtsitors and. by Grand Lodge action last year. work has been commenced under direction of this Committee to put the cemetery in a presentable condition: Brush and debris have been cleaned up and hauled
away, a large oak tree trimmed. and an engineer's survey made. The
latter was necessary to establish the correct boundary lines so that a
picket fence. corresponding to that in front of the cemetery, and the
old schoolhouse grounds, could be installed. Contract has been let for
this fence and it is scheduled for completion by the end of October,
1962. Incidentally, the survey disclosed that a piece of land 76 x 156
in front of the cemetery is included in the Grand Lodge title and should
be placed on record. This could probably be used for a parking lot.
It will be recalled that at the 1961 Communication Grand Lodge
authorized an appropriation of $3 .000.00 for work on the Columbia property. The amount already contracted for is included in the present requested appropriation of $5,385.00 detailed in the following recom~

Activity of our Committee in the other two categories, referred to
in paragraph three of this report, is usually confined to specific cases
brought to our attention. For example, in Grass V alley a cemetery
owned by Madison Lodge No. 23 is reported to us to be in a neglected
state and it is recommended that the Lodge in question be instructed to
set up a program of rehabilitation. Another instance, of which there are
many, is a situation in which a Lodge holds title to a Masonic section
and sells lots to its members. Obviously it is the duty of such Lodge
to see that the section is maintained in a proper manner to avoid reflection on the Fraternity.
The third category includes such problems as an old cemetery in
Hueneme, which is owned by a corporation established some sixty years
ago. The individual stockholders were Masons in Hueneme Lodge No.
311 , which was consolidated with Oxnard Lodge No. 341 in 1902. The
cemetery is neglected and little used now and the whereabouts of most
of the original stockholders is unknown. The name of the corporation.
however, is "Hueneme Masonic Cemetery", and it is desirable that the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

word "Masonic" be eliminated from the corporate title. This poses a
legal problem and it is our recommendation that the matter be referred
to the appropriate Grand Lodge Committee to work with the Inspector
for that District and determine what can be done. A Past Master of
Oxnard Lodge is president of the corporation and several of the directors are Masons. A similar situation exists in Modesto, except that here
our Committee has not yet had an opportunity to complete its investigation. Another facet under this third category is the establishment of
Masonic sections in new cemeteries. In such cases the cemetery corporation sells the lots and our interest is to ascertain whether a perpetual
care trust fund has been established and that the Fraternity shall not
be used as a means of commercializing the sale of grave sites. Your
Committee sees no objection otherwise. Two recent instances are: New
cemeteries at Chico and Fullerton, both projects being high grade and
well managed operations.

REPORT OF BOARD OF
LIBRARY COMMISSIONERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . & A. M. of California:
The Masonic Year 1961-62 will probably go down in California
Masonic history-as far as the Grand Lodge Library is concerned-as
the year in which our Lending Library at long last went into orbit.
After ·several years of preparation---<:omprising the gathering of a representative selection of books, properly cataloging and indexing them,
developing a practical and effective method of operation, securing the
necessary assistance from among the brethren to man an adequate
Library staff, and developing the proper working tools-it is gratifying
to be able to report that we are now, as the saying goes. "in business."
As a result, an increasing number of Brethren from all over the Jurisdiction have been making use of our Lending Library, and the many
expressions of appreciation that we have received from those who have
begun to take advantage of this new facility is very satisfying to your
Board. With the continued support of the Grand Lodge. and the continued interest on the part of the Brethren, our possibilities for service
to the Craft show every promise of increase as the years go by, and as
the resources at our disposal become greater and greater.
A new issue of our BOOK LIST has been made avilable and widely
circulated, cataloging the books that can be had on loan by mail. arranged and classified as to subject matter for convenient selection. By
means of generous publicity in the California Freemason, and frequent
notices in Lodge Bulletins around the Jurisdiction. numerous requests for
these BOOK LISTS have come in. To the California Freemason, and to
the Masters of Lodges who have given us this much-needed and most
effective publicity, we express our most heartfelt gratitude.
Thanks are also due to those who have given so generously of their
time and energy to man the variou·s stations and perform the many
arduous tasks connected with the operation of a working Library: to
Brother William H. MacMaster, who has been in general charge of the
Library and its records, and who has faithfully kept the Library open
to visitors one day a week; to Brother Paul R. Kruse, a professionally
trained and practicing Librarian, who has helped to put the cataloging.
indexing. and shelving of our books on a scientific basis; to Brother
William H. Scott, who has attended to the mailing and keeping the records of the Lending Library; and to Brother Andrew Burn who has
recently made it possible to keep the Library open one additional day a
week. Brother Philip Salzman has also aided ma terially in the mechanical work connected with our book shelves. As a result of the
availability of these dedicated Brethren, the Library and Museum is
now open regularly from 10:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. on Mondays and
Wednesdays. As the demand increases, and as the supply of self-

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

213

sacrificing Brethren increases with it, we may eventually reach our goal
-that of keeping the Library open to visitors every day in the working
week. Needless to say, volunteers are always welcome, and we should
like to hear from others living around the Bay Area who may be in a
position to devote some portion of their spare time in helping us keep
the Library open for an additional day or two during the week.
Our Lending Library has so far necessarily confined itself to the
lending of books that are of more or less general interest, and that a re
easy or inexpensive to replace if lost or accidentally damaged; and the
lending has been confined to members of California Lodges residing in
the State. In this connection, an important decision was taken by this
Board at its meeting on May 12 of this year, at which time it was decided that the Lending Library would be made available to all members
of California Lodges, whatever their place of residence, in or out of
the State of California, since it was their dues indirectly that made the
operation of the Grand Lodge Library possible. It was also decided that
the Lending Library would be made available to Sojourners in California, to stimulate their interest in this activity of the California Grand
Lodge. and through that means. in California Masonry in general. Such
loans of books to Sojourners. however, would only be made upon personal application, and not by mail. and under satisfactory safeguards,
at the discretion of the Librarian in charge. Needless to say, this action
by the Board should be of assistance to the Grand Lodge Committee
on Sojourners, and should recommend itself to the Officers of California
Lodges who undouJ:>tedly would all like to see a greater participation on
the part of Sojourners in the Masonic life of the Jurisdiction.
With this progress that has been noted in the operation of a Lending
Library, the development of a Masonic Reference Library has not been
neglected, for the permanent accumulation and preservation of worthwhile works for the generations of students and readers that are to
come after us; and thus. by purchase and by gift, we can now report
the possession of over 1.600 volumes in our Library to date, not counting the numerous volumes of Proceedings of this Grand Lodge and of
other Jurisdictions in this country. Over the years, this modest beginning
can grow to respectable proportions.
Some of the items on our shelves, we might mention, are of unusual
interest. To take but one example at random. there is the two volume
Diary of the Englishman, John Evelyn, born in 1620 and a contemporary
and friend of the famous Sir Christopher Wren, a writer on architectural subjects and other matters of interest to the Masonic student, reflecting in his Diary the social and intellectual atmosphere of an era
when Specula tive Masonry was just beginning to be born .
Our stock of books was increased this year alone by the accession
of 35 books by purchase, and 428 books by gift from various Brethren

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

or their families, including a gift from the Iowa Masonic Library of
some of their duplicate copies. In addition, we have been able to borrow
from this world-famous Library in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, certain works
for which we have had requests but which we did not as yet have on

Among the generous gifts of books that have come to us from all

recently donated by Brother William T . Corbusier of Long Beach,
representing some seventy items. This includes not only many worlcs

donated by Brother Corbusier, and it is hoped that the Brethren attending this Communication will take advantage of this opportunity to view

Similarly interesting items have been added to the Grand Lodge

Two items of interest came to us last year but have not as yet been
reported to Grand Lodge and are therefore mentioned at this time. One

Luke of Concord Lodge No. 117, Sacramento, and his wife, in memory
of her brother, Jonas Sharp Miller, also a member of Concord Lodge.
This organ was originally purchased by Mrs. Luke's grandparents in
the I 870's and was played at a reception on the occasion of their golden
wedding anniversary in 1904. The other item of interest is a metal box
recently unearthed from the Cornerstone of the old Masonic Temple in

Stockton. containing a host of relics of varied historic value, both general
and Masonic. For example: a map of Stockton dated 1879, and several
other maps of the period; copies of fifteen different California newspapers dated 1883; Rosters of Officers and Members of various Masonic
Bodies of Stockton, both of the Craft and of Concordant Orders; and
even a box of some eighteen old coins going back to 1771, and a denture
set in gold plate of obvious interest to the dental profession. Thus is
California Pioneer and Masonic history preserved for future generations.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON MASONIC INFORMATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F . 0 A. M. of California:
The work of the Masonic Information Committee has been somewhat
of a contemplative nature this year, which is a description I am sure is a
familiar one to most of you.
Following a year of considerable activity, it was your Committee's
feeling that this year we should direct our attention toward three areasand calculate accomplishment, if any, in these areas only:
1. To determine just how far we, as Masons, should go in the field
of communications.
2. To set up a procedure which would accomplish this objective.
3. To handle news releases of Grand Lodge activities.
Within these three areas, I have the following to report:
First is the determination of just how far we should proceed. This,
my Brethren. is not purely an academic question. Most of us, I am aware,
feel that we have been lacking for some years in properly telling our
story to the non-Masonic public and of not using our best efforts in the
creation of a good public image for the Masonic Fraternity. It was to
correct this that the Committee on Masonic Information was created.
There are others. however, who do not think we should put forth any
effort in the creation of a good name for ourselves; that we should avoid
all forms of public communication; and that we should keep all thoughts
and utterances Masonic wholly unto ourselves. It was, and still is, the
program of your Committee on Masonic Information to reconcile these
two schools of thought; and reconciled they must be, Brethren. This is
a Fraternity among whose members there should be no contention . We
must not create a division wherein a majority is called upon to rule. We
must find a path upon which we can all walk.
Our first step was the publication of a booklet which was, with only
a few (very few) minor changes, an address given before this Grand
Lodge by Theodore Meriam prior to his election as Junior Grand Warden and while he was a member of the Committee on Masonic Information. It is titled, If Freemasonry Is Good. Let Us Talk About It. A copy
was mailed to the Master of every Lodge in this jurisdiction with the
request that he read it and hand it to the other Officers of his Lodge
with the suggestion that they also read it. If you have not read it, may
I suggest that you have your Secretary dig it out of his files and permit
you to read it, even now.
This booklet does not say, Brethren, that we should erect any billboards, carry on any advertising campaign, establish any widespread
publicity or advertising program. It says we should clean the birds' nests

218

219

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

off our window sills. We should act the part we actually do play in our
communities. We should conduct ourselves always to create the image--

is planned for later this fall. By this time next year we should have two
cooperating Masonic Press Clubs in California--0ne in the south and
one in the north.
Third, is the releasing of such general publicity as is determined to
be right and proper. We have prepared stories which have been sent to
the press. Some have been used.
. .
To carry out this program the Committee requests an appropriation
in the amount of $3,500.00 for the ensuing year.
The opportunity of serving the Grand Lodge this past year _has. been
appreciated. We are starting slowly. Brethren. It is not our obiective to
make a big splurge all at once. Rather, we want to determin~ first where
we are going, and then, how we are going to get there, taking all members of the Masonic Fraternity with us-the old timers and the new
Master Masons. I hope the Committee which carries on this work next
year will enjoy the assignment as much as we have.
R espectfully submitted,

"QUALITY, DIGNITY, SUBSTANCE."

We proposed also, in our effort to establish an area or field of work
to publish a booklet on what a new Mason could and should tell hi~
friends. A newly raised Mason is enthusiastic. He is filled with good
thoughts and a general love of the Fraternity. He goes to work the morning after his raising and his fellow workers. who may or may not be
members (usually not), ask him what it was like. what they did, did he
"ride the goat." And, what can he say? ... "It was all secret." We think
perhaps he can say something about our great and consuming interest in
public education, in the Constitution, in our state and national history,
in the good things we stand for, and that we are not a religion but a
fraternity based upon moral truths, etc.
Midway during the year, however, the Grand Master asked that
stress on this particular project be handed to the Committee on Masonic
Education. I am sure you will be seeing something along this line very
soon, if indeed you have not already.
Second is the setting up of a procedure whereby we could best
accomplish this objective. Should all public statements be made from
Grand Lodge? Should they be originated on the local level only? Should
there be a combination of these and, if so. how should it be done? The
Committee feels that news is local. The people of Lodi are more interested in their o·wn local Lodge's Public School Week activity than they
are in a meeting of the Grand Lodge in San Diego, shall we say, and
rightly so. So are the papers in Lodi, which is more to the point. So, the
Committee on Masonic Information has set out to prepare for you. the
Masters of the Lodges in this Jurisdiction, a manual on how to write a
news story, what to write, what you should avoid, and how to get it into
the papers. This manual. or the first copy of it, has now been written.
It was prepared by the Masonic Press Club of Los Angeles with Brother
R. W. Latta, Vice-President of the Masonic Press Club, as Chairman
of the Committee which actually did the work. It is now under review
by members of the Committee on Masonic Information . When the manual is as free of bugs as is possible, it is our plan that it be sent to you
in the hope that it will be of assistance to you. We expect this will be
accomplished before the end of this calendar year.
We mentioned the Masonic Press Club of Los Angeles. We are
very proud of this active Masonic organization. It is well organized,
capably run, and a credit to our Fraternity. It is our hope and plan to
c rga nize a similar club in Northern California. Brother A. W. Bramwell, a member of Leland Stanford Lodge No. 784, Chico, and publisher
of the Chico Enterprise-Record. is Chairman of the Organizing Committee. The first meeting of this Committee has been held and another

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON COLUMBIA TEMPLE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
This year Lodges from many Districts have made their pilgrimag_e
to the Masonic Hall in Columbia to confer the various D egrees of this
Craft. They have enjoyed not only the qu~intnes.s of th~ S~irit of '49
that prevails in this area, but have also enioyed its hospitality as well
as the scenic beauty of The Mother Lode Country.
Fate has dealt rather harshly with The Columbia Temple Committee this last season and it is with deep regret we report the deaths of
Brothers Alfred Mailloux, Arthur Clink, and Cecil Mathews, Chairman
of the Committee.
In spite of these hardships. may we report tha t progress is be.ing
made to establish a Masonic Museum on the gro und floor of the building. When such plans are complete and in accord with the State Park
authorities, it is hoped that each Lodge in this Jurisdiction will have
6ome item of importance they would like to have displayed.

220

We wish to thank the Officers of Grand Lodge, th~ Officers and
members of Tuolumne Lodge No. 8, the Inspectors, and Buck Nelson
our custodian.
'
To all Lodges, we extend greetings and a cordial invitation to have
you confer a degree in this historic shrine.
With regard to the appropriation for Columbia Temple this next fiscal
year, we are at a loss to submit a comprehensive report due to the sudden death of Brother Cecil Mathews, our Chairman, and lack of sufficient records at this time.
Brother Buck Nelson informs us that the California State Park
authorities insist that approved type fire extinguishers, fire exit signs and
the steel doors at basement be installed without delay as this has been
their third request on this matter; also, the dehumidifier in the vault must
be replaced before the rainy season. the present one having been in
operation continually since the vault has been in use. These are items
that should have been taken care of under last year's budget at an estimated cost of $285.00, which would have shown an expenditure of
$1.465.90 instead of $1.080.90.
With due consideration as to operating and maintenance expense for
this next year, we respectfully request the sum of $1,500.00 as previously
budgeted for Columbia Temple. Should the plans for the Masonic
Museum be consummated this year, additional funds would be required
to carry out this project.
R espect f u 11 y sub m1tte

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON SOJOURNERS
To the Most Wor~hipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Once again it is our pleasure to report to you on the progress of
our Committee. Our principal project was the publishing of a brochure
on the sojourner problem, basing our conclusions and recommendations
upon data in our past files as well as upon current suggestions. This
brochure was sent to all Lodges. We trust it has been put to good use.
Our Committeemen made their usual appearances before various
Masonic bodies and associations, lending encouragement to the efforts
of the brethren to implement our program.
That our work is successful can be seen in the affiliation figures for
the past year. There were the usual transfers within the State, approximately 1600. However, there were 838 out-of-state affiliation•s, up from
780 in 1961. When we consider that the total net gain (including plural
members) was only 896 for 1962, we can easily see how important this
item is for our continued growth pattern.
We received reports of very successful "Sojourner Nights" from
various parts of the State. It appears, however, that only some of the
Lodges are carrying the load for all the rest. Once again we commend
the former, while urging the remainder to particpate in this very important activity.
Respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM A. CoHENDET
FRANCIS H. GENTRY

It is requested that an appropriation of $150 be made to cover anticipated travel and other expenses of your Commission.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TAXATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Since filing our report for 1961, there have been no changes in the
pa">".roll tax laws or the Federal Admissions Tax which apply to our
various Masonic organizations.
As has been our custom in past years, we present, for reference purposes, the usual schedule of tax rates and wage bases for the various
payroll taxes which will be in effect during the calendar year 1963 and
thereafter. We again present in our report a section on Federal Admissions T ax.
FEDERAL WITHHOLDING (INCOME) TAX
All wages paid to employees of a Masonic Lodge are subject to Federal income tax withholding. In order to determine the amount of income
tax which is to be withheld from wages paid to its employees, the Lodge
should ask each employee to complete and file with the Secretary of the
~dge a Federal Form W-4, Employee's Withholding Exemption Certificate. Refere~ce to withholding tax tables furnished by the Treasury
Department will enable the Secretary to determine the amount to be
withheld.
FEDERAL INSURANCE CONTRIBUTIONS (SOCIAL SECURITY)
An employee of a Masonic Lodge is subject to tax for each calendar
quarter during which he earns $50 or more. The tax rates shown below
are applicable to the first $4.800 of wages paid to each employee during
the calendar year. These ra tes are to be paid by both the employer and
the employee.

Per Cent
