1968 and thereafter...................................................... 4%
There is a possibility that changes may be made by the Congress in
the wage base and/ or percentage rate applicable to the year 1963.
FEDERAL UNEMPLOYMENT T AX
Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if they employ four or
m~re individuals w~o are paid $50 or more per calendar quarter. For
this purpose, all paid employees of the Lodge, including the Secretary

CALIFORNIA UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE TAX
Masonic Lodges will be subject to this tax if the total wages paid
during a calendar quarter to taxable employees are in excess of $100.
For this purpose a taxable employee is one who is paid $50 or more per
calendar quarter. However, whether or not elected or appointed officials
of a Lodge are to be counted as taxable employees will depend upon
w hether or not the Lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax
Act.
If the Lodge is not subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act,
then the wages paid to an elected or appointed official will be exempt
from California Unemployment Insurance Tax unless the wages paid
to these officials ~ceed $100 per month.
If the Lodge is subject to the Federal Unemployment Tax Act. then
the wages paid to an elected or appointed official will be subject to
California Unemployment Insurance Tax if the wages paid to these
officials amou nt to $50, or more, per calendar quarter.
For purpose of this tax, the term "elected or appointed official" will
include any official of the Lodge who is compensated for his services.
Those usually compensated for their services are the Secretary, Tiler,
Organist, and Soloist.

terior decorator, improvements are taking place, such as re-'Covering
furniture, replacements of old furniture, better lighting. repainting, and
rea£1ranging of equipment.
In addition to use by the students, the use of the club house facilities has been extended to the East Bay Masters and Wardens Association. Berkeley-Albany Masters and Wardens Association, Masonic
Lodges, University Square Club, and the DeMolay. It is the hope
of the Board that many Masons attending their Grand Lodge Communication this year may find time to visit the club house and see for
themselves the excellent facilities available for use by the students.
The budget for the fiscal year ending July 31. 1963, adopted by
the Board, and previously submitted to the Finance Committee, is
attached hereto a s Exhibit Number One and is incorporated as a
part of this report.
The Board recommends, in furtherance of its objective of obtaining a greater use of the club house at Berkeley, that an annual letter
from the Grand Master. preferably timed to be read at the June Stated
Meetings, be mailed to the various Lodge Secretaries, reminding California Masons about the two club houses, and particularly calling to
the Craft's attention the fact that those eligible to membership are
Masons, the sons, daughters and blood relatives of Masons. that personal membership in the Masonic Order is not a requisite, and that
the club is co-educational.
The Board also recommends that the foregoing information and
other suitable publicity about the two dub houses appear annually in
the summer issue of the California Freemason.
Your Board of Directors deem it a privilege to serve this worthy
Masonic activity.
Respectfully submitted,

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS
OF THE MASONIC CLUB
UNIVERSIT Y OF CALIFORNI A AT LOS ANGELES
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
It has been several years since we have given a brief resume of the
Club's activities, and therefore we submit the following:
A full social calendar is provided during the school year with
Coffee Hours on Tuesday and Wednesday afternoons, Friday and/or
Saturday night parties, dinners before Council Meetings (open to all
members}. Monthly Dinners before all General Meetings. The ~mmmer
program includes beach parties, bridge parties, and trips to the Hollywood Bowl. Greek Theater and baseball games.
Following are some of the year's highlights:
There is an orientation program at the beginning of each semester,
during which pamphlets of our Club are sent to all students entering
the University. A booth is maintained on campus to distribute liternture
and acquaint the newcomers with the Club and its activities.
A Thanksgiving dinner is held for under-priviledg ed children, each
Club Member paying for his own and one child's dinner.
A Christmas Party is held for parents, initiation of new Member-s,
and various honor awards. This usually has an attendance of about 275
people.
The Reception for the Grand Master is the highlight of the year,
and also has an attendance of about 275 people.
Last year, our Club participated in the Mardi Gras at UCLA and
received two trophies. The proceeds from this activity were used to help
maintain a camp for needy children.
There is a Spring Initiation of new Members, at which further
honor awards are made.
These are but a few of the various activities that help to keep our
members occupied.
There has been considerable comment in our last few reports about
the Masonic Club movie. This movie was shown to the members at last
Grand Lodge, and appeared to be well received. The purpose is to make
available to all Lodges something that describes the Club and its
activities. This movie has been shown by four Northern California
Lodges, nineteen Southern California Lodges, and various DeMolay,
Job's Daughters, Rainbow Girls, Eastern Star and service groups. We
are quite pleased with the picture's reception, and the various favorable
comments that have been received from these groups. The picture is
available to anyone who would like to show it at any Lodge or other
Masonic group. A request to our resident hostess will secure the picture.
Shown below is our 1962-63 Budget with explanatory footnotes.
Again, it has been a distinct pleasure for your Board of Directors
to have served during the past year. It has been a rewarding experience
for all of us, and we are gratified for having been given the opportunity
of serving.

ROBER T NORMA N GRAHA M WALKE R. Bob Walker was
raised a M as ter Mason in June, 1939, in Palo Alto Lodge No. 346 and
served as Master of that Lodge in 1945. He was also a Past Master of EI
~amino R esearch Lodge and was a member of other Masonic organiza tions. He was commissioned as Inspecto r in July, 1948, and continue d
t~ serve J?istrict 368 until the end of December, 1957. During tha t time
his capacity to serve, and deep interest in the Brethren in his Lodges.
endeared him not only in his own D istrict but thro ughout all the Lodges
in the Santa Clara Valley. It came as a shock to many to know that Bob
had passed away on March 3, 1962, at the comparti vely early age of 57
years. His large heartedn ess inspired kindlines s and a strong spirit of
fraternit y among his Brethren , and Bob Walker is missed very much in
Santa Clara County.
WESLE Y WILLIA M KERGA N. A very well known and highly
respected Mason, particula rly in East Bay Masonic Circles, was called
from labor on April 3. 1962. Brother Kergan was raised a Master Mason
in Sequoia Lodge No. 349 on Decembe r 2, 1912, and served as its
Master in 1920. H e was commissioned Inspecto r in 1921 and continue d
~o serve in the old 35th District until 1939-fo r 18 years. H is help and
influence were real factors in molding the fraternal spirit in East Bay
Masonry. In 1947-48, when Most Worship ful Chester H. Warlow was
Grand Mas ter, he served this Grand Lodge with distinctio n as its Grand
~arshal. He served the cause and spirit of M asonry long and ably, and
his labor has not been in vain in the Lord.
WILLIA M NICKSO N PEDDE R was raised a Master Mason in
Anchor Lodge N o. 273 on November 25, 1926. In 1937 he affiliated with
Temple City Lodge No. 612, a nd served as Master of that Lodge in
1945. H e was commissioned an Inspecto r in May, 1950, and served
Distric.t No. 538 for four years. Brother P edder passed away in Port
of Spam on the Island of Trinidad on July 16, 1962, and funeral services,
conducte d by Temple City Lodge No. 612 , were held in Temple City
on July 30, 1962.

LEO ELLSW ORTH SIEVER T. a Vice Presiden t of the Santa F e
Railway, and an outstand ing civic leader, passed away in Karachi,
Pakis tan, on M ay 2, 1962. after a very brief illness. Brother Sievert was
raised a Master Mason on April 7, 1920. was a charter member of San
Marino Lodge No. 685, and served that Lodge as its Master in 1947.
During the years he was Senior Warden and Master of his Lodge-1946 and 1947- he served as a member of the Grievanc es C ommittee
of this Grand Lodge, and 1949 through 1954 he was a Director of the
Berkeley Clubhou se. At the time of his death he was a member of
the Grand Lodge Retireme nt P lan Committee. An outstand ing attorney
and business executive. Brother Sievert had served on many importan t
universit y and civic committees and received many honors for his distinguishe d service. His family home was in San M ateo and he is survived by his wife, three sons and two da ughters. This Grand Lodge
lost a very able member and Californ ia an outstand ing citizen when
Leo Sievert was taken from us.
HARRY G . WILSO N. The City of Redland s was saddened by
the sudden death of its Councilm an and former Mayor, H arry G.
Wilson, on August 13, 1962. Brother Wilson was a member of Redlands Lodge No. 300 and served as its Master in 1957. H e was a member of the Grand Lodge Committ ee on Research from 1958 to 1960.
Redland s was s hocked by his death and the present Mayor of the
City wrote, "In my opinion, he was one of the kindest persons I have
ever known and also one of the most unselfish with his own time and
consider able ability. H e never said ' no' when it was somethin g for his
Church, his Lodge, his clubs, or his commun ity.
SAMUE L EDWAR D LEDDE L. Just before this Grand Lodge
convened word was received that Brother Samuel E. Leddel of Long
Beach passed away on Septemb er 28th. Raised a Master Mason on
October I 8, 1932. he served Los Cerritos Lodge No. 674 as its Master
in 1939. H e was Senior Grand Steward during the year 1955-56 when
Most Worship ful Edgar V. Stewart, Jr .. was G rand Master. For a number of years he had served on the Cemeter ies Committ ee of this Grand
Lodge and since I 960 has been Chairma n o f that Committee. At the
time of his death Brother Leddel was also a member of the boards of
the P sychiatric Clinic for Children; Long Beach Memoria l Hospital ;
Jewish Commun ity Federation and other civic committi es. His death
at the early age of 52 is a real loss to both his city and to our fraternity .

o f us will know some whose names are there. They were Brethren
with whom we served and to whom we were closely bound by ties of
friendship. We cannot escape a measu re of the sense of loss, but we
are not of those "who, hopeless lay their dead away." We would not
sit in sadness but rather be thankful that we have been privileged to

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

IN GRAND LODGE
MORNING SESSION-THURSDAY, OCTOBER 11, 1962
At 9 :30 a.m. Grand Lodge was called on. the Grand Master presiding. The invocation was delivered by the Grand Chaplain. The minutes
of the morning session of Wednesday. October 10th, were read and
approved.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON GRIEVANCES
(Items reported on at different times during the Communication are
consolidated to facilitate reference.)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M . of California:
Your Committee on Grievances reports as follows:
This Committee has considered 52 trial records. This omnibus report will cover 36, and the others will be the subject of special reports.
We again urge Lodges to proceed diligently in all disciplinary matters. We do not advocate rushing a case, but unpleasant business should
not be postponed unduly. Every year a number of trial records come
in during the last month or two prior to the Annual Communication,
some of them having been pending for as much as a year.
We also urge that copies of charges filed be sent at once to the Grand
Secretary, as req uired by our Code, and that form s for procedure be
secured from the Grand Secretary.
In the following trial records all procedure has been substantially
correct, and there is evidence sufficient to support all findings. We find
no miscarriages of justice:
No. 1699~A member of El Cerrito Lodge No. 705, Expelled. November 6, 1961.

To the Mo st Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
A member of All States Lodge No. 593 was expelled by the Lodge

plea in the Lodge and the Master made sufficient investigation to sup~

The accused has filed a letter which he calls an appeal and also a
petition for restoration. The appeal was filed too late but we have considered the file and find no errors.
Although a Lodge ,c annot restore a suspended member until the
suspension has been affirmed by Grand Lodge, it would appear that
Grand Lodge has the inherent power to affirm an expulsion and forthwith grant a petition for restoration which has been properly filed and
noticed, such hasty action should be taken in rare cases only. In this
case the Lodge is opposed to res toration of its former member.
We offer the following resolution:

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1735

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
The accused in Trial Record No. 1735 was a member of North Hollywood Lodge No. 542. The specification on which the accused was tried
was based on the conviction of the accused in the Municipal Court of
a misdemeanor offense.
Nine commissioners were duly elected and the trial was held with
all nine commissioners present and participating. The transcript of all
the testimony in the criminal case was introduced in evidence before the
com missioners.
On the issue of guilt the vote of the commissioners was "guilty-I,"
"not guilty-8" and on the issue of unmasonic conduct the verdict was
unanimous "not guilty."
At the opening of the trial counsel for the accused after interrogation of two of the commissioners objected to their qualifications to serve.
The objections were based on the claim that they were prejudiced in
favor of the accused. The Trial Master over-ruled the objections.
It has been urged to this Committee that the commissioners to whom
objection was made should have been disqualified and that findings of
the commissioners should be reversed and the matter retried.
Although it may be conceded that there is a sound basis for disagreement as to whether the objections should have been granted or
denied by the Trial Master by reason of the unanimous decision of the
nine commissioners we have determined that their decision should be
affirmed and we offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the finding of "not guilty" by the Trial Commission in Trial Record No. 1735 be affirmed.
Adopted.
TRIAL RECORD NO. 1764
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
In Trial Record No. 1764 the accused, a member of West Gate Lodge
No. 335. was under amended charges, charged under the following specifications:
1. That as an insurance agent he wilfully and falsely failed to cover
the accuser with Workmen's Compensation Insurance for which he
received payment of premium and retained said payment for his own use.
As a result thereof the accuser was uninsured on January 6, 1958. when
his employee was injured in the course of his employment. This caused
a financial loss in the sum of $7,500.00 to the accuser.
2. That on or about October, 1960, the accused filed a petition in
bankruptcy for which he included in his list of unsecured creditors the

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

255

accuser's claim in the amount of $7.500.00 which he stated arose from
his failure to secure an insurance contract for the accuser.
3. That during the year 1959 the accused forged the name of a cosigner on a personal note.
4. That during the year 1961 the accused did without cause or justification instigate an investigation of the accuser by the Internal Revenue
Department.
A trial was held before commissioners in which both the accused
and accuser were represented by competent counsel. They found the
accused guilty on ,specifications 1 and 2 and not guilty on specifications
3 and 4 and guilty of unmasonic conduct with the penalty fixed at
suspension.
The evidence presented at the trial shows that the accuser filed a
civil action against the accused for failure to cover him with Workmen's
Compensation Insurance and obtained a judgment in the amount of
$7.500.00 based principally on the accused's negligence.
This entire record indicates that all the facts in specifications 1 - 4
arose out of a business dispute between an insurance broker and one of
his clients. As stated in Section 684 ( d) CMC. "To warrant an appeal
to Masonic censure, the case must involve a willful and deliberate disregard of moral and Masonic duty and an intention knowingly and
wilfully to cheat and defraud a Brother."
A thorough examination of the Trial Record fails to reveal any evidence of fraud on the part of the accused. The money which he received
was applied to other insurance policies which he obtained for the accused.
None was retained for his own personal gain or benefit.
Nor does the record reflect any illegalit'Y in the filing of the bank~
ruptcy petition which the accused testified he did on the advice of his
counsel.
Your Committee is of the opinion that there is not sufficient evidence
in the record to support a finding of guilty on specificatons 1 and 2 and
of unmasonic conduct.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the finding of guilty of the Trial Commission in
Trial Record No. 1764 on Specifications 1 and 2 and of unmasonic
conduct be reversed and that a finding of not guilty be substituted therefor.
Adopted .

TRIAL RECORD NO. 1771

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 8 A. M. of California:
The accused in Trial Record No. 1771 is a member of Natoma Lodge
No. 64. The onginal charge contained five specifications of which two
were of doubtful validity as constituting only civil disputes.
Approximately seven and one-half months after the five charges
were presented a further charge based on a plea of guilty to petty theft
entered by accused in a case in the Municipal Court (Santa ClaraC u per ti no Judicial District) for which he was fined.
The accused pleaded "not guilty" to all six specifications. Nine
trial commissioners were elected but only six were present for the trial.
As to the first five specifications no evidence was presented by the
accuser. As to number six, the only evidence was the petty theft plea.
The accused presented a sworn written statement which detailed his
defense of each specification.
As to each specification l to 5 inclusive, the verdict was unanimous,
"not guilty." On specification No. 6, on the issue of guilt. the vote was
unanimous, "guilty," and on the issue of unmasonic conduct the vote
was, "guilty" 5, "not guilty" I. The vote on the issue of "expulsion"
was "aye" l, "no" 5.
The first vote on the issue of suspension was "aye" 2, "no" 4. The
Trial Master noted that the vote lacked a majority of the nine elected
commissioners and called for a second ballot on "suspension" which
resulted in "aye" 5, "no" l.
It is to be noted that the criminal charge originally filed against
the accused (Specification No. 6) was forgery based on a check for
$87.00 payable to cash and purportedly signed by the accused as
maker. H e at all times denied the offense but on the advice of his
attorney pleaded guilty to PETTY THEFT, a misdemeanor.
There has been presented to the Grievance Committee documentary
evidence by an expert witness on questioned documents, whose opinion
is that the defendent did not sign the check previously referred to nor
did he write any part of it. We have also received an affidavit by the
merchant who accepted the alleged forged check which recites that it
was presented to him by the estranged wife of the accused.
We would question the action of the commissioners in taking a

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

257

second ballot on the issue of "suspension" after the first ballot was 2
"aye" and 4 "no" ( 72 l CMC) but in view of our other fin dings we
need not rule on this point.
We are of the opinion that the trial record in itself would require a
reversal and re-trial but by reason of the documentary evidence presented on the appeal and without detailing all the evidence we have
unanimously det ermined that the accused never committed the F ORGERY on which the plea of guilty of PETTY THEFT was made and
that he was not guilty of PETTY THEFT to which his attorney advised
a guilty plea.
.
.
It is our conclusion tha t the Lodge should not be required to re-try
the matter and that the decision of the commissioners on specifications
I, 2. 3, 4 and 5 be affirmed: their decision as to specification 6 be reversed and the charge dismissed ( 761 CMC).
We offer the following resolution :
RESOLVED. that the decision of the Trial Commissioners on
specifications 1, 2. 3. 4 and 5 be affirmed; that the decision on specification 6 be reversed and the specification dismissed.
Adopted .

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON JURISPRUDENCE

DECISION No . 2
The Grand Master ruled that "capital gains" distributed by certain
mutual investment trusts and corporations, whose securities are held as
an investment of life membership funds are not "income" under the
meaning of that word as used in Section 404. California Masonic Code.
and that hence such capital gains are not to be included as revenue in
the calculation of the amount available for "refreshment and fraterna l
intercourse" within the purview of Section 412, California Masonic
Code.
He further ruled that distribution by such investment trusts or corporations of "ordinary income" may be included in the calculations
mentioned in Sections 404 and 412, California Masonic Code.
We concur with the conclusions so reached by the Grand Master
and move approval thereof.
Adopted unanimously.

(Items reported on at different times during the Communication are
consolidated to facilitate reference.)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your Committee expresses its gratitude to the Grand Master for his
consideration in submitting to this Committee in ample time for our study
the decisions made by him during the course of the year. We would
hope that his practice in that respect may be adopted by his successors
in office. We commend the practice to them.
We report on the Grand Master's decisions as follows:
DEc1s10N No. 1
The decision holds that the provisions of Section 403 of the California Masonic Code apply to Lodge Temple Associations and to
Masonic Temple Associations. but that no Lodge. Lodge Temple Association or Masonic Temple Association is required to submit to the
Investment Advisor used by Grand Lodge, proposed investments in
savings accounts in, and investment certificates and shares issued by
building and loan and savings and loan associations.
We concur with the Grand Master and move approval of the decision.
The Grand Master declared the clarification of Section 403 CMC
an emergent matter and the following was submitted:
By reason of the interpretation by the Grand Master in his Decision
No. 1, and the concurrence of your Committee therein. and in order to
clarify Section 403 of the California Masonic Code, your Committee
offers the following resolution:
RESOLVED: That the next to last paragraph of Section 403, California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
"Should a Lodge, Lodge Temple Association or Masonic Temple
Association elect to invest in funds under the provisions of Sections 2,
or 3 (a), or 3 ( b) hereof. it shall confer and counsel as to any such
proposed or contemplated investments with the professional Investment
Advisor used by Grand Lodge, whose fees will be paid by Grand Lodge."
We move the adoption of the resolution and urge a yes vote.
Adopted unanimously.

DEcis10N No. 3
In his Decision No. 3, the Grand Master held that:
" ... cornerstone laying and dedication ceremonies for public school
buildings or other exclusively public buildings may be conducted on
Sunday, if in the discretion of the Grand Master, the same may be done
without infringing the spirit of Masonry."
We concur with the Grand Master in his decision and move its
approval.
Adopted unanimously.
DECISION No. 4

The Grand Master held that Sec. 334-c, CMC. does not prohibit the
listing of the business or occupation, business address and telephone
number of members in a Lodge roster. We concur with the Grand
Master.
The mere possibility that such a roster may be used for commercial
exploitation does not affect the legality of such a roster.
We move approval of the decision.
Adopted unanimously.
DECISION No. 5
The Grand Master ruled that where a deceased brother died in good
standing, having had a long and distinguished career in Masonry, and
who had willed his body to a university for medical research, a proper
request having been made for burial with Masonic honors, such request
should be granted. regardless of the disposition of the brother's remains
and of the fact that his remains may not be present at the funeral service.
We concur with the decision, and move its approval.
Adopted unanimously.

consolidated to facilitate reference.}
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
TEXTBOOKS FOR THE PHILIPPINES

That portion of the report of the Committee on Public Schools, relative to the letter addressed to our Grand Master from the Grand Master
of the Philippines, has been referred to the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes.
The writer states that during the last war the Japanese systematically
destroyed all textbooks in the English language and that despite the
efforts of many Americans to replace them the situation has never been
substantially alleviated. resu lting in such a shortage that. on the average, three children are forced to use one textbook.
He asks that the Lodges of California undertake the collection of
used textbooks and states that arrangements have been made with the
United States Navy for their transportation, free of charge.
The Committee on Public Schools feels. as does the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes, that this request is challenging and
worthy. and that every effort be made to assist our sister Jurisdiction in
this endeavor.
We, therefore, recommend that the Committee on Public Schools be
encouraged to activate the program among the several constituent Lodges
of the Jurisdiction and that the Lodges be urged to cooperate.
We recommend the adoption of this report and a yes vote.
Adopted.
Respectfully submitted,

CANDIDA TES' INSTRUC TION

We agree that there is a conflict between the duties of Inspecto r and
of Secretary . The Inspecto r is represen tative of Grand Lodge in his
District. Under Section 161 of the Californ ia Masonic Code, he must
examin.e th.e books and records of the Lodge , kept by the Secretar y, to
determin e 1£ the manner of transacti ng the business of the Lodge and
of making returns conform to our laws, and he must report to the Grand
Master any violation s of law. As Secretary , he must obey the will and
pleasure of the Worship ful Master, but as Inspecto r he must inspect
the work and correct the same and report the working condition of the
Lodge to the Grand Lecturer . and he may even require the Master to
convene his Lodge for inspectio n. We do not believe the performa nce
of all these duties can be properly placed in the sam e hands.
We, therefore . approve the policy repor ted by the Grand Lecturer
as to this matter and move adoption of this report.
Adopted .

The Committ ee on Policg and General Purposes :
There has been referred to your Committ ee on Policy and General
Purposes the portion of the Grand Lecturer 's Report in which he reports
to Grand Lodge that, with the assistanc e of the other members of the
Committ ee on Ritual. he has formulat ed and is putting into operatio n a
system of instructio n and educatio n of candidat es through the coaches
of the constitue nt Lodges, including the use of a handboo k for coaches
and for the candidat es which has been prepared by the Grand Lecturer .
One of the members of the Committ ee on Policy and General Purposes has reviewed the material included in the handboo k and your
Committ ee has consider ed the proposed system of instructio n. We
highly commend the Grand Lecturer and the members of the Committee on Ritual for the excellent work which has gone into the preparation of this material.
We thorough ly agree with the Grand Lecturer that if Masonic
educatio n is to be effective . it mus t commenc e upon the candidat e level
and during the time w hen the candidat e is receiving his degrees and
is most recepti ve to instructio n.
We , therefore , recomme nd the approval of this portion of the Report
of the Grand Lecturer and move the adoption of this report.
The Committ ee on Finance indicated their concurre nce in the recommend ation.
Adopted .

COLUMB IA TEMPLE MUSEUM

The Committ ee on Policg and General Purposes:
In his reference to the Columbi a Masonic Temple, the Grand Master
has reported that the Universi ty of the Pacific has presente d a plan
whereby the University would use the ground floor of the Temple as a
Museum . featuring historical items dealing with early Californi a History.
A curator would be provided for the Museum and his services would
make it possible for visitors to view the Lodge Hall. which privilege is
not now available at all times.
This proposal would require consider ation by the Universi ty, the
Grand Lodge and the approval of the proper division of the State of
Californ ia as lessor.

CEMETERY AT JAMESTOWN

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Committee on Masonic Cemeteries has recommended that the
Grand Lodge acquire title to a cemetery at Jamestown. approximately
three miles from Sonora. No information is given except that title is said
to have been in St. James Lodge No. 54 which surrendered its charter
on February 20. 1875. It is stated that no burials have been made in this
cemetery since 1876 and it is so overgrown that it is impossible to ascertain how many graves are there or the condition of headstones.
In the absence of adequate information as to what may be involved
in acquiring or clearing title. and thereafter maintaining the cemetery.
your Committee cannot make a recommendation what the policy should
be. We. therefore. move that the matter of the cemetery at Jamestown
be referred to the Committee on Masonic Cemeteries for further investigation and report.
The Committee on Finance indicated their concurrence in the rec ommendation.
Adopted.

O[SPLAY NATIONAL EMBLEM

( 14)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes. to which was referred Resolution No. 14. reports as follows:
The Resolution would require the display of the National Colors
from an appropriate flagstaff. on top or in front of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple. on every day of the year between the hours
of sunrise and sunset. except in inclement weather.
The preliminary paragraphs of the Resolution recite the traditional
devotion of Masons to patriotism and love of country and call attention
to the fact that our Temple is dedicated to those members of our Craft
who gave their lives in defense of their country.
As required· by California Masonic Code 554w. the Flag of our
Country is displayed at all Communications of Grand Lodge and at all
meetings of our Lodges; on frequent occasions it is formally presented at
the Altar of the Lodge by the Marshal. There is no question but that
the Fraternity by every appropriate means urges upon and inculcates
in its members devotion to the United States of America. It does not
seem to this Committee. however. that flying the Flag on or in front of
the California Masonic M emorial T emple. not only when the Grand
Lodge offices are open- as is done at the present time, but also on Saturdays. Sundays and holidays .. from sunrise to sunset," will significantly
impress our members or the public at large with any additional reverence
for the Colors or devotion to patriotism. Moreover. it is obvious that it
would be necessary to employ an additional building custodian to fully
perform the duty of literal compliance with the Resolution. which would
require th e Flag to be flo wn as early as sunrise every morning. to remain there until sunset of each evening "on every day of the year."
We recommend that Resolution No. 14 be not adopted or approved.
The Committee on Finance indicated their concurrence in the recommendation.
A majority voted against the resolution.

ferred to your Committee on Policy and General Purposes.
The recommendation would add four new sections to the CMC.
It proposes technical changes in the corporate organization of the Masonic Club at Berkeley. including increasing the number of directors from
nine to fifteen. a nd providing for staggered three year terms. It grants
to Grand Lodge more effective control and supervision over an important
Masonic activity which has been maintai ned and supported by Grand
Lodge from the beginning.
The Board of Directors of the Club concurs in the recommended
changes and has already taken the necessary preliminary steps to change
the articles and by-laws of the corporation.
Your Committee moves the adoption of the recommendation and
recommends a yes vote.
The Committee on f urisprudence:
RESOLVED: That a new article be added to the Ordinances in
the California Masonic Code to be numbered ARTICLE IV - B bearing the title " D irectors of the Masonic Club of the University. Berkeley,
California" and that the following sections be added thereunder:
Section 231. Appointment of Directors. The directors of the Masonic
Club of the University. Berkeley, California. consisting of fifteen shall
be appointed by the Grand Master for terms of three years each, provided. however, that the terms of one-third of the directors shall expire
at the close of the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge each year.
Where a vacancy occurs the appointee shall serve for the remainder of
the unexpired term. The Grand Master may remove a director at any
time.
Section 232. Board of Directors and Title to Property. The duly
qua lified directors shall constitute the Board of Directors of the Masonic
Club of the University, Berkeley, California. a corporation. which shall
hold title to all assets of said corporation.
Section 233. Organization of the Board. Said Directors shall organize
by the election of officers each year at the close of the Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. They shall adopt by- laws for their own guidance
and for the management of said corporation , which by-laws they may
alter or amend at any time, all subject to the approval of the Grand
M aster. They shall have the right to incur indebtedness, but not to borrow money without the consent of the Grand Master. The Grand Master
shall at all times have the right of visitation and inspection, and the
supervision of the entire management.
Section 234. Annual Reports. The Directors shall submit a printed
Annual Report in detail to Grand Lodge at the beginning of each Annual Communication respecting operations and the condition of the
assets and lia bilities of said corporation, together with a proposed budget
for the ensuing year which shall be referred to the Committee on Finance
for appropriate consideration by Grand Lodge.
We move adoption of the resolution and recommend a yes vote.
Adopted 5/ 6 vote.

MEMBERSHIP QUALIFICATION
(4)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 4 proposes that Section 511 of the California Masonic
Co~~ be amended by adding thereto the following:
Provided that one who has served a term in the state prison and
w~o has since lived properly should not by reason of the service of said
pnson_ term be deemed ineligible for Masonry."
It is stated in .an introductory clause that Grand Lodge has heretofore made exceptions to the rule of ineligibility of felons to receive the
degrees and two references are made to the Proceedings of the 1958
Communication. When one of the proponents of the resolution appeared
b:for~ our Committee, it was pointed out to him that in neither of the
cited instances had the applicant involved been convicted of a felony
and. b:ing trained in the law, he conceded such to have been the case.
. It is apparent from the resolution a nd the proponent that the resolut10.n has it~ genesis in the fact that the proponents know of one pros?ec~1~e applicant whom they consider worthy of admisison, but who is
mehg1ble because some years ago he was sentenced to and served a
term in a state prison.

However. the policy of the Grand Lodge must not be determined by
the situation of one or even a dozen prospective applicants. The question is: Will Freemasonry be benefited by opening the doors of its
Lodge rooms to those who have served time in state prisons? It is the
considered opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes
that such action would be a disservice to Masonry. There are hundred~
of thousands of men who are not Masons who have not served prisor
terms and the policy of ineligibility of felons. which has stood unchanged
since the inception of this Grand Lodge, should not now be changed
because of sympathy or liking for a given prospect.
We recommend a no vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
RESOLVED: That Section 511, CMC. be amended by adding at
the end of said section the following:
"Provided that one who has served a term in state prison and
who has since lived properly should not by reason of the service of said
term be deemed ineligible for Masonry."
For 87 years. since 1875. our law has been:
"One who has served a term in state prison is not under the tongue
of good report, and it is not proper to receive his petition." ( 511-g CMC)
This resolution 'Nill repeal this law.
This law ha& never been contradicted by Grand Lodge albeit the
proposers of this resolution erroneously contend that Grand Lodge has
made exceptions.
The proposers of this resolution attempt to equate the rights of an
uninitiated felon with those of a brother by contending that a brother
who serves time in prison may be restored to M asonic status by Grand
Lodge. We should remember that there is a fellowship which extends
a helping hand to a fallen brother.
If adopted, this resolution will create dissension within Lodges and
invite shame and ridicule by having it said that felons can gain membership.
We ask you to always remember our precepts: that to become a
Mason is a distinct honor and privilege-not a matter of common right;
that a candidate mus t be "under the tongue of good report" is a Masonic
requirement as old and as honored as the Fraternity itself and is a bulwark of protection of the Order and of every member thereof; and that
unimpeachable character and conduct are synonymous with Masonry
and must ever remain so.
We move adoption of this Resolution No. 4 but urge a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

PROCEEDING S OF THE

BURIAL WITH MASONIC HONORS
(10)
The Committee on Policy and G eneral Purposes:
Your Committee on P olicy and General Purposes has considered
Resolution No. I 0, proposed by three Past Masters of South San Francisco Lodge No. 212 , to provide that where a member in good standing
is alleged to have committed murder and then suicide, the Master and
W ardens of the Lodge are to determine whether or not the deceased
shall be buried with Masonic honors.
The fact that a member is in good standing and of general good
repu tation is no guarantee that he has not committed the a lleged crime,
nor that the suicide is not itself an admission of his guilt. Obviously
there can be no legal determinatio n of the guilt or innocence o f the deceased member, since he cannot be prosecuted.
We believe that the proposed interpretatio n is wholly unnecessary ,
since the Master and W ardens, under Section 604 of the CMC. already
are given the r ig ht to determine as to the propriety of burying a suicide
with Masonic honors. We have such provision, even though at common
law suicide was a felony and even though in the minds of ma ny people
today suicide carries a moral stigma.
We would suggest. however. that in a case of this kind the Master
and Wardens should be extremely cautious in the exercise of the right.
because in giving a Masonic burial to one alleged to have committed
murder the attendant publicity could adversely reflect upon the Fraternity.
We move the adoption of the resolution but we recommend a no
vote on the resolution.
Th e Committee on furisprudence:
RESOLVE D :
That Sec. 604 CMC be amended as follows:
Insert at the end thereof the following language:
In the event that it a ppea rs that an alleged felony has been committed a nd the accused thereupon committed suicide. the Master and
the Wardens are to determine whether or not the accused is to be
buried with M asonic Honors. As our Civil La ws protect the accused.
in that a man is innocent until proven guilty of the crime of which
he is accused, it must be borne in mind that a Police Report is an
official preliminary investigatio n but does not necessarily establish
the fina l proof o f guilt of the accused, nor the conviction of the accused for the crime. Furthermore , if there is reasonable doubt of the
accused's guilt because of alternate or remote possibilities involved.
he should receive proper consideratio n to be buried with Masonic
Honors, provided that he was a Master Mason in good standing at
the time.

GRA ND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

281

This resolution would introduce a set of facts relating to one particular case only. Facts are probative and a s et of hypothetical facts
should not be included in the law.
A s our law now stands the Master and W a rdens have the power to
determine facts in all cases and the discretion to bury a suicide . We think
our law as it now exists is sound and that our Masters and Wardens
are reliable.
W e move adoption of the Resolution but urge a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution .

In summa ry Resolution No. 11 would eliminate paragraph 18 of
Section 385 CMC which now req uires that none but a Past Master of
a C a lifornia Lodge is eligible for election as Master or W arden of a
Research Lodge and provide that if such Master or Warden is not a
Past Master of a Cali fornia Lodge he must produce a certificate of proficiency in the opening and closing ceremonies. The resolution then seeks
to amend paragraph 10 to fu rther clarify the distinction between one
who has served as Master of a Resea rch Lodge and a Past Master of
other constit uent Lodges.
Th e effect of this resolution would be to further distinguish Research
Lodges from other constitue nt Lodges. One may well argue that if they
are to be constituent Lodges then Research Lodges should follow the
general rules applicable to constituent Lodges. On th~. other ~and, th.e
first sentence of Section 38 5 states in part as follows : A special class1fication of constituent Lodges is hereby established ... " . T his, together
with the many restrictions and the qualification s fou nd in Section 385,
indicates that it wa s never intended that the Research Lodges and the
other constituent Lodges were to be governed by the same r ules.
The members of your Committee on Policy and General P urposes
are persuaded that th is legislation is necessary to preserve some of the

the position of Master or Wa rden. We. therefore, move the a doption

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

After painstaking work and research. new legislation was presented
during Grand Master Drapeau's year and was adopted as law ( 1952
Proc. p. 326). It is recorded in Sec. 385 CMC.
Ever since, it seems that some members of Research Lodges have
tried to change the law. In 1953 they sought and were granted exemption
from minimum annual dues (Sec. 385-17 CMC). This was an advantage over regular Lodges. They sought representation in Grand Lodge.
This was rejected ( 1960 Proc. p. 260). They have another Resolution
No. 12 now before Grand Lodge in which it is asked that an appropriation or subsidy of $500.00 be extended to each Research Lodge to establish a Masonic library. This seeks advantage over regular Lodges.
No regular Lodge is entitled to nor has sought subsidy. It is fundamental
that Lodges should be self-sustaining. So should Research Lodges. They
have still another Resolution No. 9 now before Grand Lodge seeking
appointment of an Honorary Marshal to present the flag during Installation Ceremony. In such ceremony the Lodge has been opened and the
flag is in the Lodge. To present another one would be cumbersome.
This is an intrusion into the affairs of a Lodge by Research members.
The Resolution No. 11 now before us. seeking amendment of Sec.
385CMC,isinthreeparts (A), (B) & (C).
(A) would amend paragraph 10 of Sec. 385 CMC to read as specified in the resolution. This language is completely unnecessary for OU'.!'
law as it now exists amply covers the proposals, as follows:
1. Sec. 8 CMC (Constitution) defines members of Grand Lodge.
Officers and former officers of a Research Lodge are not among them.
2. Sec. 490 CMC defines a Past Master and a Past Master of a Research Lodge is not included.
After this resolution has been acted upon by Grand Lodge, if necessary, we shall present a resolution in just a few words which will
clarify all.
( B) would amend paragraph 5 of Sec. 385 CMC and require proficiency certificates from an Inspector for Officers of Research Lodges
who are not Past Masters. This would place an additional burden on
our already overburdened Inspector's and should not be required. As
our law now stands this is not necessary.
(C) would strike paragraph 18 of Sec. 385 CMC which reads, as
follows:
"18. None but a Past Master of a California Lodge is eligible for
election as Master. Senior or Junior Warden of a Research Lodge."
This legislation was adopted in 1960 ( 196() Proc. p. 256). In 1961
members of Research Lodges asked repeal and were voted down by
Grand Lodge ( 1961 Proc. p. 296). They are again asking repeal.
We think this section should not be repealed. In our Lodges the
Officers pass through the several chairs to the Master's Chair. The pur-

pose of this is to enable the Officer to become acquainted with our rules.
regulations and precepts and to learn how to govern the Lodge. Research Lodges exist by the sufferance of Grand Lodge and they are expected at all times to be Masonic in character. The operating officers
should be experienced Masons.
We move adoption of Resolution No, 11 but urge a no vote.
If the foregoing resolution is rejected, present the following :
RESOLVED:
That Sec. 385-5 be amended by inserting therein the following
Code Sections: 8 and 490.
A simple majority voted for the resolution. Failing a 5/6 vote, the
matter was held over until the 1963 Annual Communication.

SERVING OF LIQUORS
(15)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 15 has been referred to the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes.
This resolution proposes to delete from Section 408 of the California
Masonic Code that portion which reads. "nor shall any such liquors be
used or served at any Ma·s onic banquet or gathering."
We feel sure that the proponent did not realize the full implication
of his resolution, but a literal interpretation would mean that liq uor could
be served at any Masonic function. including Stated Meetings, the conferring of degrees or even in Grand Lodge at its communications.
It is stated by the proponent that our law regarding liquor " does not
reflect the concept of our modern way of life."
Your Committee could argue at length on our objections to the reso~
lution, but feels that it is sufficient to say that the Fraternity does not
change its cu.stems and laws because of what society generally has a ccepted as proper and further. that the serving of liquor at Masonic fu nctions would be offensive to many of our members.
The resolution would accomplish no good purpose but would do
irreparable harm to the Craft.
We move the adoption of the resolution, but your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes recommends a no vote.

That Sec. 408 CMC be amended, as follows:
Strike the last words in the section reading. as follows:
"nor sha ll any such liquors be used or served at any Ma·s onic
banquet or gathering."
We move adoption of the resolution but urge a no vote.
A majority voted against the resolution.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

SPONSORSHIP OF DE MOLAY
(16)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolu tion No. 16 proposes an amendment to what is called Section
333-r of the California Code. Aside from the fact that there is no such
section, the letter "r" is merely a designation of an annotation under
Section 333, we call attention that it has been the established policy of
this body since the Communication in 1956 that Lodges may sponsor
chapters of the Order of De Molay. but may not expend Lodge fund s to
that end. It, therefore. appears to your Committee on Policy and General
Purposes that the adoption of Resolµt ion No. 16 is not necessary in order
to authorize sponsorship of De Molay Chapters by our Lodges and we
shall discuss the resolution only as to permitting expenditure o f Lodge
funds.
We are satisfied the need of the Order of De Molay in California
is that Freemasons give of themselves to support that Order rather than
that they make the somewhat impersonal gift of funds from Lodges. The
Order of De Molay needs and deserves the time and energies of additional qualified members of our fraternity who will serve as chapter
advisers and assist in the formulation of programs and activities. This
is a gift of greater value than the appropriation o f Lodge funds.
W e further believe that the opportunities of participation in activities
and the use of paraphernalia of the Order of De Molay will be far more
appreciated by its members if they themselves earn the cost thereof.
We . therefore, move the adoption of Resolution No. 16 and recommend a no vote with the understanding that the Grand Lodge thereby
will not alter the present policy of permitting sponsorship.
The Committee on furisprudence:
Your Committee reports on Resolution No. 16 by H . E. Darling
et al as follows:
This resolution seeks to legislate upon or amend a decision of a
Grand Master. This is improper. A decision may be repealed but not
amended. Legislation is an Ordinance and should become a part of CMC
bearing a section number. Decisions and edicts are listed by letters under
section numbers.
Under Sec. 333-f. sponsorship of De Molay by a Lodge is forbidden.
The language following the word "NOTE:" is mere policy and comment by the Code Commission and is not law.
Therefore. in order to accomplish the intent of the resolution we
shall present two resolutions as follows:
I. RESOLVED :
That Sec. 333-f of CMC be repealed.
Comment: If this resolution is adopted nothing in our law will
prohibit sponsorship of the Order of De Molay but expenditure
of funds by Lodges in such sponsorship will remain prohibited.
We move adoption of the resolution and urge a yes vote.

2. RESOLVED:
That a new section be added to CMC reuding as follows:
Sec. 331.1. Sponsorship of De Molay.
A Lodge by resolution may sponsor a Chapter or Chapters of
the Order of De Molay and may expend its funds in nominal
amounts to provide equipment, supplies and furnishings for such
sponsored Chapter or Chapters, all subject to approval of the
Grand Master.
We move adoption but urge a no vote.
Resolution l~Ad opted 5/ 6 vote.
Resolution 2-A majority voted against.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
In accordance with the provision of Ordinances, an audit of all

which ended June 30, 1962. These have been examined by this Committee and discussed with Brother Jam es E. Hammond, a general

financial position of Grand Lodge. A copy of the audit will be printed
in the annual Proceedings.

and appropriations of $372,965. 76, leaving net revenue of $16, 760.35.

of all Committees and Boards, and the Grand Secretary, for their
diligence in staying within the budget.

CALIFORNIA FREEMASON

The audit for the last fiscal year shows that cash disbursements
from publication of our official magazine, California Freemason, were
in excess of cash receipts in the amount of $1, 125.33.
We recommend that Grand Lodge approve the appropriation of
$1,125.33 to cover this deficiency.
It is estimated that approximately 311,000 individual copies of future
issues of the magazine were subscribed and paid for at June 30, 1962.
At 20 cents per copy this amounts to $62,200.00 and represents a
liability of Grand Lodge. Against this we have $35,168.22 in the reserve.
If future publication of the magazine does not show an excess of cash
receipts over expenditures, we feel that Grand Lodge should give consideration to increasing the reserve by an appropriation from general
funds.

funding the total of past service credits for all employees of Grand
Lodge and its agencies was partially responsible for the anticipated
and realized decrease in cost of some $9,200.00 from the previous
year.
For the current fiscal year we are budgeting a total of $16,900.00
to cover current service credits on all employees under the Retirement
Plan.
NEW GRAND LODGE REGALIA

There has been referred to thi-s Committee that portion of the
Grand Master's Message in which he recommends the purchase of
new regalia and equipment for Grand Lodge Officers.
We have discussed this matter with the Grand Master and are
inclined to agree with his reasons for making the recommendation. We
have been furnished with an estimate of $2, 700.00 as the cost of this
new set and have included it in the budget. We recommend approval.

MASONIC HOMES

We have examined the audit of the accounts of the Masonic Homes
of California and have reviewed the report of the Trustees. After a
discussion of the affairs of the Homes with the Trustees, your Committee is of the opinion that a renewal of the per capita of $1.00
will be sufficient to support their operating budget for the current fiscal
year.
We, therefore, offer the following resolution:
RESOLVED, that the sum of $1.00 per capita be levied for
the fiscal year ending June 30, 1963, the proceeds to be paid to
the Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California.

GRAND LECTURER'S REPORT

There has been referred to this Committee the report of the Grand
Lecturer in which he recommends the printing of Candidate and Candidate Coach Handbooks. With the approval of the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes, to which the matter has been referred, we
recommend the appropriation of $6,950.00 which is estimated to be
the cost of this program.
It is your Committee's understanding that these Handbooks are
to be distributed to the constituent Lodges at a price which should at
least return to Grand Lodge the cost of printing.

INSTAL LATION SERVIC E

(9)
proYour Comm ittee on Ritual has consid ered Resolu tion No. 9
Flag
a
for
provide
to
Service
tion
Installa
the
posing an amend ment to
presen tation at public installa tions by an Honor ary Marsh al.
disSince 1927 our law has require d that the Flag of our Countr y be

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

played at all meetings of our Lodges. and at the annual election of
officers and at such other meetings as may be deemed desirable by the
Master, the Flag must be formally presented at the Altar by the Marshal
and received in the manner prescribed by the Grand Lecturer. ( 1927:
473)
In order to open the Lodge for the ceremony of installation . the
Flag must be displayed in its proper place in the East. or it must be
presented at the Altar by the Marshal and the Deacons in accordance
with the Flag ceremony adopted by Grand Lodge.
The Flag is required to be displayed at all times while the Lodge is
open, whether at work or at refreshment. There is no logic whatever in
permitting the Flag to be informally taken out of the Lodge in order to
have it again presented by an Honorary Marshal while the Lodge is at
refreshment for purposes of installation. The proposed resolution does
not provide just how the Flag is to be taken out of the Lodge room. nor
by whom.
Our present Installation Service provides all due respect and honor
to the Flag, by requiring the pledge of allegia nce to be given at the very
commencemen t of the installation ceremony. whether it be a public or
private ceremony. We do not think the Flag should become mere paraphernalia to be carried in and out of the Lodge room. It is the pledge of
allegiance to the Flag which is important, not the act of someone carrying it about the Lodge room.
We recommend that the resolution be not adopted.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes indicated their concurrence in the recommendatio n.
A majority voted against the resolution .

CHARLES ALBERT ADAMS
By Myron E. Smith
"Let you r light so s hine before men .
that they may see your good works.
and glorify your Fa th er which is in
- M atthew 5 : 16
hea,·en. "
This beautiful pa ssage. found recorded in the fifth chapter. the
sixteenth verse, of the Book of M att hew. symbolizes for us the guiding
principle in the life of the Hreat and good man, whose memory we here
honor. Truly. the brilliant light held aloft for us by Charles Albert
Adams has lighted the pathway of our lives- just as his memory will
ever be a guiding star for our children and our children's children. And
through his good works . our Fa ther who is in heaven has indeed been
glorified. If. as we are taught, man is a ray of the divine intellect. surely
this man has been many rays of the divine intelligence.
Light comes from God . The wise ma n knows it is God who makes
light in our lives. Charles Albert Adams understood this. along wi th
George Matheson , the blind poet, who wrote.
" O . light that followest all my ways
1 y ield my flickering torch to thee .
My heart restores its borrowed ray
That in thy sunshine's blaze. its day
May brighter, fairer be."
John Wesley said that every ma n should be possessed of the lighted
mind, the warm heart and the helping hand. Charles Albert Adams was
such a man. By his lighted mind. he lifted us up to a new sphere of
intellectual and spiritual independ ence. His warm heart taught us the
real meaning of true friendship. His helping hand demon strated for
us how every ma n should pour forth comfort and consolation into the
hearts of the distressed. the afflicted and the destitute.
So it is that we hono r a radia nt and victorious personality. What a
glorious life his has been! H ow inspiring is his biography! Carlyle said:
" Biography is the only true history. " Emerson said: "There is properly
no history- only biography." In a very real sense , the biog raph y of
C harles Albert Adams is mu ch of the his tory of this grea t city . sta te
and nation . the public schools a nd Masonry.
Our beloved brother, who has meant so much to us . was born o f
pioneer parents, Amos and Regina Adams, in the California "Mother
Lode" town of Mokelumne Hill . in Calaveras County, on November
25, 1867- more than 94 yea rs ago.
His father was the judge of the old Eleventh Judicial District, comprised of Amador, Calaveras and El Dorado Counties. In 1875 the

304

GRAND LODGE OF CALI FORNIA

family moved to San Francisco. where he e\'er after resided, except for
a short time in Oakla nd.
H e received his education in the public sc hools of San F rancisco
and Oakland, and in 1887 was graduated from the University of California's Hc:stings College of Law and admitted to the practice of law.
The devoted protagonist of public education. he was for several years
chairman of the sec ti o n of education in the Commonwealth Club . an d
for many years a me mber of th e executive comm ittee of the Public Education Society of San Francisco. He was a former member of the State
Board of Education <111d. as chairman of its text- book commi ttee took
a promin ent part in the controvery and subsequent litigation with reference to the adoption of text-books and which ultimately resulted in a
decision by the Supreme Court. whic h confirmed and definitely established the right of the State Board to adopt such text-books as '~:ere
believed by its members to be bes t- even though they were not, and
could not be printed by the State Printer.
A member of the Order of Coif. he was at the time of his death
the oldest practicing a ttorney in the City and County of San Francisco.
and one of the oldest active attorneys in th e United States. honored
and respected as one of the great leaders in his profession in his na ti\'e
California.
His Masonic caree r has been an unusu ally long and active onein our Grand Lodge probably unique. because there has not been a
year since he entered Grand Lodge as Jun ior Warden o f Excelsio r
Lodge N o. 166. in 1907. that he has not been either a member of an
importa nt committee or board. or an officer of Grand Lodge .
A s a great M aso n. he will be especially remembered for two superb
achievements: The institution, while Grand Master, in 1920 of the
Annua l Public Schools Week in California ( significantly being observed throughout the State during the week of his death) and service
of more than four d ecades as a Trustee of M asonic H omes of California.
A teacher of teac hers, he recognized that the public school is the
people's school. a \'ital keystone in the structure and preservation of
our way of life- the g reat unifying force in America, a bright light in
a world shadowed by the dark clouds of wa r ;rnd the uncertainties of
an uneasy peace. Because of his influence, the citizenry of our state
will not countenance a ny jeopardy to our public schools.
It has been said th<:1t to truly live is to live in the lives of others.
"Charlie", as all of us affectionately knew him, was twelve years older
than the average age ( 82) of the residents of our Home for the Aged .
During his more than forty years on the Homes Board, .over •4,00~ app.licants received aid a nd assistance from the Board. guided by his wise
counsel and advice. Three generations older than the children in our
Home for Children. his interest in young people never diminis hed and
he has been the friend and counselor of hundreds of graduates who have

loved him dea rly. How glo riously our Brother truly lives in the lives of
others!
Charles Albert Adams knew that the glo1y of life on this earth is
achievemen t in growth of character an d in service to our fellow men.
He never ceased to grow and he never stopped serving his fellow man .
Youth. he understood so well, is not a time of life. It is a state of
mind . You th may be in a man of ninety- as it was in "Charlie"- mo re
than in a boy of nineteen. Men do not grow old from years bu t by desertion of their ideals. Charles Albert Adams never deserted his ideals.
He had an unmatched sense of moral courage.
A kindly. gracious gen tleman. he loved his home. H is love and
devotion to his wife, who predeceased him. were tender and beautiful
beyond words to express. To his son a nd daugh ter a nd grandchildren .
whom he dearly loved, we extend our warmest and deepest sympathy.
It was Plato who said : "Those having torches will pass them on to
others." F or the Greek runner o f old. to cross the finis h line was not
enough. He was the winner who first reached the goal with the torch
in his hand s till lighted. In the long wa r between the good and the evil ,
between light and darkness. between knowledge a nd ignora nce, Charles
Albert Adams has fought the good fight and won- with the torch of
his faith still s hining brig htly. He has passed it on to us. A s with one
illustrio us in Masonry long ago, no one man can ever replace him or the
lig ht he bore. It will require all the light of many men to approach tha t
of this great servant of God and man.
In the search for truth, Charles A lbert Adams never ceased climbing
up the mountai~side toward that light which radiates from H im w hose
holy name ligh ts our Lodge. We shall th ink of him as ever climbing.
ever advancing in wisdo m, streng th and beauty of character, in the
Great Grand Lodge on High where, as St. John. the Patron Saint of
l'vtasonry,recorded:

CHARLES M. WOLLENBERG
By Alfred F. Breslauer
We meet this afternoon, in accordance with Masonic custom, to offer
up to the memory of Charles M. Wollenberg, a tribute of our love and
affection. The beautiful ritual of the service carries a message that is
warming and complete. Yet. in addition, let us remember together some
of the actual incidents of his life which have in turn enriched the lives
of all who w ere privileged to know him.
Some of us assembled here are attired in the habilaments of a Mason.
However, his activities and influence were not circumscribed by any
one affiliation, and all men. regardless of sect or creed, w ere the recipients of his goodness and understanding.
The records tell us that Charles Wollenberg was born in Castroville, Monterey County, California, on March 13. 1873. almost 90 years
ago, the son of pioneers who had come to California in 1858; that when
he was tw o years old, the Wollenberg family moved to Prescott. Arizona.
where he attended grammar and high school. In 1891 the family returned
to California. whereupon young Charles attended the University of
California, graduated in 1894 with a degree in pharmacy. and obtained
his certificate which he proudly held until the day of his passing.
But the statistics cannot tell us of the early influence of Masonic
teachings in his life. through his father, Louis Wollenberg. who was a
member of Confidence Lodge No. 203 in Castroville and had served v.s
Secretary of the' Lodge; or of how many years later, after Charles became Grand Master. ''Wollenberg Night" was a frequent event in
Confidence Lodge. attended by many members of the Wollenberg family
a nd their ho st o f fri end s in that a r ea .
The sta tistics say th at Charles lived in Prescott, Arizona , from the
age of 2 until 18, but we mu st dra w upon o ur o w n pow ers o f insight to
compr ehend th e influ en ce w hi ch th is immedia te a n d persona l conta ct
with the p io neer West h ad in moulding his life o f limitless energy an d
courageous purpose-indeed, what it mean t to this boy to live a t a n
isola ted military o utpost , o ver 100 miles from a railroad , in th e he a rt o f
the Indian country, w h e re h e actu ally lived through the experi ences
a bo u t w hi ch the youth of toda y can only read . His stories of this per iod
of his life were legion. a nd h e was never happier than whe n r elating
some expe rience with the India ns or another episode in the life o f the
expand ing Wes tern Frontie r.
After he became a prac ticin g pha rmacist in S a n Fra ncisco. h e married Romild a J udell in 1899. and their happy life of more th a n sixty
y ear s tog ether was insp iring to all w h o knew t h em . The combined W o llenbe rg-Judell family wer e a la rge. d evoted g roup. w ho looked u p on hi m
as "Pa pa Char lie" a n d upon Mrs. Wollenber g as ''Mother Roe."

311

PROC EEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALI FORNIA

Even had he not been called into public service. but remained the
quietly practicing pharmacist, his was a dist inct and impelling personality which would have asse rted itsel f whatever course his activities
might have taken .
He was so strong ly motivated by his own deep-felt convictions of
what was right and what \\'aS wrong in the realm of human rela tions,
and so courageously asserted these pri nciples which he believed to be
just. that as the years went by more than a few people in high places
became familiar with his dau ntless spirit and firmness .
H e had a profound insight into human nature. He was a great and
sympathetic soul, and as we say in our installation service, he was truly
one "to whom the burdened heart could pour out its sorrow, on e to whom
distress could pre fer its suit. one whose hand was guided by jus tice and
whose heart was expanded by benevolence."
That he was literally catapulted into a life of public service to help
and comfort the dis tressed. is a matter of record in the annals of San
Francisco history. One day, A pril 17, 1906, he was peacefull y carr ying
on his professio n as a pharmacist on Sutter S treet. On the follow ing
day the earthquake struck this area. followed by disastrous fire. Twentyfour hours later, General Funston swore in Charles Wollenberg as
chief civilian aide to the S urgeon General of the United States Army
of San Francisco Earthquake Relief. Then followed more than forty
years of outstanding service in relief and welfare activities: first. two
years with the Red Cross. then from I 908 to 1943 he was su perintendent of the Laguna Honda H ome. and concurrently with this post held
that of D irector of Institutions for the City and County of San Francisco. One cannot begin to estimate the countless number of persons
receiving assistance and comfort during the span of years when these
institutions were under his direction. A man of more average energies
and enthusiasm might have been satisfied to expend such energies and
enthusiasm on one job. But one job at a time was never the pattern of
Charles Wollenberg's activities. either before or after his so-called
" retirement" in 1943. In fact, he had ha rd ly become aware that he had
reti red, when Earl Warren. then the newly-e lected Governor. appointed
him State Director o f Public Welfare. a post whic h he held for five years.
Du ring a ll the years, no one who ever sought his guidance . counsel
or assistance was turned away if it was within hi s power to help. If
anyone could be called a "humanitarian," surely it was Cha rles Wollenberg. in every sense. For one example we see his intense interest in the
Masonic Home for the Aged at Decoto. Charles Wollenberg was an
active member o f the Board of Trustees for more than fo r ty years. served
as President of the Board . a nd continued on as T rustee Eme ritus until
his death. During the Annua l Communication of Grand Lodge. held
only two weeks ago, the hospital a t the H ome was re-dedicated. and it
w ill be known as the C harles Wollenber g Memorial Hospital.

Charles Wollenberg loved and understood young people too. The
Masonic H omes of California. of which the H ome a t Decoto is a part,
also includes the H ome for Children at Covina , Ca lifornia. He was
proud o f the Covina Home a nd the children there were his particular
interest. During the many years of his active guidance. he made it a
point to know personally every boy and girl residing there. Many were
the hours he spent in helping these young people plan and prepare for
their futu re. He gave much of his time and effort in helping them choose
a career. and he found his reward in the joy that he felt when in later
yea rs they came to see him. successfu l business or professional men and
women. or happy housewives and mothers as the case might be. T hese
young people will be a living memorial to his accomplishments in the
field of yout h gu idance .
His contacts with the civic life of the community and this state are
hund red-fold. His years in retirement were not only marked by holding
the distinguished post of State Director of Public W elfare, but also
by his activities as executive director of the He brew Nursing H ome. a
director of Mt . Zion H ospital. one of the founde rs of Maimonides Health
Center , a governor of the Commonwealth Club . and numerous other
orga nizations.
His love for his fellow-man was clear in his response to the idea ls of
fraterna l service. The earthquake o f April. 1906. not only had its significance in setting him forth on a lifetime of public service. but gives us
an interesting anecdote in connection with his Masonic career. H e joined
Starr King Lodge No. 344, on March 14. 1906, and received his Second
Degree on Aprif 11th. He was scheduled to receive his Third Degree
on the evening of A pril 18th. That nigh t. he a rrived a t the Lodge , after
walking a great distance, only to find that the rear wall of the hall was
down and the roof gone! He finally received his Third Degree when
the building was restored on May 30. 1906. His great interest in Starr
King Lodge resulted in his appointment to the line of officers, and in
1913 he was elected as Master o f the Lodge. Thereafter he became
interested in Grand Lodge activities, being appointed to the Board of
T rustees of The Masonic Homes in 19 17. He was elected as Junior
Grand Warden in due course . and served a s Grand Master of Masons
in California in 1929. His year will long be remembered as one in which
he traveled throughout the entire state, visiting many small Lodges in
the mountains and Mother Lode Country-Lodges which had not had
a visit from a Grand Master for many years. His friendliness and gen uine interest in Masonry endeared him to the many thousands of Masons
who had the opportunity to meet h im persona lly on his travels.
He gained grea t pleasure when he pa rticipated in the Degree work
at the time his sons, Albert, H arold an d Ralp h. were made Master
Masons. He had particular gratification when he was also privileged

310

312

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

to participate in the ceremonies in which his grandsons, Albert Wollenberg, Jr. and Harold Wollenberg, Jr., received their Third Degrees.
He was active in the Scottish Rite, serving as Venerable Master of
the San Francisco Lodge of Perfection and Master of the Consistory,
and in 1925 was coroneted with the 33rd Degree.
His was truly a distinguished Masonic career, and one in which he
put into actual practice the beautiful lessons and high principles of the
Order.
Yes-Charles Wollenberg has a host of witnesses to the fact that he
was a very special man. He gave of himself. all of his life, those qualities
of mind and heart that make life for those who knew him more significant-more worthwhile.
Concerning our personal friendship. I will not elaborate. To me the
strong affection, the high regard, the invaluable assistance, the spiritual
inspiration are sacred things, not to be talked of but rather as the years
go on to recall to the mind's eye, to sense again and to say to myselfmy life has been better and richer for the privilege of knowing him.

fund balances of MASONIC HOMES OF CALIFORNIA, a California nonprofit corporation, as of June 30, 1962, and the related statement
of revenue rece ived and expense disbursed for the year then ended.
Our examination was made in accordance with qenerally accepted
auditinq standards, and accordinqly included such tests of the
accountinq records and such other auditinq procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstancea.
In our opinion, the accompanyinq statements present
fairly the ·asset.s , reserves, and fund balances of Masonic HOlll8s
of California at June 30, 1962 arising primarily from cash
tranaactions, and the revenue received and expense disbursed by
it and the chanqes in reserves and in f und balances dur ing the
year then ended, . on a basis consistent with that of the preceding
year.
